I accepted a new job with a 401k that the match didn't kick in until after the first year and by implication, you couldn't contribute until after 1st year. During the onboarding process I asked the HR person if I could contribute to the 401k (to get the pretax benefits) without a match for the first year. He said that he had never had that question before but would go up the chain. End result was that I was allowed to contribute without a match for the first year. This was not a small company. Ask your new company, HR may have interpreted the no match to be no contribution.

topic_title: New job doesn't have 401K for first year - options?
content: Is it possible that you can contribute in the first year but the employer match is zero or is not vested in the first year? Seems odd to only offer 401k to employees who have been there longer than a year. If so, might indicate there is high turnover.

topic_title: New job doesn't have 401K for first year - options?
content: If you were planning to make a pre-tax contribution to Traditional 401(k), and you want to have a pre-tax contribution now, and neither you nor your spouse was covered by an employer retirement plan, you can contribute to Traditional IRA, and deduct the contribution no matter how high your income is. Of course, you can only contribute $6000 and it would mean that you won't be able to contribute $6000 to Roth IRA anymore. But if you were planning to make a $19500 pre-tax contribution to Traditional 401(k) and a $6000 contribution to Roth IRA, that means most of your contributions were planned to be allocated to pre-tax, so that now that you are limited to only IRA contributions, making most or all of it as deductible Traditional IRA contributions is a roughly equivalent allocation.

topic_title: IRS PUB 926: Paying the employee's share of social security and medicare
content:
I have an arrangement with my child's nanny that we will pay her share of the social security and medicare taxes. This is allowable according to the IRS and falls under the section "not withholding the employee's share" (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p926#e ... k100086743). They have a very clear example of this:
In 2022, you hire a household employee (who is an unrelated individual over age 18) to care for your child and agree to pay cash wages of $100 every Friday. You expect to pay your employee $2,400 or more for the year. You decide to pay your employee's share of social security and Medicare taxes from your own funds. You pay your employee $100 every Friday without withholding any social security or Medicare taxes.

For social security and Medicare tax purposes, your employee's wages each payday are $100. For each wage payment, you will pay $15.30 when you pay the taxes. This is $7.65 ($6.20 for social security tax plus $1.45 for Medicare tax) to cover your employee's share plus $7.65 ($6.20 for social security tax plus $1.45 for Medicare tax) for your share. For income tax purposes, your employee's wages each payday are $107.65 ($100 + the $7.65 you will pay to cover your employee's share of social security and Medicare taxes).
The crazy thing about this is that the math doesn't work the other way. Let's say that I have a formal agreement to pay the nanny $107.65 each week and that I will be withholding social security and medicare from her wages. If I do this, then I would be withholding $107.65 * 0.0765 or $8.24 in taxes! I'm a bit confused. This only just became a problem since my nanny needs a paystub as proof of income for a lease application, and I cannot make the numbers work. If I want to make sure that my nanny can pocket $100 in take-home pay, then the gross pay should actually be $100/(1-0.0765) or $108.28.

I'd prefer to stick with the IRS guidance since that's what the nanny and I agreed would apply (plus, it also results in slightly lower taxable income for her). It just seems like contradictory guidance from the IRS when you compare the "withholding the employee's share" vs "not withholding the employee's share" sections. Am I reading this correctly?

topic_title: IRS PUB 926: Paying the employee's share of social security and medicare
content:
In the paragraph right above what you quoted, it says:
Not withholding the employee's share. If you prefer to pay your employee's social security and Medicare taxes from your own funds, don't withhold them from your employee's wages. The social security and Medicare taxes you pay to cover your employee's share must be included in the employee's wages for income tax purposes. However, they aren't counted as social security and Medicare wages or as FUTA wages.
In other words, if the employEE pays those taxes, they will have to pay SS and Medicare taxes on these taxes. But if the employER pays them, neither the employer or employee would pay the SS and Medicare taxes on these taxes. (The employee would also have to pay income taxes on their wages and the SS taxes and the Medicare taxes in either case.)


Give your nanny a pay of $107.65 for each $100 earned, unless s/he will earn over the maximum SS wages for the year.

I'm not sure on the math there. I think you're incorrect though.
Let's say someone has an S-corp and they take $100,000 wages with no K-1 income. How much net business earnings (revenue minus expenses) are needed for this salary? $7,650 employer payroll taxes are owed, so the answer is $107,650. (The employee payroll taxes are taken out of the wages, so don't matter.) What's the ratio of wages to net business income? $100,000 / $107,650 = 0.928936.... Not 0.9235 as Schedule SE says.

Now let's say this same person operates as a sole proprietor rather than being incorporated. They earn $107,650 net business profit. What are their effective wages? $107,650 x 0.9235 = $99,414.76, but for parity with a corporation it should be $100,000. This could be though of as a small advantage for sole proprietors, although it's probably too small to make a difference.

topic_title: How to be on the Board of a mutual fund or ETF?
content:
Every mutual fund I've looked at has essentially fund company insiders on the board. I believe they're required to have some board members that are independent, but it seems to me those "independent" members are only an arms reach disassociated from the fund company. Since the fund company and it's associated investment banks have to finance the start of the fund, and the companies financial interests are tied to controlling the financial aspects (fees) of the fund, the fund company will own and maintain controlling interest in who is on the board and whatever matters the fund might put to a vote. FWIW, I have a rather cynical view of mutual funds in general. Mutual funds are like taking all the expenses, principal/agent problems, and bureaucratic management waste of a business, and then adding another layer of that on top of owning the actual underlying business.
I make an exception for low-cost broad-market index funds as being different from traditional mutual funds because they compete on how well (and low-cost) they track an index from a third-party index provider, and at least the relative returns from that are transparent even if most of the other parts of the inner workings of the fund are not.

So if you want to be on a board, make friends with people that work for or are on the board of a fund / fund company.

topic_title: Eligible Designated Beneficiary and inherited ira and 401K
content:
Question about Eligible Designated Beneficiary and inherited ira and 401K

1. A person inherits a IRA or 401K as a named beneficiary.
2. The beneficiary is not a spouse
3. The beneficiary is older than the deceased.
4. The beneficiary is under 59-1/2 years.
5. The deceased died before their RMD date.

Does the person fit the criteria for Eligible Designated Beneficiary then since the requirement is that "A non-spouse less than 10 years younger". Does this mean the beneficary can take RMD over their life expectancy?

When does the clock start for the RMD? For example if the person died last year but the IRA and 401K is not transferrred until next year.

Thanks.

topic_title: Eligible Designated Beneficiary and inherited ira and 401K
content:
I am not an accountant, tax attorney, or other expert.

From https://www.investopedia.com/eligible-d ... on-5025191:

There are five categories of individuals included in the EDB classification:

1.The owner’s surviving spouse
2.The owner’s child who is less than 18 years of age
3.A disabled individual
4.A chronically ill individual
5,Any other individual who is not more than 10 years younger than the deceased IRA owner

Based upon my layperson's reading of this, if the beneficiary is older than the deceased, they would clearly meet criteria #5.

Regarding when they need to start, this article (https://www.kitces.com/blog/successor-b ... eneficary/) says:

This ‘Stretch’ provision allowed Designated Beneficiaries – and younger Designated Beneficiaries, in particular – to begin taking relatively small distributions, based on their life expectancy (as calculated using the IRS-provided Single Life Expectancy Table), from inherited retirement accounts beginning in the year after the owner’s death

Just a warning... This paragraph was in reference to the lifetime stretch prior to the SECURE act. However, if you are a EDB post-secure act, you are still able to get the lifetime stretch, so my layperson assumption is that the same rules would apply. Of course, you should confirm this with an actual expert.

topic_title: Eligible Designated Beneficiary and inherited ira and 401K
content:
Yes, the person is an EDB and can stretch beneficiary RMDs just as before the Secure Act. There is also an option to opt out of EDB status and into the 10 year rule, but that would only be beneficial in very unique circumstances.

Since death was prior to RBD, the remaining LE of the younger decedent cannot be used by the beneficiary.

I retired back in 2008 at age 45. In the years leading up to my ER, I split my overall ER plan into 2 parts. The first part (the tougher one) was getting from age 45 to around age 60, using only my non-retirement assets. After that, I would begin being able to access what I call my "reinforcements" consisting of unfettered access to my tIRA, my frozen company pension, and Social Security. I wasn't really worried about having enough money readily available starting at age 60 because I knew my financial picture would be much, much better.

I am less than a year from age 60 and these last 13.5 years have gone very well, better than I had projected. I thought I would have to dip into principal these last few years, but that hasn't happened. My taxable portfolio has been able to generate enough income to pay my bills.

My suggestion to you, OP, is to do a similar split in the timeline and make sure you can get by easily enough using only the subset of your portfolio you have unfettered access to.

Your planned spending is only 2.6% of your portfolio, which is below the historic perpetual withdrawal rate of about 3%.
While I agree that the OP is almost certainly fine, I think this kind of calculation can be slightly deceiving when talking about early FIRE people like the OP with their portfolio split between taxable and tax-deferred. Not deceiving "wrong" but more like "needs a quick closer investigation to check to be sure".

For people that far from "normal retirement age" (i.e. triggers for 401k withdrawals and Social Security), people are often better off thinking of "before 60" and "after 60" as two different sanity checks that need to be done.

The OP has $2.8 million in taxable. That's a 3.8% withdrawal rate for ages 41 to 60; i.e. a 20-year period. Off the top of my head I don't remember the SWR for a 20-year horizon. Probably around 5% or something like that? So still okay.

And if "tax-deferred" means something like a Roth where they can pull stuff penalty-free in some way then it adds even more flexibility.

I do have a slight concern about their not owning property, unless the OP is willing to move to a completely new area at some point. "Property is too expensive to buy here" almost exactly means "national CPI calculations are wrong for my situation because local housing inflation is way higher than the national average". So their own personal inflation rate could be substantially higher than the numbers you get from firecalc stuff.

Given all that I'd still say "you're fine; but you might have to move in 20 years in a worst case kind of scenario". I personally would be willing to take that risk in order to not work another 5 or 10 years.

Based on the limited info you gave us, you can retire now in my opinion.

You live in a tier 3 state and not near a major metropolis, so cost of living must be great.

You have no wife who wants to keep up with the joneses.

I added that in red, not because you’re wrong, but because others never realized that there’s a thing such as capital W work… Work with meaning. Their loss, on a continuing basis unfortunately.
Not everybody's right work is paid, or paid well enough to support their desired lifestyle. FIRE might let them explore that without an actual career or paycheck. And work certainly isn't the only way to find meaning.
No work, no wife, no kids, and 40+ more years to live. When everyone else your age is busy with their families, it might get a little depressing.
Totally disagree. I am never married with no kids, as I am not interested in either. While I liked my job for much of the 23 years I worked, it was very easy to put it behind me when I left. I hated the commute, even when I had reduced it 1-3 days per week the last 7 years I worked. Ridding myself of that was the biggest improvement to my everyday life.

The combination of economic freedom and personal freedom is unbeatable.
Personal freedom to do what? Economic freedom to do what?

“Whatever I want” is a child’s answer. The real effort is in answering that question, and then with courage often realizing that there is no reason one has to put it off until after becoming fabulously wealthy doing something else.

I’m not digging at you and your choices at all; I’m digging at the argument which too often reflects the majority of FIRE folks. FI, yes. RE means you haven’t answered the hard questions yet. Of course, most never do.
For me, Economic Freedom was the ability to have money magically appear in my local bank's checking account (like a paycheck) without having to do anything at all to make that happen. That money was enough to pay the bills with a little bit left over (and that didn't include any money already accessible in my portfolio). Simply eliminating all the downside of having to make that money appear (i.e. work, including the commute I so much despised) was a huge positive.

Personal Freedom was something I already had. That came from choices I had made years earlier, mainly to remain unmarried (although I have a ladyfriend) and childfree. When I first switched from working full-time to part-time 7 years before I fully retired, I was able to regain some personal freedom by doing some things I hadn't had the time or energy to do for many years. Fully retiring allowed me to partake in those activities more easily, without the frequent scheduling conflicts between them and my limited work schedule. Personal freedom also meant I had nobody depending on me all the time, nor did I have to depend on anyone else all the time.

So, putting these two freedoms together allowed me to enjoy the daily lifestyle I wanted to have without having to work any more for the money to maintain it. "Whatever I want" may seem like a child's answer, but it is a fully adult one because I earned it with my years of working and the choices I made along the way.

topic_title: Understanding PBGC (Pension Benefits Guarantee Corp) Protection
content:
Getting close to making the pension annuity v. lump some option decision, and trying to understand the PBGC insurance protection better. If my pension annuity will be essentially risk free, that is my preferred option. Reading the tables on the website, the maximum insured insured limits are based on your age when the Company declares bankruptcy. So first question is, can a company only default on pension payments by declaring bankruptcy? Can they default without declaring bankruptcy?

Assuming I have already started collecting a monthly pension, can My Company sell that pension obligation, to a different company, that is not covered by the PBGC?

If my monthly pension is at (or above) that maximum limit, is it certain I can collect the limit?

If the limit is above my monthly pension, is it certain that (if default) I can collect my full pension from PBGC? Can PBGC itself go bankrupt? or change the rules / limits?

topic_title: Understanding PBGC (Pension Benefits Guarantee Corp) Protection
content:
I had similar questions over a decade ago when I retired from a company. It seems it was easier then to find answers to these sorts of questions than it is now.

The current PBGC website answers the question about the pension-providing company transferring the responsibility to an insurance company. This can be done, but there is heavy supervision to ensure that the funds transferred are suffixient to pay the pension obligations. Once that transfer takes place, the PBGC is no longer involved. At that time (accd'g to the PBGC site) there may be state-level guarantees of payment.

Regarding reduction of benefits, I retired with fewer than 30 years at my company and below age 60. I forget the parameters, but given my age and actual years of service at that company, my pension would be reduced if the PBGC were to take over. I could not find this information on the current website, but I'd guess there are similar concerns today with number of years in the company and age at retirement, with reduction by PBGC if they take over and you fall below those parameters.

I hope others with expertise will chime in here. I saw this question was going unanswered and hope that this response will activate the topic and spur more responses.

Although not asked, I'd like to chime in with some thoughts about your upcoming decision. A pension as part of a diversified retirement portfolio is a wonderful thing. Certainly, the questions you are asking are important, and to the extent that the answers are not satisfying, that detracts from the appeal of choosig the pension over the lump sum.

In case it may help, I'll mention some things that may not jump out when evaluating the pension decision:

- In my case, we have 2 Social Security and 1 pension as sources of monthly income in retirement. The pension is not inflation adjusted, which I initially considered to be a major factor. We've found that the Social Security COLAs work well to over time mitigate this in our circumstances and I no longer think much about inflation relative to the fixed pension income. Instead I think of our monthly totality which is now getting close to two-thirds inflation protected. However, when one spouse passes away, one Social Security payment will cease, and taxes will increase, so that's an inevitable future inflation-protection and tax hit tht will have to be absorbed.

- The pension really provides huge peace of mind in down markets. You feel much more in control of your circumstances because of the monthly income. It's hard for me to overstate the emotional calm it provides and the resultant comfort that mitigates against panicked selling and worry.

- While there's no guarantee of this, the same factors that would cause your company's pension plan to go bust would likely (but not certainly) be causing the economy as a whole to swoon, so that the money from a lump sum invested would probably also suffer at that time.

- For sure, our cicumstances and our pension providers are probably different, and the sequence of returns we experience will probably be different, so keep researching the answers to your questions and thinking about your personal circumstances. For me the pension was the right decision, but that does not mean the same will be true for you.

Best wishes!

topic_title: Understanding PBGC (Pension Benefits Guarantee Corp) Protection
content:
Retired mid fifties in 2008 with two pensions from a company (worked for two different subgroups) that I viewed as very poorly run but had a major stream that I projected would last until 2013 keeping the company viable and hopefully the pensions until such date. I don't think the PBGC rules have changed much but the age reductions can be severe if the company fails before you reach 65. It appeared that PBGC would consider my two pensions as one if the company went bankrupt. For me, I had options to 'Levelize' each pension. This basically front loaded the pensions in early years until age 62 at which time they would reduce to a little more than half of what I got in the early years. I chose this option since I expected a company bankruptcy and if it came about I would only have a couple of years with substantial potential reductions, and only a modest reduction from what I would have gotten at age 62. Taking the normal pensions (which would have been roughly midpoint between my pre and post age 62 levelized pensions) would have put me at risk for losing some given PBGC rules for bankruptcy until I was roughly age 70.

As it turned out the company lasted a year more than my projection. To my surprise, the post bankruptcy company continued paying the original pensions and providing cadillac health care insurance. I guess there were enough corrupt individuals at the top that were not fully vested and now eligible for full pension cashouts (were not available to me) that they did not worry about shareholders (reorganized company has recently recovered dramatically to perhaps one-third of the post bankruptcy stock valuation). Once I was 64 I was fully PBGC covered. The company did reduced the post 65 health coverage from cadillac level to a $1400 annual pot. Having the big pension early I was able to not need my IRAs/401k in the 2008-2009 market meltdown. I wish I could say I did not mess with them at all other than doing some nice Roth conversions in the down market.

PBGC rules can be changed. Lots of talk about that in the past, but little has been done.

Go in person. One, it’s a good experience. Two, at many closings you need to present ID. Third, you need to transport the check yourself. Fourth, if something comes up you want to be present. Why do you need to be at the closing to sign the documents?

I've closed on several properties:
1.) the documents were FedEx'd to me - I had to sign them in front of a Notary of the Public (I did this at my local Bank - after making an appt to do so)
2.) I arranged to meet with a representative of the local Title Company - I could have had them come to my office (or home) but I opted to go their office (it was near by). They printed out all the documents and I signed them and the Title Company Representative "notarized" them.


What is the cost of having your lawyer be the POA verses the cost of you receiving the documents and signing them and returning them? What is most convenient for you?

If you have difficulties writing - then I can see where having someone else sign for you would be advantageous. If you can sign your name a 50 times in row - you can do the paper work yourself.

oh!!! ONE WORD OF CAUTION!! Before signing - see how they have your name displayed on the forms. You want to sign your name using that format.
At one of the closings were I was present - it was me, my lawyer, the sellers lawyer and the Title Company people...
The documents I was signing had my name as: First Name Middle Initial LastName I NEVER sign my name with my Middle Initial. The Title Company person almost had a heart attack when they realized my official signature didn't match the pre-typed up documents. The closing process STOPPED COLD. The lawyers "woke up" and they and Title Company person did some voodoo to create a new form with a list of my "alias" that became part of the closing documents - and so I continued signing my name FirstName LastName.

At the Closing where I was doing it remotely (and on all electronically signed documents) if I see they want my middle initial in my signature - I just make due and add it. I really need to create a swoopy liney Squiggle handwritten signature for myself - and then no one will know if the middle initial is in there or not....

topic_title: How is this Legal? Father added my name to Credit Card
content:
It is possible that you were added as an "authorized user" of the card. Basically it gives you permission to use the credit card account of another person.

Here is a good article on authorized users from Experian: https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-expe ... ized-user/

Key points:
1. The primary cardholder (your father in this case, not you) is the one liable for any charges on the card.
2. You can benefit from the good credit earned from the account, even though you aren't liable for the charges yourself.
3. You may or may not be impacted negatively if the primary cardholder misses payments. The article seems a bit unclear on this point.

The impact of negative information depends on how the credit bureau views that history. Experian, for example, won't include the information on an authorized user's credit report if the primary account owner misses payments, but high credit utilization—like a maxed-out credit card—could wind up damaging the authorized user's credit.

It is not uncommon for parents to add a minor child as an authorized user. First, they can give the child the card to be used in case of emergency. Second, it allows them to build up a positive credit history from a young age (assuming that the parent pays bills on time, etc). I know when I was in high school, my parents added me as an authorized user for these reasons. Then when I was in college, I was able to get my own credit card based upon my history.

In terms of permission, the article says that the primary cardholder needs to grant permission. This makes sense since they are the one who is responsible for the charges. There is no mention of whether the authorized user has to give permission or not. In any case, if you were a minor at the time, probably no permission was needed. Honestly, I wouldn't lose sleep over this as it is your father who is taking the risk, not you.

Of course, all of the above assumes an authorized user situation (which is the most likely explanation). If not, then feel free to disregard

You need to watch for the fixed fee. While free balance transfers do exists they are not common. Usually there is something like a 1-3% fixed balance transfer fee before you get to the 0% APR. Looks like this offer is actually free though. Just something to watch for for other offers

The balance will go into the new CC. There will be a minimum monthly payment to satisfy, yes. This varies from lender to lender, but usually it's something like the greater of 1% of balance or $30.

Your credit will likely suffer a temporary hit, because the higher balance will mean higher utilization ratio. This is temporary because soon after you pay the balance down, the lower balance will report and bring your utilization back to normal along with your score.

There will so be temporary credit hits from the credit pull and new account, as usual.

If your new mortgage is already funded, this won't matter at all. If not already funded, usually there is a last minute credit check before funding. If there are new inquiries or credit cards on your report they will ask about it. It's not necessarily a dealbreaker but underwriting will ask for statements/reasons for them and re evaluate. It's not a huge deal as long as you are not borderline, but it is an extra hassle and an extra hurdle that can slow things down. That is why people usually recommend waiting for funding before getting new cards.

Personally if I'm going to open a new CC, I'd rather get one with a fat sign up bonus. That will likely outweigh the interest you can earn on the little bit of interest rate arbitrage you have here. If you are trying to leverage up debt to invest into stocks, that is quite risky with the short 12 ish month horizon.

Likely if you miss a payment you'll wind up paying the 13.99%. As pointed out above, a lot of offers charge a balance transfer fee of 2%-5% so it isn't really free money.

Is the old house for sale? I'd concentrate on selling that and not solar panels for the new house and not shifting debt around.

1. Not really. There is almost certainly a 3-5% fee to transfer up front.

2. Yes, it is the same minimum monthly payment as if you purchased items on the card. It's generally about 1%, but your specific card's terms apply.

3. Yes, there is a ding to your credit score. The impact of the ding depends on the resulting size of your available credit lines that you have taken. So, you will have a new inquiry, new account, more credit, but higher usage. It could be anywhere from a hit of 15 to 100 depending on your situation. Based on what you have said, I would imagine it would be closer to 15-20.

There may be an impact on your mortgage if you take out the credit card before closing. The bank may notice a significant change in your credit profile and ask questions. If you take the new card after closing on the new house, it would not affect the mortgage.

4. Not really. One thing to make sure you do is send transfer paperwork more than a day before the due date on your old card. It can take anywhere from 3-5 business days on the short end to a couple weeks for a transfer to process, so you can end up eating interest for a couple days on the old card if you're not careful. Some cards let you direct deposit the balance transfer so you can control the timing a bit better.

5. Yes. It is possible that worse credit would affect your future credit card applications. On the other hand, actually carrying a balance may attract more offers (even if it's a 0% rate balance).

topic_title: Depreciation recapture on sale of rental property
content:
Quick question:

We sold a rental property last year, and I am now trying to fill out the various 2021 tax forms, including form 4797.

I believe we did depreciate the rental properly on our 2020 taxes, and I know we will need to pay tax at our ordinary rate (22% for us) on the depreciation recapture.

I've managed to confuse myself, though, as to whether I need to include the 2021 portion of the depreciation in the amount that needs to be recaptured.

In other words: on our 2020 taxes there was about $12K of depreciation, and that obviously needs to be recaptured because we didn't pay any tax on that $12K.

But for the $8K of depreciation attributable to 2021, we haven't filed any returns including that $8K, so it seems like including that $8K in the total amount of depreciation to recapture might mean we are paying tax twice on that $8K.

On the other hand, if we DON'T include the $8K, then we would not be paying any tax on the $7K of rental income we got in 2021.

So I think I must need to include the $8K of 2021 depreciation in the amount that needs to be recaptured, but I am still not thinking clearly about this.

Also, let me add that form 4797 sucks.

Thanks all.

Thu Jun 23, 2022 10:11 am
We sold a rental property last year, and I am now trying to fill out the various 2021 tax forms, including form 4797.

I believe we did depreciate the rental properly on our 2020 taxes, and I know we will need to pay tax at our ordinary rate (22% for us) on the depreciation recapture.

I've managed to confuse myself, though, as to whether I need to include the 2021 portion of the depreciation in the amount that needs to be recaptured.

But for the $8K of depreciation attributable to 2021, we haven't filed any returns including that $8K, so it seems like including that $8K in the total amount of depreciation to recapture might mean we are paying tax twice on that $8K.
You would not be paying tax twice. When a rental property is sold, the amount of gain attributable to depreciation deducted is taxed as an Unrecaptured Sec. 1250 Gain, subject to a maximum federal tax rate of 25%. The amount of depreciation deducted in the year of sale is included in the Sec. 1250 Gain amount.

topic_title: How are you investing to keep your retirement income below IRMAA, NIIT, AMT, etc.?
content:
What is the method you rely on to keep your retirement income below IRMAA, NIIT, AMT and any other additional taxation that you perhaps did not need to worry about before retirement age?

Retirement often triggers RMDs from Traditional IRAs that you cannot totally avoid through e.g. Roth Conversions. There may also be other investments that mature or must be sold that potentially can push up income for a year or two. So, what is your main means of controlling your income so that you do not end up paying more in tax on your tax deferred retirement savings than you would have paid if you had not deferred it?

Do you just invest in stocks that do not produce dividend income? Do you invest in real estate, although that has property taxes?

Or do you just resign yourself to paying e.g. IRMAA, a "tax" that did not exist when 401ks/Trad IRAs were first pushed as the only way to save for retirement Those retiring now, no doubt recall that Roths did not initially exist and when first allowed did not allow any means to convert from Trad IRAs to Roths. So, difficult to convert everything to Roth unless there is sufficient time before IRMAA, etc. kicks in.

topic_title: How are you investing to keep your retirement income below IRMAA, NIIT, AMT, etc.?
content:
I'm probably not the target audience for this question given that I'm a younger accumulator, but from the perspective of someone in my position, I think one of the most underrated ways to avoid these kinds of "problems" is to just increase spending earlier in life as opposed to trying to hamstring one's investments and letting the tax tail wag the total return dog. This helps with several other things, such as qualifying for student financial aid. If one creates a legitimate business and spends on legitimate legal business expenses, there are significant tax savings to be had there as well; I realize this is not apples-to-apples, but if the choice is between starting a business or maintaining a high enough savings rate to hit IRMAA and other thresholds in retirement, that may be a point in favor of starting the business earlier in life.

This of course likely depends on being able to dramatically cut one's spending in retirement, because presumably, someone hitting such thresholds is gearing up for a relatively high spending rate in retirement. Some forms of spending can be shifted earlier without much negative consequence, such as buying or paying off a home earlier. Others imply more significant lifestyle shifts, such as eating out or traveling more before retirement and then cutting back after. Personally, upon hitting FI, I intend to decide between retiring early or working to increase spending, and my long-term retirement spending equilibrium would stay pretty modest. Of course, whether that's suitable for any given person or family is entirely personal, but I think it's arguably one of the simplest, most efficient approaches in terms of taxes and fees. It attempts to stay below thresholds in the long term, but enable additional discretionary spending (and working) in a way that does not sacrifice long-term priorities.

topic_title: How are you investing to keep your retirement income below IRMAA, NIIT, AMT, etc.?
content:
One pretty basic step to reduce the taxes you mention is to avoid having to take large sums out of savings in any one year.

So if you expect to buy a $50,000 car for cash in 4 years, take $12,500 out of your IRA in each intervening year. You’ll reduce the likelihood of going over an income limit, relative to taking it out all at once.

Or, continuing the car example, if you can get a low interest loan to pay for the car then use it rather than paying the taxes.

There is never any guarantee that you’ll pay lower tax rates in retirement than when you were working. That’s why so many advocate here for a balance between tax-deferred, taxable, and Roths. There are not many who suggest converting all tax-deferred accounts to Roths.

We ended up paying a small amount in NIIT for 2022. While the 3.8% sounded significant, it applied to only a small percentage of our actual income.

Use tax software to estimate the effect of Roth conversions, realizing capital gains, etc. BEFORE you take any action.

topic_title: How are you investing to keep your retirement income below IRMAA, NIIT, AMT, etc.?
content:
Retired, so no chance of an unexpected pay raise or hefty Christmas bonus.

Pension, SS and RMDs are entirely predictable at the beginning of the year. Interest on CDs and individual bonds are also predictable. QCD amount is under my control. CG distributions are unlikely with the index equity funds I hold. So the only real unknowns are the taxable dividends from mutual funds. I make an educated guess (based on the previous year’s numbers) as to what those will be and add it all up. The difference between that number and the next IRMAA level is my first cut at Roth conversions. Of course, I throw in a healthy fudge factor so I don’t inadvertently go over the cliff. I wait until as late in the year as possible to do the conversions lest I have an unanticipated need for a big MF redemption to buy a new car or something like that.

Thanks, there have been many thoughtful replies. I'm resigned to most likely paying some IRMAA. I agree that NIIT may not produce a large amount of additional tax, but would prefer not to have to deal with NIIT as it is more time consuming than it is worth (well unless you are mega-rich). Hopefully AMT will be indexed sufficiently for inflation.

The problem with NIIT is that the threshold is not indexed for inflation. The problem with IRMAA is that the brackets were not indexed for inflation for many years and most likely are not now indexed to keep up with the increases in the IRMAA "tax" rate, since the IRMAA "tax" rate will be at medical inflation rates. Also, IRMAA is a cliff tax and you have no way of knowing the actual bracket amounts until two years after the income has been set in stone.

It's the complexity that causes issues and the fact that these taxes did not exist when employers and financial institutions began pushing employees into traditional IRA/401ks with required minimum distributions. The ability to convert to Roths has been spotty over the years, including the latest change that does not allow for the recharacterization of a conversion. For someone who is single, IRMAA really hits significantly for someone with MAGI between 91,000 and 170,000, bumping up effective marginal tax rates significantly.

And IRMAA allows no exception for those who must pay for long term care, with thousands of dollars in care expenses (which are not covered by Medicare). IRMAA is based on MAGI, so no deductions are allowed before determination. And RMDs are counted, even though IRMAA did not exist originally when the trad IRAs were funded. So, no allowance for anyone who is being bankrupted by long term care (with added withdrawals and cap gains on sales of assets). And that is really hard to explain to someone in long term care who incurs very little in Medicare claims. But it is what it is.

QCDs, Roth Conversions, I Bonds are good possibilities. And as others have pointed out, a sense of resignation, may help. But can't help but keep hoping for more clarity and less complexity. Thanks for all the insights.

It's fortunate that AMT is much harder to run into at least for the time being than it used to be, since it's so complicated.

Then I modulate capital gains recognition not to likely end up just over a threshold, correcting my risk position by adjustments in things without immediate tax consequence.

I think you can and should separate your opinion about tax policy from management of your portfolio to best suit the policy as it is. For example I try not to factor in, at all, how I feel about the 'fairness' of IRMAA. I just try to avoid additional charges without 'tax tail wagging the investment dog'. I have a strong opinion about features like that in the code, but I'm not giving it and I try to exclude it from my portfolio management. I would not rationalize my failure to pay attention to the IRMAA brackets as 'well, I should be happy I'm in a position to get charged this extra money', or use a case of ending up a few $'s above a threshold as the basis for going off on how IRMAA shouldn't exist. content: FWIW, we set a target AGI for the year based on the IRMAA cutoffs, break it down to a monthly target, track AGI, and then make monthly Roth conversions up to the target. Late in the year, I'll check the projected distributions from mutual funds in our taxable accounts (I've found them reasonably accurate) and adjust the November Roth conversion if needed with the December conversion right at the end after all the MF distributions. We've done enough Roth conversions that by the time the first of us reaches 72, we should be able to stay below the first IRMAA threshold even with RMDs and both of us receiving SS. Taxable is fairly small and will sell all that (and therefore no more taxable MF distributions) after we move to a state with no state income tax in early 2023. So after that, income will be very predictable. Only possible issue is a future inheritance in the form of an inherited t-IRA (small six-figure at best) which we'll probably take evenly over the ten years so that we don't push a single year over the top - that will reduce conversions but in the long run make no difference as until we both start SS, we will need to draw down retirement funds so all it does is change where the funds are coming from, not the amount or tax status. By the time we reach RMDs, most of our assets will be in Roths.

It's interesting that so many seem to think that if you are paying IRMAA that you are well off, i.e. no worries about expenses. Is this just those who are married who think this, because those IRMAA brackets are double the single brackets?

Because for single brackets, while $91,000 is certainly not poor, for anyone who has seen income and assets gobbled up quickly by long term care costs, $91,000 does not come close to paying for one year of care. In that situation the person is on the way to bankruptcy. And as mentioned, Medicare does not pay for Long Term Care. And the need for Long Term Care is not a life changing event.

In any event, it seems a single person does need to plan for how to budget for/minimize such expenses as IRMAA, if they are to allow for future costs that are not covered by Medicare. And no one should want to have to apply for Long Term Care without being able to private pay for at least a few years, so that they will actually be accepted by a facility and kept at that facility if they ultimately must apply for Medicaid.

I guess with the latest increase in Medicare rates, it just seems more likely that IRMAA wil become a larger portion of income related taxes more quickly than I originally thought. And this is particularly true if one is single. So, while IRMAA is inevitable, it definitely requires more planning going forward. And whether it is Savings Bonds maturing after decades or a real estate sale or unexpected capital gains on other investments, or unexpected expenses requiring even larger retirement plan taxable withdrawals the tax planning may be challenging/no easy answer.

Better to be aware that these taxes are more likely than not to impact funds available in retirement. Has anyone found other income or nonincome related taxes that can popup in retirement other than IRMAA, NIIT and AMT?

Senior citizen property tax break cutoffs can effectively function in this way. They are all over the map and can vary widely based on jurisdiction.

In my state (NY), the cutoff for senior property tax breaks is actually quite close to the current IRMAA first tier, though "income" for that purpose is computed in an idiosyncratically different manner. (For some weird reason, IRA distributions don't count, but 401k and other retirement plan distributions do!) Also, the income cutoff has changed from year to year in ways that don't correspond to any rationale I can think of. A few years ago, the cutoff was $92K, for 2022 it is $90,550. Also, whether you are single or married does not matter.

My state also has a free senior pharmaceutical program (EPIC) which backstops Part D plans by limiting out-of-pocket costs. EPIC also gives you the option to switch your Part D and/or Part C and/or go back to original Medicare at any time during a calendar year. Income cutoff for that is $75K for single and $100K for married. And yet another idiosyncratic definition of income for that purpose (start with AGI, add the untaxed portion of your SS, but subtract your Medicare Premium payments for Parts B and D.)

Lots of other state and/or local programs out there with income limits of various kinds.

content:
I can see making charitable contributions via QCDs due to IRMAA if your income pops above an IRMAA threshold, such that you will end up with less money, if you are required to pay IRMAA, than if you hadn't had the amount of income above the threshold in the first place. So, you can pay IRMAA and end up poorer than if you hadn't had the additional income, or you can make a QCD to a charity back to $1 below the IRMAA threshold and end up with more money than after paying IRMAA and the charity gets a contribution.

So, income/MAGI is $91,001, IRMAA is 964.80, you can either a) pay IRMAA with Net result of $91,001 - 964.80 = 90,036.20
or b) you can make a QCD of anywhere up to 964.80 and end up with more money, e.g. QCD $500, MAGI $91,001 - 500 = 90,501, so no IRMAA, the charity receives $500 and you end up with 90,501 instead of 90,036.20 after IRMAA. Not an enormous difference, but someone paying long term care bills could no doubt use the funds, since LTC is not covered by Medicare. And again $91,000 is not rich if you are paying long term care bills, if you are paying that expense on 91,000 you are going to eventually go bankrupt.

The costs of care are a huge problem for the elderly and as stated, they are not covered by Medicare except for possibly a short term rehab. If you are many years from retirement, Roth seems to be the way to go as long as the tax laws governing Roths don't change and you meet the criteria to be able to contribute or convert to a Roth.

Practically that's unlikely of course, income is usually too hard to predict to that level of accuracy. I agree if somebody perceives zero inherent benefit to giving to charity but would QCD $10k (maybe $7k after tax cost) to make sure they ended below an IRMAA threshold and saved less than half that much in Medicare costs (for a couple even): irrational. But I doubt it's the actual aim of more than a small % of posts talking about IRMAA v QCD.

Likewise if somebody suggests retiring at an earlier age because of higher taxes due to higher income/assets, this is part of the basic economics of taxation. People at the margin *will* decide to work and earn less due to taxes on what they earn than if those taxes were lower. Most people see work, set aside from pay, as a net negative and pay as the offsetting positive that makes it worthwhile ('I love this job so much I'd do it for free' is rarely literally true). And the only pay that counts is the pay after tax, including secondary and tertiary taxes on that income (taxes on investment returns on already taxed income and potential third round, estate tax). The public policy debate about that, which we can't get into here, is the trade off between subjectively determined 'necessary' tax revenue and the disincentive to produce caused by taxes. But on an individual basis it's altogether rational for some people to decide to work less than they would if taxes were lower. Their decision wouldn't necessarily be the right one for somebody else though. Some people are less sensitive to tax rates in their work decisions, ie closer to 'I'd do this for free' than others are.

content:
You could put bonds and to some extent International stocks in your IRA/401K to maximize your degree of control I suppose. Others have mentioned charitable giving, let me expand on Roth Conversions. For Roth Conversions, you would have to make assumptions about future life expectancy, returns, tax laws, heirs' tax rates, ACA premium credits, etc. and develop a model of cash flows and taxes year by year. Future uncertainties will overwhelm your planning, so much of your efforts are to learn about the tradeoffs, the details of future years are not actionable.

Even with static assumptions, there are many different Roth Conversion paths that end nearly at the same place. For instance, for us, it's almost the same for our final estate values after heirs pay taxes to make Roth conversions steadily to the top of the 2nd IRMAA tier throughout versus convert to the top of the 24% bracket now, then to the NIIT threshold for a couple years, then to top of the 2nd IRMAA tier until age 70 and then age 70 and 71 stay within the top of the 0% LTCG bracket and then back to the top of the 2nd IRMAA tier after RMDs start. This modeling of later years is somewhat wasted in that things will change, but within our ability to make predictions, staying in the 22/24% range will all work about the same in the end.

content:
Interesting that at least some seem to think that 91,000 single or 182,000 married will provide extravagant lifestyles in the US. It appears that some totally discount the very real possibility of having to finance medical issues or significant long term care issues in retirement.

The complexities of dealing with the reality of a single person or a couple where both must pay for long term care is daunting at best. And as mentioned previously unless there are millions in assets at the time care is needed, will certainly ultimately lead to bankruptcy. And the process of financing medical expenses and particularly long term care, leads to retirement plan withdrawals and sales of assets that all trigger every one of the taxes that are supposed to only hit the truly wealthy.

True they only hit those who are not multi-millionaires for several years at which time all the assets are gone and the person must depend on Medicaid. But it truly is in the person's best interest to be able to stay off of Medicaid as long as possible in order to be able to stay in facilities that provide better care. And to do that one would need to minimize the taxes triggered by MAGI regardless of taxable income after deductions, which would most likely be zero.

I guess either many have not witnessed the need for a decade of long term care or a couple both in long term care or believe that it won't happen to them or that Medicaid will be sufficient. But the reality is that some people will require this care and their 91,000 or 182,000 will be spent every year plus additional assets will be sold/withdrawn and taxed. A couple would need at least 250,000 per year, probably more like 300,000. A million will be gone in no time. It's only if long term care expenses are totally ignored as a possibility or one is fine with thinking they can totally rely on Medicaid, that even 182,000 for a couple could be considered to provide a life of extravagance.

It's true that tax on these retirement savings/investments would have to be paid sometime, but while the person needs care, it would be in their interest to not have to pay "extra" MAGI triggered taxes, just because they are paying for their care. But as mentioned previously it seems the best way to deal with this possibility is to have had the time and ability/eligibility to have most savings/investments in a Roth IRA at least 2 years before age 65.

If one did not have that opportunity, there does not appear to be anything as significant that one can do after age 63. So, at that point, it appears to be more an issue of working around the edges and being aware and budgeting for these MAGI triggered taxes as much as possible. So, various suggestions have been helpful, but it looks like after age 63, the tax planning just gets harder.

I do agree that that hardest scenario financial is if one spouse needs LTC while the other still is living independently.

We have LTC insurance that will cover each of us for 3 years. We hope that will greatly lessen the chance of putting the independent spouse in financial jeopardy.

What we really hope, though, is that the insurance goes unused.

topic_title: Pause retirement savings or PMI?
content:
Keep in mind that you can't "back fill" your retirement accounts. PMI has an end date.
Have you calculated/guesstimated your PMI amount? And how that compares to a year of contributions to your retirement accounts? Really. This is how you would answer your question yourself. It's hard to give advice since there are so many different situations... we don't know your situation.

I dont' know what makes the most sense for you... but I'd guesstimate that it would be better in the long term to pay PMI for some period of time.

(my observation is that PMI gets a bad rap - because the person paying the PMI doesn't keep track and have it removed (assumes the lender will do it automatically) or is surprised by the cost of getting it removed because they have to go thru the expenses of doing a refi to get rid of it OR have to pay some fees/charges to have the lender remove it. OR that they take a loan that requires PMI be paid for the entire length of the loan but assume that it doesn't work that way - and are surprised that the only way to get rid of it is to refi - which may have expenses/fees and a not as good interest rate on the new loan).

My advice is if your loan has PMI - fully understand what it takes to have it removed (and if any fees will need to be paid - the lender may not quote you a price because they don't know what the $$ will be in the future) before you sign the closing documents.

I'm am sure other more wise (and less math challenged) people than I will have more to say.

content:
Here's a PMI calculator:
The average cost of private mortgage insurance, or PMI, for a conventional home loan ranges from 0.58% to 1.86% of the original loan amount per year, according to Genworth Mortgage Insurance, Ginnie Mae and the Urban Institute.
https://www.nerdwallet.com/article/mort ... calculator

A niece took a mortgage that had PMI of about $60 per month (a 5% down payment) . She paid $60 per month for 2 years ($1440). She was able to refi the mortgage and get rid of the PMI at that point. She opted to spend $1440 spread out over 24 months rather than save up (or stop retirement contributions) another 14K to get to 20% down. PMI let her keep her finances the same (the same contributions to retirement, etc...) for a relatively small monthly expense.

** the housing market and interest rates are not what they were a year or two ago... so your mileage may very - you may need to carry PMI for a longer period of time... and even then if you refi - there will be expenses and an unknown mortgage rate. There are lots of variables. PMI is a tool. If used correctly and appropriately it can be very useful. There is no shame in using PMI (But, I would say there is some shame in NOT knowing how it will effect YOUR particular situation when using it. You can't assume you know how it will work based on hearing how it worked for other people.)

You are asking the wrong question. You should be asking;

Should I buy this house or (insert your plan "B" here").

Since you can easily afford the house the big question is what you will do if you do not buy it.

The next biggest question is what your spouse(if you have one) wants to do and I would also give give that a lot of weight.

That said when I have been looking for a house to live in I have always taken the approach that within my budget it is better to find a great house at an OK price than settle for a just OK house at a great price. As long as you expect to live there 10+ years then finding a house that costs 10% less but does not "check all of your boxes" is a poor trade off.

It is even possible that you could live there the rest of your lives so that any financial impact will mainly impact your estate some day.

Good morning Mike,

I had another look through the report, based on your feedback. I'll document it as I understand it, for the benefit of other people that might have the same questions as me:
As I mentioned in my original post, at the top of the report there are two PIA at benefit date amounts - Wage-Indexed Formula and Special Minimum. Thanks to Mike, I know I can ignore the Special Minimum amount. However, it is not clear whether the Wage-Indexed Formula includes the impact of the Windfall Elimination Provision (WEP).
If you scroll down to the Wage-Indexed Formula section (in my report, that is on page 6), there are a few more mentions of PIA:
- PIA at eligibility. This is what the PIA would be at the date you start taking your Social Security benefit IF you did not have a "non-covered pension". Note that this does NOT include any adjustments for CPI increases between now and your eligibility date.
- PIA after windfall. This reflects the impact of WEP on your PIA at eligibility. You can easily verify this by adjusting the "Date of entitlement for non-covered pension" field in the Supplemental Worker Information form to be a date later than your eligibility date and running Calculate Estimate again.
- PIA at benefit date. This reflects the application of CPI increases between now and your eligibility date to your PIA after windfall amount.

So the net of all this is that the Wage-Indexed Formula PIA on the first page of the report DOES reflect any WEP adjustment.

One other thing, for those that know as little about Social Security as I do (and Mike, please confirm if this is correct). The PIA is NOT the amount of benefit you will receive. The estimated benefit that you will receive takes the PIA and adjusts it to reflect if you take your benefits before you reach Full Retirement Age or after that. This value is shown on page 1 of the Detailed Benefits Calculator report, in the "Benefit after rounding" field on the first page of your report.

Thank you again for your help Mike. I hope that this information will help other users of this outstanding website.

topic_title: Your experience with teaching your kids about money and how it works
content:
So I am thinking about how to teach my kids about money, since they are at a point where they are asking about how money works. I was thinking about how I learned about money. My parents did not talk about finance, but there was always talk about not having money, so I was under the impression that money was a scarce resource. When I was a few years older than them, I had jobs and saved money at an early age.

I currently make more money than my parents, but I tried not to show it. I don't drive luxury cars and the kids go to public school. We go on normal vacations and don't dine out too much. Despite this, I recognize that the lifestyle is considerable better than when I was their age. I am more interested in instilling in them the same ethics of not living beyond their means. What do you suggest? How have you taught your kids?

The other question is how do you deal with Santa . My son wanted me to buy something but I told him it was too expensive, but he thought Santa could get it for him. I basically told him that Santa doesn't usually do big ticket items. When I was a kid, there was no such thing as Santa. He was just a fictional character called Father Christmas that I read in books.

topic_title: Your experience with teaching your kids about money and how it works
content:
When I was growing up, my parents told me that Santa brought the gifts but they had to pay him for them. We had an approximate “budget” that we had to stick to when coming up with our wish list.

I’d also consider giving your child a small allowance and allow them to either save it (and pay them an interest credit on it) or use it to buy things that they may want.

topic_title: Your experience with teaching your kids about money and how it works
content: We tend to remind our kids that they are pretty privileged (getting to go on trips, dine out at a non-fast food resturants) though they live in an area where many of the kids are in similar situtations so it's easy to think everybody lives that way. We also tell them that parents have to pay Santa for presents and they don't magically appear. I suspect we spend less on our two kids for "Sanata" than my parents did when I was kid despite much high incomes. We aren't a fan of kids bragging that Santa brought them X very expensive gift.

It is odd, but what I recollect is that my mother gave me quite a financial education and that all of it was in the form of sound bites--just a couple of sentences.

She would say things like "while we had the mortgage, it was interesting to watch each month as the money went toward principal and interest, and at first almost all of it went toward interest, and then as time went on more and more of it went toward principal." And that would be that.

I don't remember exactly what we did with our kids, but they both seem to be doing what we'd want them to do. They did get an allowance. My son had a paper route, not a very big or long one. There was a toy store in town that allowed kids to buy things on layaway, which I thought was pretty much OK... and they were a nice store.

One day my son, he might have been eight or so, bought a toy on layaway and was very disappointed with it. I said he should go back to the store, quickly, with the receipt, and explain that he was disappointed because on the TV ad the toy could be taken apart into eight lions (?????) and the toy he got didn't disassemble at all. but money is a scarce resource . I know what you mean but it is important to remember that the first economic lesson is The Fundamental Economic Problem which is we have unlimited wants but limited means. We all can want things that we don't have the money to buy. Even Mr. Buffett who google says is currently worth $93,400,000,000 can't buy something he wants if it costs $93,400,000,001, right? (not without borrowing, which means he has to find additional money somewhere to pay that back, possibly with interest too).

I don't have kids but I heard recently on a podcast that you have to start with where your kids are at developmentally.

So you don't state their ages, nor what they're exactly asking about money and how it works.

Presumably they see you go to work and they see you buy things. You can start to help them connect the dots that the reason you go to work in part is to earn money to buy the things they need/want.

You don't have to teach them about Keynesian economics or Milton Friedman's ideas on the history of the US monetary system from 1867-1960. Not yet at least.

You can offer to provide an allowance if you like. That gives them some control over handling money, especially when the stakes are small. If they spend it and later regret how they used the money, it's better to learn that lesson with a handful of dollars than after they've bought their first Lambo.

They might think money grows on trees if you don't explain how the family gets their money (you don't have to give numbers of how much you get, etc).

I had an adult friend who took their kids (about 8 years old?) on a very expensive vacation to disney. When they got back they went out somewhere and the daughter asked the mom for some small amount of money to get a toy/trinket out of some machine and the mom barked, "We just spent thousands of dollars on you at Disney!" That didn't change the fact the kid still wanted the toy from the machine for 50 cents. Nor the kid didn't at that time understand there was a difference between the toy and the Disney vacation. If anything, she walked away confused thinking the toy was somehow more expensive than Disney because the parents splurged there but couldn't afford the trinket. Obviously, you don't want to be "that guy".

I think if you make it interesting it helps. My parents taught me to save a part of whatever I earned when I was young. They gave me an allowance ($1 a week) in exchange for me doing some chores around the house (some will disagree you shouldn't get an allowance for stuff like that, but at the same time, you don't just get money for not doing anything either do you? except with your investments, but not from your employer).

my parents had me open up a savings account and taught me that I'd get interest (more money) for keeping money with the bank.

I had absolutely no clue why I was earning money (so the bank could lend my savings out to others who wanted a mortgage, car loan, etc and the bank would make money on my money. I just liked that I was making money on my money).

does that help? what are they asking, what are you telling them? what are their ages? Start with where they're at, what they can handle. Add more information over time. Some kids are interested in learning and some are not. Some kids want to make money, earn interest, etc. Some just want money to spend. Everyone's different.

when they're ready you can ask them the following question:

Would You Rather Have A Penny That Doubles Each Day For A Month Or $1 Million?

topic_title: Your experience with teaching your kids about money and how it works
content:
Bit by bit as it was helpful. We started our kids with savings accounts as soon as they were able to sign their name in the book. Token allowance given in coins that could easily be split into percentages. By the time they were teenagers, we gave them enough to budget for their own personal needs. (They could see we had no more than they did at that point.) They are all adults now. Paid their own way through college with scholarships and jobs and began saving into tax advantaged retirement accounts with their first full time jobs. Two of them are starting to talk about buying houses. One is doing a major career transition and moving half way across the country this week. She has a 6 month emergency fund if things don't work out. I'm glad that we were able to show them some things and give them some opportunities that my parents were not able to do for me and siblings.

From a perspective that I do not have, I'm guessing that it's harder to teach some of this stuff to young kids if there appears to be a family "money tree" that keeps on dropping money. Or maybe it works out in a similar way or maybe it depends on the individual kid.

They are in elementary school. They seemed to know that their parents have to work to make money and that different parents seem to have different levels of money. They know that $100 is more than $10, but don't yet understand if something is expensive or cheap.

topic_title: Your experience with teaching your kids about money and how it works
content:
When my kids were young, we gave them a small allowance. Since we bought everything they really needed, we told them they could spend it on anything they wanted other than candy. At one point the older one asked for a boombox. We told him to save up his allowance until he had enough to pay for it. It took about 10 weeks, then he bought the item. We went through the same thing with the younger one about 2 years later, with the same result. This taught them about saving and delayed gratification. They also took very good care of those boomboxes because they knew how long they would have to save to buy a replacement. They both grew up with good financial habits, saving for retirement, etc.

When the older one was about 12 years old, we had a larger than usual credit card bill one month after returning from vacation. I showed him how much the bill was, and also what the minimum payment required by the bank. I told him "it looks real easy, just to pay that small payment doesn't it?" Then I explained how much interest I would have to pay if I did that, and that I would not get anything in return for spending money on interest. He is in his 40s now and I believe he has ever paid credit card interest.

A while back, there was a thread on using UTMA accounts for kid's savings. As a part of that I described how we handled teaching our kids about money. Not necessarily recommending it for anyone, but it has worked out very well for us. We started this when the kids were about 7 or 8, they are now both gainfully employed in good careers, living well below their means, and saving a significant percentage of their incomes:
We used them (UTMA accounts) as way to teach our kids about finances. The schools do a great job of teaching math, sciences, humanities, etc., but there is no curriculum on personal finance, so we took it upon ourselves to try to teach our kids.

At an early age we gave our kids an allowance (salary) and made them responsible for some of their expenses, the amount and the expense they were responsible for grew as they got older. By about age 13 they were handling just about all of their expenses except housing and eating at home (going out, clothes, electronics, etc.). They were also given the option of forgoing some portion of their "salary" to be put into the UTMA account. Whatever they chose to put in their got doubled (think of it as a 401k with 100% match). We also add additional funds from time to time (profit sharing plan!). I have always viewed this as their money, so no concerns about loss of control. I think of it as a 401k plan, with cliff vesting at age 21.

Over time, they have learned to differentiate between wants and needs. They are pretty frugal about how they spend their money (comparison shop for what they need). They have a very high savings rate, which we hope will continue when they have real jobs. They have learned to prioritize their wants, we are happy to see that they value experiences over stuff.

They have also learned a lot about investing, Asset Allocation, power of compounding, etc. At age 16, I let them start managing the investments as well. So far, they are adhering to a boglehead type investing regimen.

Sure, there is the risk that their behavior might turn on a dime at age 21, but I am OK with that. It has served as a useful tool for our parenting style. Certainly not recommending this for anyone else, just describing one possible use of it. This was completely separate from 529 plans set up for their college expenses.

I talk about money and related topics like taxes and insurance all the time. I think hearing the language is important even if they do understand it all.

I talk a lot about relative values. The house cost X times more than the car, how much things cost relative to the median HHI, how much we have saved for college in terms of years it would pay for.

Today something came up (I don't even remember what but something about someone could spend $1,000 on some want), and I said I wouldn't just do that without thinking and that's why I have emergency savings for XYZ.... They know about saving money. When they get spending money, I say they could have X-many of this or Y-many of that, which do you want/think is better? Or maybe you want something else later? I talk about waiting on it and will they really want it tomorrow? Amazing how much what they want changes when they wait a little.

You can make a chart if they are saving for something and they have to fill in the boxes to visualize the progress.

topic_title: Your experience with teaching your kids about money and how it works
content:
When our children showed an interest (age 5), we began giving them an allowance of $6/week. Set up 3 envelopes - Saving, Spending and Donating with $2 going into each envelope.

A lot of lessons came out of those envelopes:
(1) how to exchange multiple $1 bills in the envelopes for larger bill denominations
(2) buying their own small impulse purchases (or choosing not to) from the Spending envelope when running errands at stores with us. Taught them how to handle making a purchase and verifying change. Or to delay gratification and save up for a bigger purchase.
(3) periodic trips to the bank to make a deposit from the Savings envelope into their UTMA bank account and to see how interest accumulates. The free lollipop was an added bonus. When a little older, how to use the ATM card. In high school they learned to access account online.
(4) being charitable and making decisions on how to donate their Donating envelope $. A lot of thought went into their decisions!

Made it easy when they went to college as they had an account, knew how to write a check, use the ATM, use the debit card feature. They spent time educating their friends as many never had a bank account until the week before they went to college so they didn’t know how it worked.

I sent them to college with an Authorized User card on my credit card so they could start building credit history. Along the way they opened a Fidelity Roth IRA (we matched contributions and helped them understand low-cost diversified passive investments). In their senior year, Fidelity gave them their own credit card with low limit to continue building credit history and learn to manage their bills. They eventually closed the B&M bank account and moved to a Fidelity CMA. They use cash very little now and everything is online so the CMA works well for them.

Did their tax return filings with them as needed over the years until college graduation then they took over that responsibility.

A lot of impromptu conversations and sound bites over the years on various financial/investment/tax topics.

All these steps build on one another. Glad we raised financially-astute kids. My spouse and I received no education on investments and taxes growing up so we wanted to be sure our kids had a better foundation in those areas than we did.

We've tried to work money conversations into our regular daily/weekly talks. Not lectures, just stuff like, "Well, if I buy X today, then I won't have the money to buy Y in a few weeks, which I've been saving for."

One thing we did when they were younger: Grandma would give them spending money for vacation (usually Disney World). We would hold the money for them, and let them pick how to spend it. It was funny how the "I want!" demands dropped when it was THEIR money! Not to mention, their thoughtful choices were much more appreciated by them.

As kids grow older, the money needs/wants also grow. Our youngest, now 16, just got his first job (crappy HS job in fast food). So, he also got his first debit/checking account. He's thrilled--and saving his money to pay for the Boy Scout World Jamboree in South Korea next year. OTOH, his 19yo sister spends money like it's water--works at Starbucks, spends at Starbucks. Clearly, she's still a work in progress. But, we have a vacation coming up in a couple weeks, I know she's going to wish she had more spending money. Oh, well!

I think the important thing is to allow them to handle money, make choices, and even "fail", when they're younger. Small kids--small $$ amounts--small failures (like spending on coffee drinks--a huge waste, IMHO).

Many kids grow up seeing money coming out of ATM machines but don't understand how it works (the modern equivalent of "money grows on trees"). One time we took our daughter shopping for school clothes. We were looking at out-of-season sale items. I showed her an item that was marked at one third its original price. I asked her which she would rather have. One item bought in season or three of them bought out of season for the same cost. She understood very quickly.
We never paid our kids an allowance for living with us and never paid them for doing household or family chores such as housecleaning, grass mowing, wood splitting or stacking (we had a fireplace insert), etc. (Our oldest child now takes a decidedly different approach and started to pay our grandson an allowance for household chores.)

Our kids frequently accompanied us on grocery shopping at very early ages and we took this as an opportunity to impart basic education about foods (fruits, vegetables, meats, canned goods, and how they grow, get to market), different jobs people have, and how money is used to pay for items (it was easier back then to explain money when they could actually see cash currency exchanged with the grocery cashier). Our kids were required to work part-time during school or full-time during the summers when they could get work permits at 15. Employment and saving at least 50% of their take home pay were family requirements notwithstanding that they had demanding academic and extracurricular activities. It was always funny to see their shock in reading their first wage statement and realizing that the Government takes a cut of their pay. When they went to college, they all had their own checking and savings accounts; I think we helped them file their first tax return while they were in college, and never saw another one from them. We never funded Roth accounts for them but each of them started their own Roth accounts when they started gainful full time employment.

School bus chatter generally took care of Santa’s existence though our youngest child didn’t stop believing until 12 years old. At Church, they became exposed to additional gift giving and tithing. When our children were 12, 9 and 8 we took them Xmas shopping at Walmart— we gave them a $100 budget to buy gifts for family and friends. They shopped on their own and the looks on their faces when they came to the cashier was priceless that first year. One child was always over budget but now as an adult he’s the most frugal minded one in the family.

I think there are ample opportunities to instill good personal finance habits and skills in raising children throughout ordinary childhood activities. You want a lesson in entrepreneurship: the kid lemon stand, newspaper route or lawn mowing for the neighbors are good launching pads. You don’t need a rule book for this.
