Here's a few considerations, @SurferLife.

You have two inflation-adjusted life annuities with your military pension and your VA disability compensation. When you reach Social Security age you'll start a third one. They all use the same algorithm to calculate the cost-of-living adjustment. In the last 20 years, my military pension has risen a compounded total of over 54%. In the 1970s with even higher inflation, military retirees received some COLAs twice per year.

I think you're hedged pretty well against inflation.

I'm not an expert on Big Island farmland, but I'm pretty sure that its value will grow with inflation... unless you're close to Halemaumau or the east rift.

Finally, yes the stock market could drop. (It can also rise quickly, as we've seen several times in the last few years.) If you're investing in the stock market for the long term (>10 years) then do you think it'll be higher in 10 years? I'm confident it will, and that's another asset class which hedges against inflation.

Your military pension and your VA disability compensation are the equivalent of the monthly income from a portfolio of I bonds or TIPS. (It's an imperfect analogy since both of those have maturities, but it's good enough for asset-allocation considerations.) With such a huge amount of bond-like income, you can afford to keep your investments (TSP, IRAs, taxable accounts) in a higher allocation to equities. You still have to be able to sleep comfortably at night with short-term volatility, but mathematically & logically you could go as high as 80%-90% equities. It'd have a lot of volatility, but if you're planning to leave it there for a decade then you don't have to care about volatility.

My spouse and I are in a similar income situation as you (two military pensions, a little VA disability income). We're on Central Oahu with a primary residence and a rental property with a miserably low cap rate of 2%-3%. Because of that income and assets, our other investments (two Roth IRAs and a taxable account) are >95% equities. We keep just enough cash on hand to pay the bills. After 20 years of this, we've gone from "enough" to "way more than enough for the rest of our lives."

Pick the fund which makes you feel better.

I might be over-interpreting your question, but let me give you the different answers.

If you’re asking how much your military pension will be, that’s the High Three calculation:
https://militarypay.defense.gov/Pay/Retirement/

If you’re asking about VA disability compensation, that depends on your rating and your family members. It starts on the date you leave active duty, and those tables are here for your spouse and unmarried kids under 18 (or in college):
https://www.va.gov/disability/compensat ... ran-rates/
If you’re curious about how the rating is calculated, that’s a different hairball of a discussion for a separate thread.

If you’re asking how to value the lifetime value of a series of inflation-adjusted payments, I’m not. There’s a formula for figuring out the life value of an inflation-adjusted annuity, but you probably don’t care about the complexities of a discounted cash flow.

Instead you could consider your military pension (and any VA disability compensation) as the equivalent monthly income from a portfolio of TIPS or I bonds. (It’s an imperfect analogy because TIPS & I bonds have maturities, but it’s good enough for an asset allocation discussion.) Pick an interest rate for either one that’s a reasonable long-term number, like 1.5%-2.5%. (Recent I bond rates are far above the last 25 years of I bond interest rates.) That will give you the asset-allocation equivalent of the bond portion of your portfolio (from your military pension & VA disability income) and leads to a conclusion that you could invest the rest of your savings in equity funds.

You could also take a look at Part 3 of this post:
https://militaryfinancialindependence.c ... y-pension/
and the section “How To Calculate The Present Value Of A Military Retirement Pension” in this post:
https://themilitarywallet.com/military- ... -millions/

topic_title: Tax loss harvest question. Can use it to offset IRA -> Roth IRA conversion?

topic_title: Tax loss harvest question. Can use it to offset IRA -> Roth IRA conversion?
content: I agree with the other comments. Losses offset gains. Any losses in excess of gains can offset up to $3000 of ordinary income, including traditional to Roth IRA conversion income. Any losses in excess of both are carried forward to future years, then repeat the cycle.

topic_title: Traditional IRA to Roth IRA conversion
content:
I have been contributing to my trad IRA and converting the contribution to Roth (the so called backdoor Roth conversion) for sometime now. I always kept the balance in my trad IRA 0 to keep things simple but this year I performed a 401k rollover to my IRA and have a non-zero pretax dollar amount in my IRA. I want to know are there any gotchas I should be aware of if I try to do the backdoor conversion this year?

If it helps, I have setup different IRA accounts - one with Fidelity another with Vanguard. The rollover I performed went to Fidelity and I can do the backdoor conversion in my Vanguard account which has 0 balance in it.

A separate question I have regarding Form 8606 which I will have to file.

The IRS page says:

Basis. Your basis in traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRAs is the total of all your nondeductible contributions and nontaxable amounts included in rollovers made to these IRAs minus the total of all your nontaxable distributions, adjusted if necessary (see the instructions for line 2, later)

So IIUC the rollover I did does not affect the basis since the amount rolled over was pretax. Is that correct?

topic_title: Traditional IRA to Roth IRA conversion
content:
You should probably NOT use the backdoor process while you have this other money in the rollover IRA.

For tax purposes, the IRS considers all traditional IRAs (which includes the rollover IRA) as one IRA. Putting them at different brokerage houses does not change that.

If you do a Roth conversion (second step of the backdoor process), then the Roth conversion will be pro-rated with the money in the rollover IRA. You probably do not want to do that.

So IIUC the rollover I did does not affect the basis since the amount rolled over was pretax. Is that correct?
The basis is not "affected", but the backdoor maneuver is affected substantially and most people want to avoid that.

Unless there is something unusual in your situation, you should. not be using the backdoor any more. Put that contribution in taxable instead.

A Controlled Group exists if the spouses together control more than 50% of one of the business. Note the word "together".

Even if each spouse controlled 100% of his/her own business, if they have a child under 21, then the ownership attribution rules would make the businesses a Controlled Group.

My understanding is that both of your businesses (based on your description) are in a Controlled Group--technically a "Parent-Subsidiary Controlled Group".

Most 401(k) plans (e.g., Vanguard) provide that the plan is not only for the adopting employer but but also certain affiliates (in the Vanguard plan "Related Employers"). If there is a Controlled Group, one plan should be used for ALL businesses in the Controlled Group. E.g, my wife and I each have a Schedule C business and based on ours facts those businesses are considered to be in a Controlled Group. So, our businesses use one Vanguard plan. It would be a mistake for each of our businesses to have a separate plan--because if we did each plan would be in non-compliance with the Related Employer provisions.

If you are looking for complex estate planning, it's possible that the local attorneys are not equipped for that. If they are offering you their services for those more basic "first" steps, then that might explain it -- they want your business for the more basic legal work.

If you need sophisticated work requiring the establishment of an inter vivos or testamentary irrevocable trust, then it makes sense to integrate your will and other estate planning with that document.

Typically, lawyers prepare Medical Powers of Attorney and Advance Directives (aka Living Wills) to conform to your state's requirements. Most states have enacted statutes governing the enforceability of such documents and it is best to follow the relevant state's requirements very closely, including requirements for proper execution.

With regard to Financial Powers of Attorney: in addition to a general FPOA that also, generally, conforms to your state's requirements, most here strongly recommended that you obtain and properly execute the FPOA form required by each financial institution at which you hold accounts. This will avoid any potential problems with validity or acceptability of your own general FPOA.

As to a revocable trust: I am at a loss to understand why you would need one if your aim is to establish irrevocable trusts for your purposes.

topic_title: Basic estate planning vs. Advanced estate planning
content:
In my experience, there are 2 types of trust & estate attorneys - those that deal with large taxable estates, and those that deal with smaller non-taxable estates. Generally speaking, you should seek out a firm that fits your personal situation, and you absolutely should try to work with a single attorney/firm on the whole plan, and not split it up.

If you are looking for an attorney that works with taxable estates, try searching the ACTEC database, and I'd recommend interviewing at least 3 different attorneys. This will be an ongoing, long term relationship so make sure it's a good fit from the get-go. I can tell you from personal experience that the wrong firm will cost you much more in the long run, so take your time finding the right fit. One additional suggestion - try searching for attorneys in secondary/tertiary markets. SF/LA/NYC partners are routinely billing $750-1000+/hr, which adds up fast, but there many highly qualified people in smaller markets at half those rates. Either way, be prepared for a large expense, but it's cheaper than the estate tax!

With the possible exception of asset protection trusts, any firm with a good trusts and estates practice does all of these things on a regular basis.

One would almost always do the basic planning first. The same decisions that you make in your Wills (or in your case since you're in California, a revocable trust) would carry over to whatever advanced planning you do: the degree of control you want your spouse to have, the degree of control, and at what age, you want your children to have, and your choice of trustees (and executors if you weren't in California).

Even at the level of the estate tax exclusion amount scheduled to be in effect in 2026 (half of what it is now, indexed), very few people will have taxable estates. So very few people have to do any advanced planning. However, as noted above, for those who expect to have taxable estates, the decisions they make for their Wills (or revocable trusts in California) will carry over to whatever other trusts they may create.

If you trust your beneficiary with a swap power, why not trust them with the IRA?
By accumulating the IRA distributions in the trust, they will stay out of the beneficiary's estate and there will be creditor protection. By granting swap power to the beneficiary, the distributions from the IRA that will be accumulated in the trust will get taxed at the beneficiary's favorable income tax rates.

If the IRA was passed directly to the beneficiary outside of trust, then there will be estate inclusion and no creditor protection.

I concur with hiring a neutral executor - best yet an attorney if the heirs are behaving like this. In the end, this will save everyone aggravation. Having a neutral party will help cut back on "when am I going to get my share" and it will give the OP peace of mind.

In VA, the recommended fiduciary fee for settling an estate is 5% of the first $400,000 and it slides down to 2% of the value over $1M. That's a lot of $ the sons would not see if they lived in VA, but its their fault. By way of example: https://arlingtoncommissionerofaccounts ... mpensation

The other thing is that having an attorney might just cut down on the sons suing each other. In my family - cousins - two sisters sued another after the estate was settled. The judge threw the first suit out, so they sued again and again it was tossed out, now none of them are on speaking terms.

Also, be sure your burial plans are in the estate plan to prevent arguing.

(True story, my uncle was a Commissioner of Accounts (in VA they settle estates). I went into his home and noticed a beautiful circa 1770 mahogany breakfront. When I asked where he got it, my aunt said he took it out of an estate he settled as his fee. Too bad the deceased did not have a will to specify who gets what. Lesson learned by me, almost everything has a little sticker under it with a color code of who gets what and its approx. value if its collectable. All specified in a will of course.)

knswamy,

Good questions. I think this is common in corporate world. You do a very good job and get great raises till you price yourself out. In a technical corporate job, voluntary early retirement is a norm. I have rarely seen people above 55 unless they are extremely technical. The company only need a handful of those. You can take management track instead, but it is grueling out there and again no guarantees. Few survive.

My advice is to explore adjacent paths within the corporate structure that you enjoy the most. To elaborate, if you enjoy something (say finance, data, treasuries, HR, people, capital planning, etc.), anything, take up some special projects and grow in that area. You do that while you are doing your current job. It is more fun that way, extends the career run way, and who knows where it might lead. You can be a generalist as well.

You can explore second career outside of your primary job. But as you said, they dont pay as much. You can try and start that now to get it all set up in a couple of years. Remember that you will have to have something to do after your retirement - and this might be a better long term option.

Part of your situation is that you have likely been working for around 20 years now and the novelty and excitement of doing any job has worn off.

When you were just starting out when you finished a big project that was likely pretty rewarding. Now when you finish a big project that is just another project out of dozens or hundreds of projects that you have done in your career.

If you start a different career then it might be a bit more interesting for a while but at some level it may still been seen as just being another job and it may not been all that rewarding unless you are doing something like saving babies as part of your job.

If you are looking for more fulfillment then looking for it in your outside activities and with your family while still working in your current field is likely a better choice. That would also carry over better when you eventually retire.

I purchased my first (and current) home over 30 years ago, at about age 40. The mortgage is paid off. There are four risks to staying here:

1) Love or List It: eventually, the house needed a major renovation (kitchen, bathrooms) and I faced the dilemma of renovating or moving; renovating was a huge headache and I wish I had moved instead

2) Neighborhood changes: luckily, the neighborhood improved over the years, but it could have gone either way

3) Lifestyle changes: the layout was fine when I moved here but, over the years, it has become less than ideal

4) I am facing a potential capital gains tax when I sell -- I have spent enough on home improvement projects to reduce this if I sell in the next few years; it is an incentive for me to sell sooner than later (I live in CA where cap gains are treated as ordinary income and home prices tend to go up and never down)

1) Love or List It: eventually, the house needed a major renovation (kitchen, bathrooms) and I faced the dilemma of renovating or moving; renovating was a huge headache and I wish I had moved instead

2) Neighborhood changes: luckily, the neighborhood improved over the years, but it could have gone either way

3) Lifestyle changes: the layout was fine when I moved here but, over the years, it has become less than ideal

4) I am facing a potential capital gains tax when I sell -- I have spent enough on home improvement projects to reduce this if I sell in the next few years; it is an incentive for me to sell sooner than later (I live in CA where cap gains are treated as ordinary income and home prices tend to go up and never down)
I could have written that first sentence ... "over 30 years ago" ... "about age 40" ... "mortgage is paid off." I have always called this my first-second house, because it was more than I thought I would ever be able to get in a first house.

Regarding point #1: About 10 years ago I decided to do a whole-house renovation. Freshened everything and made a few minor changes that I wanted for myself. Told contractor I intended to remain here AT LEAST 10 years. If I do ever move, I figure it would be to a continuing care place.

If you like your house and, especially, location, why change? Use the money you save not "buying up" to make changes to your home that will make it even more yours.

content:
I don't have data to back this up, but I see a lot of people in my "circles" - friends, co-workers, acquaintances, etc. - upgrading houses every so often - say 7 years at each place, each time starting the 30 year amortization over and increasing the house value each time. Combine that with the transaction costs, moving costs, new furnishings, landscaping, improvements - it seems like a recipe for not getting ahead. My parents stayed in one modest house their whole adult lives and paid it off early - housing was never an issue. Buying one reasonable house and staying put seems to be a good step towards getting and keeping your finances in line. Of course every situation is different - needs and wants change, jobs change - but I think you've save a lot of money in the long run by avoiding extra house sales in a lifetime.

On the other hand, perhaps if you keep buying new houses you can offset this by skipping out on the more expensive maintenance. We've been in our house 9 years, and the house is about 20 years old, so flooring, HVAC, roof, etc. all add up too.

Stock returns have historically been much better than real estate, esp personal real estate. After expenses, real returns for an owner-occupied home have been about 1%, while globally diverse stocks have returned about 4% after taxes.
That's not including, I would guess, net rental yield*. Which you are consuming by living in in the house. Which is the basic reason not to think a bigger house than you need is going to boost your investment returns in the long run. In contrast there's no particular reason to believe that rental real estate, levered to equal the risk of stocks (ownership interests in *levered* corporate assets) will return less than stocks risk for risk. There are various other reasons to prefer or avoid owning rental real estate, and you don't have to do just rental RE or just stocks you can do both. It's not some inherent superiority in stocks as an asset class.

Otherwise, there are two potential financial penalties to owning the same house too long, mentioned separately in earlier posts:
a) to the extent it would make you ignore better career opportunities in other places. Although you might have other reasons not to change areas.
b) as long as there's a fixed $ exemption from capital gains on owned houses eventually sold during your lifetime (currently $500k per couple, we're way past that in our house of 29 yrs). That could offset the transactions cost of buying/selling more houses along the way.

*what you'd get in rent minus cash expenses (prop tax, maintenance, landlord paid utilities, etc) if you rented out same value properity(ies) to somebody else. The easiest example is a $1mil house you live in vs. a $500k one you live in and a $500k rental-suitable property you rent out. The big penalty in the first case is not getting net rental yield on the second $500k, not that rental properties are inherently inferior to stocks.

content: The saying “don’t outsmart your common sense” comes to mind. Just curious as to what investments you are using leverage for? I’ve hashed it out every which way and the only thing that really makes sense is to not overspend on a home (avoid lifestyle creep) and pay it off. All of the extra cash flow then go to investments. It’s not necessarily an all or nothing approach though. There is a lot of antiquated or just flat out bad advice floating around out there regarding homes. One that comes to mind is that a low mortgage rate is practically paying you when inflation is more than the rate. This is such absurd thinking, I can’t decide if those that mention it are just trolling or actually believe it. On the surface it sounds good, kinda like investing instead of paying off a mortgage. Peel back a few layers though, run through some scenarios and then decide for yourself.

Even then it might not be a bad decision if you've found the place you want to be for the life you want to lead.

topic_title: Is it financially bad to live entire life in first house purchased?
content:
As others have said no, it is financially advantageous in most cases. Besides the transactions costs, resetting the amortization table on the mortgage is probably the biggest drawback to moving--in your first house you stay in 5-10 years and pay the highest interest years on the loan, then take out a new mortgage and start it all over again. You lose and the bank wins.

As someone who recently moved at age 40 and considered this heavily, there is no doubt staying put is better financially. However, things change in life. A house that you purchased at 25 without kids and early in careers may be viewed very differently 10 years later with two kids in terms of size, layout, schools, etc. Also while I'm a big proponent of paying off debt money isn't everything. A house that better meets your needs can have a big impact on your quality of life.

As others have said no, it is financially advantageous in most cases. Besides the transactions costs, resetting the amortization table on the mortgage is probably the biggest drawback to moving--in your first house you stay in 5-10 years and pay the highest interest years on the loan, then take out a new mortgage and start it all over again. You lose and the bank wins.
Correct me if I'm wrong, but I don't think the amortization schedule itself makes a difference, only the size and terms of the mortgage. In fact, assuming no changes to prevailing mortgage rates and ignoring fixed refinance costs, refinancing to a 15-year mortgage 15 years into a 30-year mortgage with the same remaining balance would likely reduce the interest rate and therefore the interest cost. It only seems like resetting the amortization schedule is worse because people tend to move up in house earlier in their journey, so in absolute nominal terms, their interest costs do go up. But if that was a concern, one could always just buy a smaller home with a bigger down payment or take out a shorter-term mortgage.

This is obviously quite logical, but it's incredibly easy to forget in the heat of searching for a new home because there's so much social and industry pressure to put down a standard amount like 20%. We kind of mistakenly forced the realization into our minds when we bought our home because we ended up buying a cheaper home than we originally anticipated, and we were also surprised by some local lending quirks that required us to put a higher amount down in order to get the cheapest rates. We ended up putting a bit over 30% down, and were pleasantly surprised to find that our mortgage payment on our 3-bed/2-bath house in a decent neighborhood was the same as the rent for our previous 1-bed/1-bath apartment above a seedy liquor store. We didn't expect or plan it that way, but it kind of made us realize how even in a seemingly unaffordable market, as long as one can save a good amount, one can eventually afford housing payments and reduce total interest costs by simply putting more down on a house (at the expense of having to wait and save longer, of course).

topic_title: Is it financially bad to live entire life in first house purchased?
content:
In most cases, living in the same house your whole life is a good move financially. Round-trip transaction costs for buying and selling a house are very roughly 10%, so the fewer of these you have in your life, the lower your housing cost. If you want leverage, you can borrow against your house in various ways.

The best financial drawback discussed here is the $250/500k capital gains exemption. But, if you live in the house your whole life and leave it to heirs, they get a step-up in basis, so they don't pay capital gains either. One could postulate other drawbacks, like not moving to chase better/higher paying jobs, but I'd say that's beyond the scope of the question.

Stock returns have historically been much better than real estate, esp personal real estate. After expenses, real returns for an owner-occupied home have been about 1%, while globally diverse stocks have returned about 4% after taxes.

There are various other reasons to prefer or avoid owning rental real estate, and you don't have to do just rental RE or just stocks you can do both. It's not some inherent superiority in stocks as an asset class.
1. But there is no way to for most people to be as well diversified as landlords as they can be in stocks/bonds. It's really easy to be globally diversified in stocks and bonds, but to do the same as a landlord would require massive amounts of capital to own rental properties all over the world. Almost no one has those resources.

Being a landlord is also a major PITA since it oft requires major time, effort, and oft borrowing, while investing in stocks/bonds is relative simple and requires minimal maintenance. To be a landlord requires either significant borrowing which as you said increases risk or you need to have significant money for rental properties which means you're forgoing investing in stocks and bonds in favor of real estate; an opportunity cost.

2. I'd rather keep it simple by avoiding the risk and potential leverage of physical assets like real estate and just invest in globally diverse stocks/bonds without using leverage. The latter is simpler and less risky.
1. The first two paragraphs obviously IMO fall into 'there are various reasons to prefer or avoid owning real estate' and aren't news to anybody least of all me. I would note though the diversification one is sometimes based on a misunderstanding of diversification. If a person has two rental properties in their neighborhood as their whole investment portfolio that's undiversified. If the two properties are 25% of their investment portfolio and 75% financial assets I'd argue that's more diversified than the person with 100% financial assets. IOW you seem to have ignored both the statement I made about there being reasons to avoid RE for some people, plus my also obvious statement nobody has do *just* RE or *just* financial assets like stock/bonds.

2. Financial assets are simpler, they are not necessarily less risk. Unlevered RE is generally less risky than stock for the reason I already gave, stocks are ownership interests in corporate assets already levered by the corporations' borrowings, and often the assets are more volatile themselves. Although clean data is a problem in evaluating RE vol v stock vol (raw RE price data will be only a small fraction as volatile but that's partly because price discovery isn't as continuous in RE) it's not reasonable posit that unlevered RE and unlevered stock are equal risk. Stock is significantly more, and some degree of leverage is needed on real estate to make the return comparison to stocks apples to apples.
A globally diversified portfolio split evenly among stocks and bonds is much less risky than any kind of investment real estate most people can access.
So you keep asserting, but it's not so on the individual asset level. Unlevered rental properties have significantly lower price volatility than stocks historically, much lower if you look at raw statistics (Case Shiller Index's volatility is a small fraction that of the S&P, though you do have to somehow correct for the averaging effect in reporting property prices, 'cleaner' commercial indexes are more like 40-60% as volatile as stocks). There's an element of truth in your claim if you artificially assume the person either must invest in a few properties and no stocks, vs all stocks and no properties. Then there's a lot of idiosyncratic risk from the few properties not offset by any diversification into other assets. But that's also false under the entirely realistic (applies to my portfolio) situation where there's significant exposure to rental properties *and* stocks. Then there's actually added diversification over just the things that drive the stock market. Some of those things drive real estate in the same way, others don't as much.

Always keeping in mind I said right from the outset: *some* people have good reasons to avoid being rental property owners. But a blanket statement 'stocks are less risky' isn't true.

It is financially optimal to live your entire life in the first house you purchase.

Shoulda, coulda, woulda wished I might have done that.

Bought a house in 1974, sold long ago, that is now worth more than 50 times initial cost.

Several houses later, things worked out better than I might have hoped for, but that first house might have been optimal.

Many years ago, I leveraged investments.

During my third trimester of life, there is no need whatsoever to use leverage.

Everything we own was fully paid for a long time ago, and we sleep well at night.

Home equity is part of net worth, by definition. Bogleheads tend to be independent-minded do-it-yourselfers, but some take this too far by inventing their own definitions for terms that do not align with generally-accepted use. Net worth is the value of everything you own, minus everything you owe. Excluding assets from net worth solely based on the type of asset should not be done, and is confusing to others who don't know your proprietary definition. There can be reasonable debates about how to account for particular assets, for example subtracting likely taxes owed from a pre-tax account, or subtracting transaction costs for a piece of real estate. Or, maybe, some assets can be excluded based on a negligible value. For example, maybe I exclude my wardrobe from net worth, because the value I (or my heirs) could get for it relative to the time it would take to sell it would be miniscule. But marketable assets with non-negligible value should be included, by the generally-accepted definition. There are other terms that can be used that exclude home equity, like "investable assets". (I think you agree with this, but saying this for the benefit of everyone else reading.)

Excluding home equity from an investment portfolio is completely different. There are plenty of assets I exclude from my portfolio - float in checking accounts, emergency fund, 529s, cars, home equity, etc. Partly this is for convenience - it's not easy to rebalance home equity, loans would be required, let alone rebalancing car equity, etc. Partly this is also because of the purpose. The purpose of my portfolio is to grow. It makes much more sense to manage a set of assets when they all have the same purpose.

topic_title: How good is First Republic Bill Pay
content:
I use First Republic Bank as my primary bank, having switched from Bank of America in 2013. First Republic is extremely customer-focused and I would have no hesitation recommending that you make the switch as well.

When I switched in 2013, it was clear that the "rails" behind Bank of America and First Republic's bill pay were the same. They recognized the same types of merchants, could do eBills for the same merchants, etc.

While Bank of America certainly has a larger digital budget, First Republic's app and website are regularly updated and tend to be more customer-focused, in the sense that there are no extra fees for most types of transfers, higher limits that work for their clientele, and easily accessible customer support.

topic_title: Is it possible to undo direct HSA contributions and contribute through payroll instead?
content:
I quit my job at the end of last year and subsequently maxed out my HSA Jan 1 via a direct contribution (not through payroll) because I wasn't sure whether I'd look for another job this year and wanted to get the money invested as soon as I could.

However, I did get another job which has a very generous HSA match (as well as savings on FICA) if I contribute via payroll to the HSA. Does anyone know if I can withdraw / undo my earlier contributions and contribute through payroll starting from 0% contributed? Can't find any info on this scenario online. If so, what steps should I take?

topic_title: Is it possible to undo direct HSA contributions and contribute through payroll instead?
content:
I assume yes, but I'd start by contacting your HSA administrator (the prior one from the old job).

And for clarity, you can only contribute to an HSA if you qualify (by having an eligible plan). I'm assuming you are on some sort of interim health insurance, with an HSA eligible plan. If not, you need to get your contribution back as you actually were not eligible to even contribute to an HSA...

And going forward, my understanding is you are limited to the prorated amount. So if you'll end up being covered by an HSA eligible plan for say 7 months, you can only contribute 7/12 of the annual maximum (since you were only eligible for 7 out of 12 months).

topic_title: Is it possible to undo direct HSA contributions and contribute through payroll instead?
content:
Yes, you can.

You will have an excess contribution in the HSA which will need to be removed by your next tax filing deadline, your custodian will have a form for this.

content:

topic_title: Accounts opened fraudulently at CapitalOne - next steps?
content: Yes. While the "Big Three" Experian, Equifax, Transunion are the most popular providers for credit reporting and locks... Wait, there's more! The other two I would recommend are Innovis and Chex-systems. The latter two are primarily used for opening bank accounts... which of course are handy for lots of other fraud. It's sad that we have to work so hard to protect ourselves. And we all pay for it (like we all subsidize shoplifting etc). If you don't have your credit locked up tight, or are OCD and like to check, run an annual credit report by rotating among the Big 3.

topic_title: do my mother need a tax ID number her trust
content:
A friend's mother passed away 9 months ago and he told me he is still waiting to get a tax ID number for his mother's trust from the IRS. Until he gets this the estate cannot be dispersed. I am wanting to avoid this if possible when my mother passes.

Apparently you file a form 1041 and ask the IRS to create a Employer Identification Number EIN which becomes the tax ID for the trust.

Questions
can this be done ahead of time or can the EIN only be created after the passing of whoever created the trust, in my case my mother?
can the trust be dispersed without the EIN?

Currently the income from my mother's trust is taxed via her social security number.

thanks for any responses

topic_title: do my mother need a tax ID number her trust
content:
If the trust were a separate taxpayer, it would get a number now, which it would continue to use.

If the trust is a grantor trust taxable to her, it may get a number now, but even if it does, it would need to get another one upon her death.

The trustee's lawyer may be able to get one more quickly.

content:

Apparently you file a form 1041 and ask the IRS to create a Employer Identification Number EIN which becomes the tax ID for the trust.
I've only had to do this once, but this doesn't sound right. The 1041 is the tax return forms for a trust, not a form to ask the IRS to give you an EIN. You can apply for an EIN online; quick google says here. The first page after pressing begin application lets you specifiy estate or trust (or several other kinds of entities). Now I can't remember if the IRS produced an EIN at the end of the online application with a follow up paper letter (which is what I think happened), or if there was just a paper letter with the EIN. In any case, it didn't take months, in my case, it took, at most, days---and I really seem to recall that issuance of the EIN was instantaneous. But my one instance of use was years ago, and the IRS may work on different time frames now.

topic_title: Megabackdoor Roth IRA double check
content:
Personally I just do the in plan Roth conversation of my after tax contributions for my mega backdoor Roth, just to make my life easier, since I have to do it every pay check. It also ensures that I have minimal growth (thus no taxes to pay) before the conversion (everything post conversion is Roth an tax free!). Having to issue paper checks and taking it to Fidelity sounds like a complete pain. At least for my plan, I can always do in service roll overs of my Roth 401k to my Roth IRA, if your plan is the same you can do this say once a year to make your life easier. I personally plan to just leave it in my 401k for now since I can find the funds I want and the ERs are lower than my Vanguard Roth IRA.

Also the mega backdoor Roth should not need to be included on Form 8606, since your 401k plan admin will issue you a 1099-R that shows whether you have any growth that was converted to Roth and needs to be taxed.

This is controlled by IRS Regulation 26 CFR § 1.401(a)(31)-1 - Requirement to offer direct rollover of eligible rollover distributions; questions and answers.

While most 401k plans allow two split direct rollovers of the employee after-tax contributions to a Roth IRA and employee after-tax earnings to an eligible pre-tax retirement plan/account (IRA, another 401k, etc...). They are not required to do this under Q&A 10:

Q-10: Must the plan administrator allow a distributee to divide an eligible rollover distribution into two or more separate distributions to be paid in direct rollovers to two or more eligible retirement plans?
A-10: No. The plan administrator is not required (but is permitted) to allow the distributee to divide an eligible rollover distribution into separate distributions to be paid to two or more eligible retirement plans in direct rollovers. Thus, the plan administrator may require that the distributee select a single eligible retirement plan to which the eligible rollover distribution (or portion thereof) will be distributed in a direct rollover. Note: Nowhere does this say it can be restricted to a traditional IRA

However, there is a way around that. A plan must allow you to use your one direct rollover for your employee after-tax earnings to an eligible pre-tax retirement plan/account and take a distribution of the employee after-tax contributions payable to you. They are required to do this under Q&A 9:

Q-9: Must the plan administrator permit a distributee to elect to have a portion of an eligible rollover distribution paid to an eligible retirement plan in a direct rollover and to have the remainder of that distribution paid to the distributee?
A-9: Yes, the plan administrator must permit a distributee to elect to have a portion of an eligible rollover distribution paid to an eligible retirement plan in a direct rollover and to have the remainder paid to the distributee.

A 401k plan has no ability to restrict rollovers to a traditional IRA. They must allow you the following three options at a minimum:
Direct rollover of both the employee after-tax contributions and earnings to a Roth IRA. The earnings will be taxable.
Direct rollover of both the employee after-tax contributions and earnings to a traditional IRA. This will be a tax-free rollover with the employee after-tax contributions constituting a non-deductible basis that must be reported. This would result in pro-rata taxation with any pre-tax balances in all traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRA accounts if you were to so any Roth conversions unless you could first rollover any pre-tax balances back into your 401k plan or another employer 401, 403b or 457b plan.
Direct rollover of the employee after-tax earnings to a traditional IRA and distribution check payable to you. You can then deposit this in a personal account and do a 60-day rollover to a Roth IRA. Both of these would be tax-free rollovers. If you are doing Backdoor Roths you would only want to choose this over option 1 if you can roll the pre-tax IRA assets back into your 401k plan or another employer 401, 403b or 457b plan.
Refer your employer/401k plan to IRS Regulation 26 CFR § 1.401(a)(31)-1, Q&As 9/10 and call them on their BS.

topic_title: Interviewing while pregnant
content:
Good employers are more than happy to wait while folks are out on maternity or paternity leave. Of course, there are some horrible employers out there as well.

You’re under no obligation to disclose any medical information until after you’ve accepted an offer. A lot of people though do talk it out during the offering period. But it is a potential risk. There is no direct analogy here, but when I’ve been in the offering process before when somebody says “just so you know, I’ve already paid for a 2 week cruise that starts a month after my start date”. And that’s not an issue for us, we can wait. Again though, some people are jerks about things……

And paternity is a thing too. Think what an expectant father should do in this case. The answer should not be any more onerous for the mother to be. Fathers who take paternity leave have never mentioned it before starting work.

It’s no shock that parents sometimes need flexibility to do parent things. And it’s no shock that people who aren’t parents, are very likely to become parents at some point. After managing for so many years, there are dozens of reasons why people need to take time of, go on extended leave, etc. Maternity is just one of them. And yep, I hired an expectant mother. She told us right after we extended the offer. I appreciated the heads up a lot but I wouldn’t have been resentful if she had waited until after the start date. She’s a great employee. So happy to have her on the team.

As a manager dealing with maternity is easier and more predictable than dealing with employees with rapidly aging parents.

topic_title: Interviewing while pregnant
content:
This is naturally a very heated, political topic - particularly when there are a lot of men on the site who don't fully understand and appreciate the nature of pregnancy - myself included.

My point of view comes from someone who is the parent of 4 kids, has hired several women and worked through maternity, as well as gotten the perspective of a 4x mother on what she thinks about "hiring newlywed women in prime child birthing years" (to quote her).

The law is reasonably clear: you are not obligated to tell them. They're not allowed to ask. They can't rescind the offer or fire you once you inform them. In general, that's mostly undisputed (I'm sure someone will contradict me, but I have no interest in a law or political debate about it).

I think the question for you and your wife is to evaluate the company's response. If I hired someone who was several months pregnant, but didn't tell me, I would be irritated and probably take some bad assumptions with me into their career. If they were a great performer and came back strong, that would get washed away. If they were mediocre, I would probably find myself being hard on them. That's a bit of human nature I think most people can't avoid. I would absolutely not blanket fire them or do anything illegal, but they'd have a higher hill to climb.

If that person told me they were pregnant before taking the offer, I'd work through it with them, understand the timing, etc. I'd also engage HR ahead of time to make sure everything is on the up-and-up so I was protected from any claims of inpropriety. I asked my wife, "would you hire them if they told you they're 4 months pregnant", she laughed and said "I think you have to, but I'd rather not".

So there you go. It's a dice roll. If it was my wife, I would probably go through the entire process, and prior to them writing an offer, I would encourage her to provide the pregnancy information. You are then effectively giving them the right to come up with an excuse not to make the offer vs. making them feel like you tricked them. My opinion is 80% of the time, the offer still comes, and you have "good faith" credit. For the 20% where they make up a BS reason - ask yourself if that's where you want to be or the boss you want to work with.

topic_title: Interviewing while pregnant
content:
And now the thread descends into pointing fingers and blaming toxicity on other people. This thread shows why there is "toxicity" at work, because people see work as a transactional tit-for-tat, not a collection of people. Empathy is at a premium. Often people just assume the worst of others at all times.

People are citing things like "what if this was in a court document", well it's not. This is a conversation around opinions.

Are there bad managers who would specifically punish and/or avoid a potentially pregnant individual? Of course. Is it right? Of course not.

Do all humans have implicit biases that are shaped by other people's behaviors and demographics. Of course. Is it right? Yes - it's specifically why many companies do implicit bias training. To help people recognize it and not have inappropriate (or illegal) responses.

Is it reasonable for a hiring manager to feel frustrated if shortly after hiring someone to fill a void, they learn that person will be taking leave? Of course.
Is it OK for that manager to take retaliatory action? Of course not.
Is there a possibility some of those feelings will creep into their perception of the individual? Of course. Is it illegal? Depends. And without context, nobody on this forum really knows.

Is it reasonable for a woman to expect to be able to raise a family without being discriminated at work? Of course.

All these things create a grayness in the world we have to navigate. It's not all on management, it's not all on employees. Any healthy relationship is a balance - not management trying to squeeze every drop of blood out of employees, not employees trying to snatch up every possible perk. Honesty, collaboration, and trust gets you there, but somebody always has to make the first move and just assume, for 1 second, that being empathetic and kind gets your to the final goal.

I literally just wrapped for the day, getting off a skip level, and my people are either legitimately happy or the best liars around. For the most part, I think they're honest with me, and I know I'm honest with them. But it all starts with being upfront and earning trust. I've written this a couple times on this forum: I'm stunned at how many people are distrustful and disgruntled at work.

topic_title: Should I setup a Joint bank account to pay Joint mortgage with girlfriend?
content:
I am neither for or against opening another account with your mortgage lender. You need to determine if it gives you enough value long term to have it.

Things to think about (not expecting a reply) :

How does the account ownership change once you are married? I'm single. I hear marrieds complain about the hoops they sometimes have to jump thru when one or both of them change their names... Maybe this isn't a concern for you.

If you open a new checking account - you may need to keep a minimum balance and you may not do enough transactions to qualify for "free checking" - which may be annoying - and the fees may be another "bill/expense".

Think about How do you expect to set up your accounts once you are married as in how do you envision getting the bills paid after marriage - will you consolidate accounts or leave things as is? Will the new account fit into that plan?

Would having what may be a third checking account that you could pay various house related monthly bills from be useful now and in the future? As in you each transfer money either from your personal checking account OR payroll transfer to the "joint" account - and that's where you make all your payments from?

If you open an account with your mortgage lender - do they have any other perks you might want to use (once you have that second "relationship" - like better CC offers or something else)?



I have a checking account with my mortgage lender. It's free and it has no minimum balance. I keep 2 months of mortgage payments as a "cushion" - this is part of my EF. On the 28th of every month I transfer the mortgage amount to the account. On the 6th of every month - the mortgage gets paid. Those dates work with my "paycheck" schedule. This is a legacy checking account - as I've had a relationship with the lender far longer than I've had the mortgage. It is NOT my primary bank.

Yes, I could consolidate this into the hot mess that is my everyday banking... but I think that would introduce some "stress" into my mortgage payment routine so I keep the extra checking account.

Welcome to the forum! And congrats on your upcoming engagement. Regarding your 2 questions, my short answers are no to tax consequences, and no good reason to open this joint account at either the lender bank, or one of the banks you are each using unless you are eligible for any bonuses or lower mortgage rates/closing costs.
I will say, that with the level of trust required for a successful marriage, I see no reason to have more than one joint checking account for your everyday household spending needs, and no reason for any individual accounts after you move in together/get married. Both my and spouse's paychecks were always direct deposited to our joint account, taxes paid from it, etc. Why add unnecessary complications to your family finance activities? topic_title: Should I setup a Joint bank account to pay Joint mortgage with girlfriend?
content:
If the plan is to split the mortgage (and presumably other associated house expenses) between you, but otherwise keep your money separate, then having a "joint" account for this purpose likely makes sense.

This is the arrangement I struck with my girlfriend (now wife): we have a joint account which I use to pay joint bills, and every month I send her a statement showing how much is being spent for what and how much we each need to contribute to keep things going for another month. We don't divide things exactly 50-50; we go by "ability to pay" which is based on proportional difference in salary times an equity multiplier.

This wouldn't necessarily be right for everyone but it works for us as DINKs. Some may say this is extra complexity, and it does add some, but it also means that there's rarely any conflict. If one of us wants to spend on something personal (a spa treatment, a gambling trip to Vegas, giving money to ne'er-do-well relatives, etc.) then we don't have to argue about whether it's necessary, so long as we'll still both be able to cover our share of running the household.

topic_title: How do you negotiate rent price?
content:
If your rent was $1,000 a month in 2016, then at a 5% increase per year, I’d be expecting to receive about $1,275 per month here after 5 years, and that’s irrespective of local market competitiveness. I don’t believe in raising rents every year on good, stable tenants, as one month of vacancy costs more than than a year’s worth of 5% rent increases. On the same token, though, it is inarguable that my costs as a landlord have risen some since 2016 so I’m probably this year or next looking to at the very least narrow that gap. I don’t mind being below market but that doesn’t mean I’ve made a commitment never to increase prices.

That said, I’d feel very comfortable asking you to move from $1,000 to $1,110/mo at this point and if you move out, I’ll make back my vacancy cost in a little less than six months of new market rate. That’s my viewpoint and framework for looking at this; I’d be happy to keep you on but I also will make more money if you leave, especially in this environment.

Your only leverage here is to move out unless you are somehow going to directly offset a maintenance cost, like keeping the lawn mowed. And even then I like to keep the professionals doing professional stuff and you just paying me rent. Then I don’t have to yell at you about not paying rent and not mowing the yard.

I don’t believe in raising rents every year on good, stable tenants, as one month of vacancy costs more than than a year’s worth of 5% rent increases. On the same token, though, it is inarguable that my costs as a landlord have risen some since 2016 so I’m probably this year or next looking to at the very least narrow that gap. I don’t mind being below market but that doesn’t mean I’ve made a commitment never to increase prices.

That said, I’d feel very comfortable asking you to move from $1,000 to $1,110/mo at this point and if you move out, I’ll make back my vacancy cost in a little less than six months of new market rate. That’s my viewpoint and framework for looking at this; I’d be happy to keep you on but I also will make more money if you leave, especially in this environment.

Your only leverage here is to move out unless you are somehow going to directly offset a maintenance cost, like keeping the lawn mowed. And even then I like to keep the professionals doing professional stuff and you just paying me rent. Then I don’t have to yell at you about not paying rent and not mowing the yard.
There is no backyard. I live in an apt. So far in 5 years no rent increase is a good deal with discount promo price right?
It's an incredible deal. And it makes it worth shaking your head at the proposed rent increase, whatever it may be, it if even comes, and asking, "wow, this is really going to stretch my budget. Would we perhaps be able to work something out on this? I can't really afford to pay more than I've been paying." Then see what the answer is.

But remember, you have no leverage. As I mentioned before, after 5 years below market without increases, your rent is significantly under what he could get from a new tenant. In fact he has room to go under market for a new tenant and still give himself a raise by booting you. When he would make more money even if you left, that's a situation you do not control. You paying on time only goes so far, because everyone ought to pay on time and frankly most folks do. (It's a myth that good tenants are hard to find. Bad ones are easier to find than they should be, but it's not like someone who pays rent monthly is a one in a million sort of customer.) And when I start seeing that my one-month vacancy cost (i.e., missing out on $1,000 rent because I didn't agree to let you pay less and you moved out; an amount made up by collecting $275 more from a new tenant in 3.6 months) is less than 6 months of a rent increase, I start thinking the odds are in my favor to begin raising rates. (This is why I'm not a big fan of $20-50/mo increases; they just piss the tenant off, are not meaningful increases in income for me, encourage you to move earlier than you might, and it takes a lot of months of a small increase to pay off a vacancy I had because I raised rates and made someone look for a house.)
So what would be a good leverage for a renter?

If your rent was $1,000 a month in 2016, then at a 5% increase per year, I’d be expecting to receive about $1,275 per month here after 5 years, and that’s irrespective of local market competitiveness. I don’t believe in raising rents every year on good, stable tenants, as one month of vacancy costs more than than a year’s worth of 5% rent increases. That’s my viewpoint and framework for looking at this; I’d be happy to keep you on but I also will make more money if you leave, especially in this environment.

Your only leverage here is to move out unless you are somehow going to directly offset a maintenance cost, like keeping the lawn mowed. Most seem like landlords here. I also want to hear from a renters perspective.
I am renting in Arlington, VA. My current lease will expire in the end of February 2022, and pretty soon I'll know my new rent amount. In the mean time, in the Washington, DC sub-reddit, people lament about rent increases of $1,000/month and more. Many of these increases compensate for special bonus rates tenants received during COVID. Also, landlords are trying to compensate for the losses during the eviction moratorium in D.C., which will end in the end of 2021. This reading indicates that rental prices will be going up and by high amounts.

On the other hand, if telework continues even as COVID subsides, people will be moving from expensive urban areas to cheaper remote areas and possibly buying their own homes. This will reduce rental occupancy. Another factor is that if some delinquent tenants are evicted in January, other landlords may not want them either. The city will hopefully find something for them, but rental occupancy overall may go down. Finally, rents usually go down in winter when fewer people are moving. If your rent is expiring in winter, you may get a lower increase.

In preparation to negotiations, look for comparable rental units on apartments.com or zillow.com. Consider locations, sizes, amenities, and the general sense of occupancy in various buildings--as well as prices. That will give you an idea of fair rent for your apartment. If, after the rent increase, you will be paying 10% less than the best place you could find on the market stay where you are.

======================================================
Indicate whether this is the first year you are eligible to make the simplified foreign tax limitation election for alternative minimum tax (AMT) purposes. Once you make this election, it applies to all later tax years and can't be changed unless you obtain IRS consent.

Choose the best answer below.

Simplified Limitation Election Eligibility:
1) First year I am eligible for the election
2) I made the election in 2020 or a previous year
3) I chose NOT to use the election in 2020 or a previous year
======================================================

From what I've read in other threads, one way to tell whether I have used the simplified limitation election in a previous year is if I only had one 1116 form for each category of income (as opposed to two 1116 forms, where one is for my regular taxes and the other's for my AMT) for that year.

However, this doesn't answer the question of whether I was ELIGIBLE for the election in previous years, which is part of Turbotax's question. How can I figure this out?

Does having only one 1116 form for each category of income necessarily mean that I was eligible for the election in that tax year? Isn't there also some criteria that needs to be meant with regards to AMT?

topic_title: How do I determine if this is the first year I'm eligible for the simplified foreign tax limitation election?
content:
archurisk wrote:
Sat Mar 05, 2022 5:41 pm
From what I've read in other threads, one way to tell whether I have used the simplified limitation election in a previous year is if I only had one 1116 form for each category of income (as opposed to two 1116 forms, where one is for my regular taxes and the other's for my AMT) for that year.

However, this doesn't answer the question of whether I was ELIGIBLE for the election in previous years, which is part of Turbotax's question. How can I figure this out?

Does having only one 1116 form for each category of income necessarily mean that I was eligible for the election in that tax year? Isn't there also some criteria that needs to be meant with regards to AMT?
I don't think it necessarily means that. If you have just the regular 1116 (per category) and you didn't file AMT/6251, then you weren't eligible for the SLE. The question of eligibility only comes up if you need to calculate AMT in the first place, correct?

Looking at the 6251 instructions for Simplified Limitation Election:
You may elect to use a simplified section 904 limitation to figure your AMTFTC. If you do, when figuring your AMTFTC, you will use the same net foreign source income for AMT that you used for regular tax. (The amount on line 17 of your AMT Form 1116 will be the same as the amount on line 17 of your regular tax Form 1116.) You must make the election for the first tax year after 1997 for which you claim an AMTFTC. If you don’t make the election for that year, you may not make it for a later year. Once made, the election applies to all later tax years and may be revoked only with IRS consent.
I added the underlining above as it seems important. It seems to say that if line 17 is the same on both 1116 and AMT 1116 (that is, for each income category pair of 1116/AMT 1116), then you elected Simplified Limitation.

topic_title: How do I determine if this is the first year I'm eligible for the simplified foreign tax limitation election?
content:
Links to cited source material at the end.

I've been trying to figure this out myself. Here's my current thinking. I might not be right.

TLDR; look for one or more 1116s for AMT. If you used TT look for "Alt Min Tax -- [income category]" centered at the top. Compare 1116 regular vs the 1116 Alt Min for lines 17. If lines 17 are the same you used the simplified AMT FTC election. See below for details.

The usual issue with the FTC is that you can only get a credit for the amount of foreign tax * (foreign income / worldwide income). That is the I.R.C. 904(a) limitation. ("The total amount of the [FTC] ... shall not exceed the same proportion of the tax against which such credit is taken which the taxpayer’s taxable income from sources without the United States (but not in excess of the taxpayer’s entire taxable income) bears to his entire taxable income for the same taxable year.")

The $300/$600 thing is not relevant to the simplified AMT FTC (unless you had less than foreign tax of <= $300/$600 and only from passive income). See I.R.C. 904(j). It says in that case you can elect that the 904(a) limit does not apply.

Now if you have more than $300/$600 of foreign tax or foreign non investment income or don't elect into 904(j) then the 904(a) limit applies and you need to fill out one or more 1116s to figure out that limit and how much FTC you get.

The complication is in that case you might also have an AMT issue. If so, what is your AMT FTC?

I.R.C. 59(a) describes the AMT FTC calculation. Remember this is done separately for each 1116 type of income. The default numerator (your foreign income) is basically your AMTI and not your regular taxable income. This might require complicated allocations and calculations for foreign income to adjust for AMT preferences and the like.

I.R.C. 59(a)(3) however allows you to elect to use a "simplified section 904 limitation." If you do so in any 1116 used for AMT you do not calculate your separate foreign AMTI but rather use your regular taxable income from the regular tax 1116 for that category of income.

I.R.C. 59(a)(3)(B)(i) only allows you to make this election "for the ... first ... year [after 1997] ... for which the taxpayer claims the [AMT FTC]." (ii) says once made the election applies to all future years and you need IRS permission to revoke the election.

An IRS internal powerpoint says "that no specific statement of election is required. The election is evidenced simply by
filing the Form 6251 using the foreign source income numbers from the Form 1116 instead
of computing foreign source AMTI." (page 17 of the link below).

This next bit makes my head hurt, so please correct me if I'm missing something. The simplified election can hurt you if you are subject to AMT but have no complicated AMTI calcs. Why? Because regular taxable income has the standard/and some(?) itemized deductions removed, but AMTI does not. So for the 1116 simplified AMT FTC your income in the simplified calc is less (because the regular tax deductions have been subtracted) but the denominator is larger (worldwide AMTI). E.g. if you used actual AMTI not taxable income the numerator would be larger and the faction of foreign tax allowed as a credit by the 904(a)/59(a)(1),(2) calcs would larger.

https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/59
https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/904
https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-utl/int_p_062.pdf [especially pages 16-18]

topic_title: How do I determine if this is the first year I'm eligible for the simplified foreign tax limitation election?
content:
To be totally clear: in order to figure out if it's the first year that you're eligible for the AMT FTC look at your PDF 1040s (or your tax file if your software still works) for each year since 1998. The first year you find an 1116 for the AMT is the year you will get your answer per my reply above. If you have no 1116 AMT previous and you do this year, then it is your first year.

Why 1997? Because the change to the IRC adding section 59(a)(3) happened in 1997 and was effective 1/1/1998. See Sec. 1103(a),(b) (PDF page 179) of https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STA ... -Pg788.pdf

alice_springs wrote:
Mon Apr 18, 2022 6:32 pm
Would I be able to take FEHB with me by "bridging" my previous years where I had FEHB with the final 2 or 3 years of FEHB, to qualify for the 5-year rule ? Would I still meet the 5-year rule if I postponed the immediate retirement annuity ?

From: https://www.opm.gov/faqs/topic/insure/i ... e98408fd0e
I know you have to be enrolled in the FEHB Program for 5 years before retirement to continue coverage in retirement. Does previous enrollment count towards 5 years or does it have to be five continuous years? This employee was enrolled for about two years in the past and wonders if this counts towards the 5 years.

It depends. FEHB law requires a retiring employee to be covered under FEHB for the 5 years of service immediately before retirement or, if less than 5 years, for all service since the employee’s first opportunity to enroll in FEHB. In the above situation, the employee’s 2 years of previous FEHB coverage would count toward his 5-year FEHB coverage requirement if he had a break in service and therefore could not have had FEHB as an employee.

For example: The employee was enrolled in FEHB from 2003-2005 and then separated from Federal employment. He returned to Federal service in 2010 and was enrolled in FEHB from 2010-2013. The 2 years he was enrolled in FEHB from 2003-2005 along with the 3 years he was enrolled in FEHB from 2010-2013 enable him to meet the 5-year coverage requirement.

However, if the employee had been continuously employed and eligible for FEHB, but had a break in his FEHB coverage from 2003-2009 because he cancelled his FEHB, he would have to begin the 5-year period over again.

Victoria
That makes a lot of sense. Does hospitalization coverage come with you in MRA plus 10 retirement?

For the past couple years, I have been using GEHA-Hiigh in conjunction with Medicare Part B. In 2021, GEHA-High reimbursed me $600; in 2022 the reimbursement increased to $800.

In other Bogleheads discussions, you will find Federal retirees who choose NOT to get Medicare Part B, because:
(1) They would have to pay high IRMAA premiums (additional Medicare Part B premiums on top of the standard ones)
(2) They consider FEHB providing adequate coverage in conjunction with Medicare Part A, which is free

My responses to these arguments:
(1) I don't have IRMAA premiums because I am delaying Social Security and using the time between retiring and collecting Social Security to do Roth conversions. I calculate my annual Roth conversions to keep my income just under the IRMAA threshold.
(2) Even if FEHB + Medicare Part A is adequate, I don't want to take chances with my coverage. I want to have some safety margin for the circumstances I can't currently foresee.

Many Bogleheads use Blue Cross Blue Shield Basic in conjunction with Medicare Part B, which is cheaper than GEHA-High and also reimburses $800/year of the Medicare Part B cost. I prefer GEHA, because BCBS-Basic does not have out-of-network coverage.

Victoria

I am not sure if it came across clearly: the $800 reimbursement is for the BCBS-Basic and GEHA-High Medicare Part B premiums. The healthcare expenses are separate.

In 2022, if your AGI in 2020 was less than $91k, you pay $170.10/month for Medicare Part B. That's $2,041.20/year, of which you get $800 reimbursed by BCBS-Basic or GEHA-High.

If your 2020 AGI were between $91k and $114k, in 2022, you would be paying $238.10/month for Medicare Part B.
If your 2020 AGI were between $114k and $142k, in 2022, you would be paying $340.20/month for Medicare Part B.
If your 2020 AGI were between $142k and $170k, in 2022, you would be paying $442.30/month for Medicare Part B.
If your 2020 AGI were between $170k and $500k, in 2022, you would be paying $544.30/month for Medicare Part B.
If your 2020 AGI were between $500k and infinity, in 2022, you would be paying $578.30/month for Medicare Part B.

These increased premia are called Income Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts (IRMAA). See https://www.medicare.gov/your-medicare- ... rt-b-costs for the details. You can see why some Federal retirees with very high incomes in retirement are reluctant to pay these high amounts for Medicare Part B.

Note that your Medicare Part B cost in a given year depends on your income 2 years prior.

Victoria

Medicare Part A is for hospitalization, and it's free.
Medicare Part B is for doctor visits and various services, and that's what the prices I listed above are for.
Note that Medicare Part D is for pharmaceuticals, but the FEHB is considered a qualifying plan and there is no need for Federal retirees to enroll in Part D. If you decide to enroll in Part D later, there is no penalty.

Withdrawing from traditional IRA is your income that increases your AGI.
Converting from traditional IRA to Roth IRA is likewise your income that increases your AGI.
Required Minimum Distributions (RMD) from traditional IRA are also income that increase the AGI.

Shortly before I retired, I created a spreadsheet where I estimated how much I will need to convert to Roth every year between the beginning of my retirement and the age of 70 when I would start Social Security. While most people do similar calculations to stay within certain tax brackets, my calculations aimed to do maximum conversions while not exceeding the lowest (pre-IRMAA) Medicare Part B band.

Note that the IRMAA income limits change every year. Normally, they increase.

Victoria

There is no one-size-all for these decisions.

While VictoriaF has decided to convert all of her tax-deferred money to a Roth, most people (couples) wouldn’t go that far. In other words, they’d have a balance between tax-deferred, Roths, and taxable accounts.

One “for instance” — if you have plans to move into a Continuing Care Retirement Community in the future, a substantial part of the deposit and monthly fees can be written off on your taxes as a medical expense. So if you draw from a Traditional IRA or TSP account to pay those expenses, you may have no or minimal taxes during your CCRC years. Ultimately, all this planning is just determining the odds as to how your life is going to play out and making decisions accordingly. The certainty is another reason to hedge your bets.

I know you have to be enrolled in the FEHB Program for 5 years before retirement to continue coverage in retirement. Does previous enrollment count towards 5 years or does it have to be five continuous years? This employee was enrolled for about two years in the past and wonders if this counts towards the 5 years.

It depends. FEHB law requires a retiring employee to be covered under FEHB for the 5 years of service immediately before retirement or, if less than 5 years, for all service since the employee’s first opportunity to enroll in FEHB. In the above situation, the employee’s 2 years of previous FEHB coverage would count toward his 5-year FEHB coverage requirement if he had a break in service and therefore could not have had FEHB as an employee.

For example: The employee was enrolled in FEHB from 2003-2005 and then separated from Federal employment. He returned to Federal service in 2010 and was enrolled in FEHB from 2010-2013. The 2 years he was enrolled in FEHB from 2003-2005 along with the 3 years he was enrolled in FEHB from 2010-2013 enable him to meet the 5-year coverage requirement.

However, if the employee had been continuously employed and eligible for FEHB, but had a break in his FEHB coverage from 2003-2009 because he cancelled his FEHB, he would have to begin the 5-year period over again.

<...>

I know you have to be enrolled in the FEHB Program for 5 years before retirement to continue coverage in retirement. Does previous enrollment count towards 5 years or does it have to be five continuous years? This employee was enrolled for about two years in the past and wonders if this counts towards the 5 years.

It depends. FEHB law requires a retiring employee to be covered under FEHB for the 5 years of service immediately before retirement or, if less than 5 years, for all service since the employee’s first opportunity to enroll in FEHB. In the above situation, the employee’s 2 years of previous FEHB coverage would count toward his 5-year FEHB coverage requirement if he had a break in service and therefore could not have had FEHB as an employee.

For example: The employee was enrolled in FEHB from 2003-2005 and then separated from Federal employment. He returned to Federal service in 2010 and was enrolled in FEHB from 2010-2013. The 2 years he was enrolled in FEHB from 2003-2005 along with the 3 years he was enrolled in FEHB from 2010-2013 enable him to meet the 5-year coverage requirement.

However, if the employee had been continuously employed and eligible for FEHB, but had a break in his FEHB coverage from 2003-2009 because he cancelled his FEHB, he would have to begin the 5-year period over again.

topic_title: FEHB in Retirement & 5-year Rule
content:
With federal retirement under the FERS your main options are:
Immediate Retirement:
62 + 5 yrs of service
60 + 20
MRA + 30

Early retirement is:
MRA + 10
If you retire at the MRA with at least 10, but less than 30 years of service, your benefit will be reduced by 5 percent a year for each year you are under 62, unless you have 20 years of service and your benefit starts when you reach age 60 or later.
Postponed retirement is at MRA + 10 years. In that case you delay collecting the pension and health benefits until age 62 or 60 (if 20+ yrs of service).

Most anything else is deferred retirement and in that case you are not eligible to receive health benefits.

In order to get the health benefits you need to have health insurance for 5 yrs. The years don't have to be continuous if you had left and returned.

And postponed retirement, once eligible can continue if you return. For example you could leave with MRA+20, then return for a year or two and then retire and carry health benefits as long as you were eligible when you left the previous time and continued to retain them when you returned to service.

I've left service twice before and on the last one qualified for a postponed retirement which I had planned to start at 60. I didn't anticipate returning for a 3rd time. This time after reaching 60 (with 20+ yrs) I plan to take an immediate retirement and start collecting my pension/health.

You do have to be on top of things. While the HR/Retirement office at my agency is pretty good, they do make mistakes. I know when I returned and asked for retirement estimates they initially said I was not eligible for the health insurance. I pointed out my previous service and they quickly agreed.

As others mentioned, I feel a bit more comfortable retiring directly from an agency than going through OPM although ultimately OPM processes all retirement paperwork. And it is processed very inefficiently since to my knowledge, it has yet to be computerized and things are done manually.

From your comments:
Previous 15+ years of federal employment, during which time always enrolled under FEHB

Stopped work in 2019 due to family issues and later the pandemic delayed my desire to return

Dipped my toe back into the job market again; found a fed job with WFH late last year (2021). Enrolled in FEHB at first opportunity

Would like to work for another 2-3 years and retire at my MRA (56 + change).

If possible, would like to retire on an "immediate annuity" but postpone receiving the annuity until age 62 to get the FERS annuity with no reduction as well as FEHB.
You can postponed it IF you leave at MRA+10 years of service and receive the pension and health insurance (assuming you had it 5 consecutive years) at 62, or at 60 if you end up with 20+ years of service. And if you had 30 yrs of service at MRA you can collect it immediately.

Personally while i know people taking the 5% per year penalty, I wouldn't do that since it seems excessive. In my case or I guess anyone who has 20+ years of service, if you left prior to age 60 and 20 yrs, my penalty is calculated from age 62 even though 60 is my retirement age. An extreme example would be if I retired one day before my 60th birthday my penalty would be 10% permanent reduction in my pension since it is calculated from 62 and not 60.

I might work elsewhere once I start the pension or just retire.

topic_title: FEHB in Retirement & 5-year Rule
content:
Maybe a bit off topic but another thing to consider with pensions, or at least how the FERS one is valued, is your high 3. If you leave the government and then go back much later in life, you will likely be making a much higher salary and that will greatly boost your pension. As a rough example when I left the government after 15 yrs several decades ago, my pension would have been something like $10,000 per year. When I returned at a much higher salary (largely just due to inflation but also at a higher grade) after just 3 years my pension went up more than 3X. Probably roughly equivalent to saving another $500K.

So going back for 5 yrs to get the health insurance at 60 is a plus and so is boosting the COLA pension. Now I will admit each time I've returned, my tolerance with government work gets lower and lower.

A big factor is what your finances and budget look like.

How much you are willing and able to work on cars yourself is also be big factor since if you can do a lot of carwork yourself it may make sense to keep cars a lot longer. I do very little car work myself so I tend to replace a car long before it dies just because taking an older car into a mechanic can be expensive.

You mentioned that you would need a car loan so one thing to watch out for is that if you buy a car with a car loan then by the time that car is paid off then the Highlander will be about due to be replaced so you may need another car loan then.

For driving around town something like a Corolla, Civic, or Elantra might be adequate and the lowest cost new car option if you can find one without a huge markup.
