If you need a car loan to buy a replacement for the Highlander then I would also get a short car loan for that and when it is paid off then try to pay cash for future cars

There is no reason that you need to replace the Highlander now but you might look at what you can sell it for anyway since used cars car getting such high prices now. You can get a quote in the Carmax or Carvana websites in just a few minutes. You might be surprised with what you can sell it for.

It is possible that the used Highlander could be selling at such a high price that doing something with it might make sense.

I did that last year for a three year old Corolla and they were offering me more than I had paid for it.

My needs had changed somewhat and I was able to find a decent deal on a Subaru Forester so I ended up replacing the Corolla with a Forester for a reasonable amount. I likely would not have done that if I was not able to get such a high price for the Corolla. This gave me a car with better safety features and a full warranty. Foresters are now in very short supply so that would likely not make sense today.

If your Highlander is a higher trim level then you might be able to sell it for enough to buy a new Corolla/Civic/Elantra for cash but you would need to research that.

If you could pay cash for a car like that you would still need a second car. Since I bought a Subaru last year I sort of follow the Subaru car market and it sounds like new Outbacks are not in too short of supply and you might be able to find a low trim level Outback (or some other car) for the low $30's without a long wait and they have some low interest rate loans available. You might also be able to buy a low trim level Outback and only have one shorter car loan that would be similar to your new lease payment.

The advantage of this that you would have two cars that should last you ten+ years and when they need to be replaced you should have been able to save up pay cash for future cars then.

That was just thinking out loud and my preference is to not have cars that are much over 10 year sold and I could do something like that with my budget, but that might not be right for you. One of the keys with this though would be that once you get both cars paid off that you actually same up to pay cash for future cars.

If the latter, I think you've answered your own question: You don't need a new car every 6 months, and that's a very expensive way to "own" a car, as the leases never end and worse, you keep starting a new lease with a newer car, and thus usually higher monthly payments. At least with a lease held to the end of the term, the monthly costs are at least a few years "old", and probably noticeably less than a brand new model of the same car leased "now". Plus building up to ... not needing to make those lease payments at all. (Separate question is whether to lease or buy; someone else mentioned getting off the monthly car payment treadmill...)

[If so, why don't they provide the car or at the least, offer highly subsidized lease terms?]

That would only be the situation the first time you switch to a "buy". After that, you'd presumably keep the car(s) for several years, and thus have some trade-in value whenever you did decide to trade it for something newer.
Otherwise, you are paying those "inflated car prices" all the time, year in, year out, with a newer, probably more expensive car twice a year...

content:
Hi,

I was enrolled in a High Deductible Medical Plan with UHC through my employer in 2021. I'm 36 yo and based in CA. I went for my annual physical exam in December after an insurance rep (who I had called for a different issue) advised me to go for one as it is covered under my plan. I was not able to get an appointment with my PCP and so booked an appointment with a nurse practitioner at the same provider. The provider is in-network with the insurance. The NP did my physical and ordered some lab tests. I did not request any of the tests myself. I just assumed that the tests are part of physical exam for everybody . Some of the lab tests were the same as for my last physical in 2019. I was on a PPO plan then and didn't pay anything for the tests. The only thing I told the NP was that I had lost a few pounds this year. To which he asked that it's a matter of concern if I lost them in a short period. I confirmed that it was not in a short time span. I got the lab tests the next day from a lab under the same medical facility in another location.

Fast forward 2 weeks and I got a bill from the hospital that I owe a balance of ~$700 for 3 of the 5 tests. I called my medical insurance helpline and the rep said that some of the tests are not considered as preventative but diagnostic. The tests in question are Metabolic Panel (CPT 80053), TSH (CPT 84443) and Lipid Panel (CPT 80061). I spoke to someone at hospital's billing department who told me to contact the doctor's office to see if they can change the codes of the tests. I'm not sure if they will/can change the codes of the lab tests. I have also contacted my company's benefits team.
Additionally, I noticed today that there is a Negative Plan Discount applied in the claim.

Posting my anecdote because my "unexpected charges for a preventative annual physical while on a High Deductible Insurance Plan" experience seems to have finally been resolved! Good luck to you - there is hope!

April 2021: Preventative annual physical. Blood taken on a 2nd visit (the next day) because they didn't have anyone on duty to take blood when I was there.
June 2021: received two bills: $25 from doctor's office for blood draw, $400 from LabCorp for blood tests.

Asked (through doctor's office web portal) what was up with the charges - it was supposed to be a "fully covered" preventative physical.

Doctor's office said the $25 was because the blood draw was on a separate visit. I replied that they didn't communicate the charge when they asked me to come back for the blood draw. The rep nicely dropped the $25 charge.

For the $400 bill from LabCorp, the doctor's office said to contact my insurance (AETNA).

After about 2 hours of hold music and transfers through AETNA's phone systems, an AETNA rep told me to contact the Doctor's office to have the tests "recoded" as preventative. AETNA couldn't tell me "the right codes" so I felt like I wasn't going to make progress when I went back to Doctor.

Sent request to Doctor's office with the vague request to have blood tests "recoded as preventative." I got a response saying they were going to update the billing and they'd get back to me, but they never did.

September 2021: I got a new bill from LabCorp that had been reduced to $100. I asked the Doctor's web portal why the bill went to $100 (and not $0). I got a response saying they'd investigate and get back to me.

November 2021: Doctor's office emailed me with a request for me to send a picture of the LabCorp bill. I sent it right back and they said they'd get back to me -- never heard anything back.

Today: Put my invoice into LabCorp's portal to find out current charges and it says nothing is due!

I guess patience is a virtue?

Will read this thread to find the right way to make sure a 'fully covered' preventative annual physical is actually "fully covered."

Given that you're asking the question in your 30s, it seems at least plausible that you might be considering retiring early with a Roth conversion ladder. Note that the ladder itself will provide you with some shielding after the first five tax years since you'll start rapidly accumulating conversion basis. It's fairly common to not fully draw your entire annual conversion amounts, so once you get five tax years past your first conversion you'll have penalty-free conversion basis as well as the original contribution basis.

So in addition to not needing to worry post-59.5, you might really only need to be moderately concerned for the first 4-5 calendar years of your early retirement if you're running a Roth ladder.

Many people on boglehead's have reported that this tax visualizer tool helps them with questions like yours. I've put in what I think your situation is (but I didn't know your filing status, although I guessed "single" since you mentioned itemizing at $15K). You can change any of the numbers, filing status, etc. and play with it.

https://engaging-data.com/tax-brackets/ ... 0&cg=13000

Some notes:

- Put anything that is taxed like wages in the "regular wage income" slot - e.g., wages, interest, non-qualified dividends, short term capital gains, Roth conversions, etc.
-Put anything that is taxed like long term capital gains - i.e. long term capital gains and qualified dividends - in the "capital gain income slot.
- Ordinary dividends = qualified ordinary dividends + non-qualified ordinary dividends, so ... since you show ordinary dividends = $1000 and qualified dividends = $1000, that would appear to be the *same* $1000 and doesn't need to appear on your list twice
-The tool shows standard deduction only, but that is the same place on the graphic that your $15K itemized deduction would go. In other words, long term capital gain + qualified dividend income "floats on top" of the ordinary income. And the deduction is drained off the bottom of the pile, so it is taken off of ordinary income first.

topic_title: Buying too much house?
content:
I think it is a choice, but a perfectly reasonable one.

Just taking a step back, I think it is important to remember every year of your life counts as much as any other. At your age, so much of what you are doing is about building for the future, and that is fine because you have lots of good opportunities to do that. But still, those years count as much as any.

OK, so if in the next long set of years you will enjoy your life more in this house than a cheaper alternative, that is a completely rational thing to want. Of course you have to balance that goal against the also rational goal of wanting to build for the future, but you are already thinking in those terms. And the particular balance point you are looking at is a reasonable one. Just as for other people, it would be reasonable to spend less on a house. You are in the range where it really depends on what you personally value.

And as a final thought--I think it is useful to sort of pick your thing or things. Like, we like a nice house and we like to travel to other countries. We do not much care about the cars we drive, having a local vacation home, or stuff like that. So, we maybe devoted more of our "every year counts" budget to our house and vacations, whereas someone else would have devoted more to cars and a vacation home. But that is all OK.

I think where people get in trouble is insisting on having the best of everything, particularly when defined in relation to what other people around them might have. Like, I want cars as nice as the Joneses have, and a house as nice as the Garcias, and vacations as nice as the Chans, and the same private K-12 and colleges as the O'Briens, and on and on. I actually think it is OK if you have friends or relatives who share your passions, and then you trade information and even sometimes make similar purchases and such . . . but then that is being done because of that shared passion. topic_title: How to Handle Inherited Accounts at Fidelity?
content:

(1) my MIL is the named beneficiary of my FIL’s traditional IRA. Both MIL and FIL are/were of RMD age. Fidelity says the IRA must be moved into an Inherited IRA for my MIL. Is this two-account process correct?

(2) my MIL and FIL have a joint Taxable account at Fidelity with equity and bond mutual funds. They live in a non-community property state. Fidelity says MIL must open a new Taxable account in her name into which they will move half the joint account’s holdings and step up the cost basis to the date-of-death market value. Fidelity will also retitle the existing joint account (which has the remaining half of the holdings) into my MIL’s name. After the step-up, MIL can then combine the two accounts. Is this two-account process correct?

With respect to her inherited IRA, transfer of the balance to an inherited IRA for her is standard procedure. At this point MIL has a choice to make:
1) DIstribute the year of death RMD from the inherited IRA as a code 4 death distribution OR
2) Elect to assume ownership of the inherited IRA and defer the year of death RMD to much later in 2022 and after she has assumed ownership. At that time she could combine the year of death RMD of FIL with her own 2022 RMD based on her own IRA's 12/31/2021 balance.

Either order is acceptable, and the choice is mainly driven by when she wants to take these RMDs. She has until year end 2022 for both of them.

Assumption of ownership and creation of the inherited IRA by Fido should be done as non reportable direct transfers to avoid running afoul of the one rollover limit which applies equally to her inherited IRA and her own IRAs for a 12 month period. She also needs to be mindful of any basis inherited from his IRA, and if so she would document it on her own Form 8606, and she must name her own beneficiaries ASAP.

For the joint taxable account, Fidelity must be dividing the assets to ease the math of the basis adjustment of this qualified joint property. However, this also creates the illusion that she could just keep these 2 accounts separate and sell only the basis adjusted shares for little gain. It does not work like that. Actually, half the value of each share, and not 100% of the value of half the shares is the proper basis adjustment, so she might as well combine those accounts and each share would have the same adjusted basis to determine her LT cap gain when she sells. Each of her shares is treated as a LT holding due to them being inherited.

topic_title: How to Handle Inherited Accounts at Fidelity?
content:
I'm sure others who have gone through this will chime in.
Fidelity generally provides good advice about the handling of accounts after death. They have no reason to make it more complicated than it should be. If they advise something that you question, you should ask the person you are speaking with to confirm it. I'm sure they will do that to make you more comfortable.

Your question 2 sounds about right. That seems like a reasonable way to give half the assets step-up basis.

Question 1 is a bit of a mystery. Ordinarily, when an IRA is inherited by a non-spouse, it certainly becomes a separate "inherited IRA" account and RMD's must be taken. However, I would think that an IRA inherited by a spouse can be merged into the spouse's IRA, then future RMD's would be based on the total value of that account. Of course, the decedent's account is required to take the 2022 RMD however the process is done. It would surprise me that merging the decedent's IRA into the spouse's IRA is a two-step process, going first through an "inherited IRA." However, I have no specific knowledge of this process and would trust Fidelity's advice in this regard after first confirming with them that this is the correct procedure. Like I said before, Fidelity has no reason to make the process more complicated than it needs to be. Just be sure they fully understand that the desired end result is a merged IRA - not an inherited IRA.

content:

My wife received two different sets of payments that require her to pay SE tax- 1) Schedule C independent contractor income and 2) Clergy income working for an employer (which is subject to SECA even when doing W2 work). H&R Block is taking her Schedule C income plus the little bit of REIT income from our Vanguard holdings, subtracting the total SE deductible amount, then multiplying by 0.2 to get the QBI deduction. Which of these is correct?

topic_title: QBI- which SE deductible amount?
content:
The purpose of QBI is to make business income rates (Schedule C, partnership, etc.) competitive with the new lower corporate rates. I don't see how W2 income qualifies.

Clergy income from weddings, funerals, and the like goes on Schedule C and does qualify.

See IRS Pub 517 on Clergy. If there is a housing allowance, it gets allocated between Schedule C and W2 income.

The purpose of having clergy pay SECA is to avoid taxing the church directly, although it still pays the employer portion for the church secretary, janitor, etc.

Clergy have a great opportunity to reduce taxes if they work it correctly with the employer. Three types of money from employer:
* reimbursement (accountable mileage reimbursement, professional books, conference attendance, etc.) -- not taxed

* housing allowance, which includes utilities (SECA, but not federal income tax)

* salary (SECA and federal income tax)

If you are willing to spend a few $, an Excel spreadsheet that I use a lot is Pralana Gold, very full featured, handles all kinds of accounts, has a strong tax package, different withdrawal strategies, historical and Monte Carlo results, and is super flexible. Allows you to model tax efficient asset placement (bonds in IRA, stocks elsewhere). You test Roth conversions year by year based on tax brackets & IRMAA tiers (if you were younger, you could also test FPL multiples that are applicable for ACA premium credits)

I've heard of some people that use MaxiFi - web based, costs somewhat more than Pralana Gold, I have not used it, so can't speak to the features.

This site offers a free spreadsheet called the Retiree Portfolio Model. Its Roth conversions are entirely manual, there are some limitations on account types and tax treatment. I found its input less intuitive than the other tools I've tried, but that's a personal opinion.

I-orp.com is free and can get you familiar with the kinds of trade-offs going on, though some folks have trouble with it. It is based on finding a steady amount you can spend each year. I think one reason some folks don't like it is since it's an auto-optimizer, it will do seemingly extreme things to get even a small return. That also means that even a small input error may drive the result. I would treat this only as a starting point and check with another tool since it's hard to see what's driving the answer.

Before you fire up any calculator, you need to think through objectives and think about what cases you want to study-
-If you are giving away your money, Roth conversions may not make sense.
-If you have heirs to plan for, particularly ones in higher brackets than yourselves, Roths may be more valuable.
-If you have lots of money and may run into estate taxes, you don't want your heirs to pay estate taxes on IRA money that has its own income tax liability for heirs.
-You may want to limit conversions to reserve some IRA money for possible long term care.
-If you think taxes will change, say due to you moving or the expiration in 2026 of the TCJA, that would affect the answer.
-Expected differences in lifespan between spouses affects the answer. Lots of years between spouses passing is lots of years of higher tax rates.

Since 27.5 year straight-line depreciation has been required for rental property sine 1986, only the very few property owners who placed their rental property in service prior to 1986 can possibly have "additional depreciation" subject to ordinary income recapture. Instead, the portion of the gain taxed as an Unrecaptured Sec 1250 Gain subject to a maximum 25% tax rate will be the lessor of the amount of depreciation allowable and the amount allowed (actually deducted), per Sec 1250(b)(3).

You didn’t acquire the property through a like-kind exchange in the past 5 years.
You aren’t subject to the expatriate tax.
You owned the home for 2 of the last 5 years and lived in the home for 2 (1 if you become disabled) of the last 5 years leading up to the date of the sale.

content:
I understand that the position of the IRS on the issue is:
A taxpayer must reduce the basis of property by the depreciation allowed or allowable, whichever is greater. Depreciation allowed is depreciation that a taxpayer actually deducted (from which it received a tax benefit) whereas depreciation that is allowable is depreciation that a taxpayer was entitled to deduct that may not have been deducted. If a taxpayer did not claim depreciation it was entitled to deduct, the basis of the property must still be reduced by the full amount of depreciation allowable. On the other hand, if a taxpayer deducted more depreciation than it should have, the property basis must be reduced by any amount deducted from which a tax benefit (the depreciation allowed) was received.
I believe that the language from 1250 (b)(3) is meant to address those cases where the IRS disallowed depreciation to the extent the amount actually allowed was less than the amount allowable. I do not interpret that to apply in cases where a taxpayer never rook a depreciation deduction. This approach is consistent with all of the IRS guidance I have seen as well as being consistent with the general principles of adjusted basis for rental real estate.

As I mentioned, I am always interested in reviewing any contrary or clarifying authority.

I understand that the position of the IRS on the issue is:
A taxpayer must reduce the basis of property by the depreciation allowed or allowable, whichever is greater. Depreciation allowed is depreciation that a taxpayer actually deducted (from which it received a tax benefit) whereas depreciation that is allowable is depreciation that a taxpayer was entitled to deduct that may not have been deducted. If a taxpayer did not claim depreciation it was entitled to deduct, the basis of the property must still be reduced by the full amount of depreciation allowable. On the other hand, if a taxpayer deducted more depreciation than it should have, the property basis must be reduced by any amount deducted from which a tax benefit (the depreciation allowed) was received.
I believe that the language from 1250 (b)(3) is meant to address those cases where the IRS disallowed depreciation to the extent the amount actually allowed was less than the amount allowable. I do not interpret that to apply in cases where a taxpayer never rook a depreciation deduction. This approach is consistent with all of the IRS guidance I have seen as well as being consistent with the general principles of adjusted basis for rental real estate.

As I mentioned, I am always interested in reviewing any contrary or clarifying authority.
I think the nuance that he's making is that yes, the basis is lowered by the depreciation allowable, but the unrecaptured gain is just the depreciation allowed. Ie you still pay LTCG on the unclaimed depreciation, just not the special 25% rate.
This is correct. The basis of the real estate property will always be adjusted by depreciation whether or not it was taken on a return. 1250 does not include depreciation that was not taken on a return as subject to 25% recapture. That is different than 1245 (machinery and other PP&E), which includes in recapture depreciation allowed (i.e., taken) or allowable (not taken).

He has no debt, owns his home that we will sell for 420,000, owns a vehicle that he wants to give to me and we will buy his new home for 250,000.

He has
$1,300,000 in a traditional IRA, invested in about 10 different positions all older than one year- I would like to convert his single stocks to mutual funds but worry about timing and tax issues
$500,000 High yield savings account
$2,600 monthly Social Security

I plan to pay all of his bills going forwards and he is fine with me taking over his assets, but I don't know if this is something I should transfer formally or just basically manage it until the day he passes (hopefully a long time from now)

Not sure if it matters but we are in a good position financially so there is no urgent issues for us related to expenses or needing access to his assets.

Any guidance or place to start here? Maybe there is a wiki or useful thread.

Thanks a bunch!
There are no tax issues for manipulating assets in his IRA.

He will need to start taking distributions from the IRA when he's 72. To reduce the tax impact, you might consider shifting where he's holding safe assets. He can slow the growth of the IRA by owning more bonds there and using some of his cash to buy stock funds in taxable.

Vanguard has an ultrashort bond fund or even a money-market fund would work.

As he needs to draw cash, he can sell stocks in taxable and swap bonds for stocks in the IRA to keep the desired asset allocation.

Just don't hold the same stuff on both taxable and the IRA. That complicates the ability to recognize capital losses. (E.g. don't have a S&P 500 fund in both.)

topic_title: Possible switch to employer offering 403b and 457
content:
You can contribute to both a 403b, 457b, and also an HSA all at once (assuming you have a high-deductible health plan that qualifies). Since you said that you're currently able to put in $27.8k between a 401k and HSA, it seems like you may have a family. Assuming an income of $100k per your example, maxing a 403b as well as a 457b would drop your adjusted-gross-income to $59k. This is low enough that you can also contribute to a traditional IRA and further lower you AGI if you so choose. You can contribute $6k to your traditional IRA and $6k to spouse's if you're married.

Lowering AGI can allow you to qualify for various credits such as the earned income tax credit, savers credit, premium tax credit, etc. I think if you post a bit more information about family (whether you're married or not, number of kids, whether you have a working spouse), it would be helpful in answering some of your questions.

As others have said, you should also know the difference between a governmental and non-governmental 457 so that you can make an informed decision as to whether or not you'd like to make use of that account.

topic_title: Mortgage: 30 yr, 15 yr, or cash?
content:
Hey, I am a first-time home-buyer looking to purchase a roughly $750k home with a bit over $1M in liquid assets (retirement excluded). I'm pretty new to the mortgage game, so I'm looking for some general advice and pointers to some reliable resources. I don't anticipate any other major expenses and any money I don't spend will likely go into a simple three-index-fund allocation. I have no intentions of moving, but I could imagine things change over the course of the years.

It seems like putting $600k (assuming 20%) into the stock market over 30 years should far surpass the amount of interest paid. I guess it would be nice to have my home paid off, but not worth the money I could make. A 15-year mortgage seems like a middle ground; not sure why I should consider that.

Other things on my mind: escrow or not, percentage down, timing, and shopping for rates. Thank you for any thoughts.

topic_title: Mortgage: 30 yr, 15 yr, or cash?
content:
Keep it simple.

Find the house and make specific decisions like this later.

Just don’t pay points. Get lender credits to cover all, much, or some of your costs. Move in. Decide later if you want a 15 or a 30 or to own it out right. Refinance into the loan you want or pay it off.

Good luck. Don’t miss the forest for the trees.

topic_title: Mortgage: 30 yr, 15 yr, or cash?
content:
How much would it cost you to liquidate the assets? If most of that $1M is in stock, then you want to minimize capital gains, which is likely a reason to put the minimum 20% down.

Otherwise, what matters is the trade-off between risk and return; see Paying down loans versus investing on the wiki. Taking out a smaller mortgage gives you a low but risk-free return, comparable to investing in bonds. You can have a higher expected return, with more risk, by buying stocks.

I would prefer a 15-year mortgage, though. The advantage is that you pay interest at a lower rate while paying down the mortgage, so it costs you less to hold the money in stocks. And given the size of your portfolio, you don't have a liquidity issue.

I made the same decisions myself. I had enough stock to pay cash for my home in 2013, but I would have had a huge capital gain, so I put 20% down and took out a 15-year mortgage. The rate was so low, and deductible on both federal and state tax, that it didn't make sense for me to pay extra...

until rates dropped. In 2020, low-risk bonds earned less than my after-tax mortgage rate, and I could liquidate cash without a tax cost, so I paid it off. (I sold stock in my taxable account for a capital loss, then moved an equal amount from bonds to stock in my employer plan, so I effectively sold bonds to pay off the mortgage.)

topic_title: Mortgage: 30 yr, 15 yr, or cash?
content:
It's fair to assume that equities will, over a long enough time horizon, outperform the interest paid on your mortgage.

It's also fair to assume that the interest you pay on your mortgage consists of (mostly and effectively) taxable dollars, whereas investment gains in non-retirement accounts will eventually be (mostly and effectively) taxable, even if at a favorable (i.e. LTCG/QD) rate. Furthermore, the interest rate you pay on your mortgage will likely far exceed the dividends received from any investment-grade fixed income you hold in said taxable portfolio to offset the risk of holding equities.

I think it is a question of risk tolerance (both practical and emotional) more than anything. Most of the answers you receive will likely (and rightly) point out that, based on past performance, the math works out in favor of investing. On the other hand, I would ask you to consider whether, having a paid off house, you would still choose to take out a mortgage simply to invest the proceeds. If not, why not? The answer to that should help you determine your risk tolerance.

Personally, I paid off the house. So far, the math has not been in my favor. On the other hand, I no longer deal with the mortgage servicing industry, so my sleep quality has improved markedly.

But if you have some months where money is tight, it'll make things a little easier. YMMV.

One oddity of mortgages is the different types (30y, 15y, ARMs) don't move in lock-and-step. One day, one might be better than the others; and a few weeks later, another type type might be more attractive. This is especially true right now with Fed activity.

For example, I've been looking for a house for the last 6 weeks. 30yr were looking the most attractive. However, we put an offer this past week and the ARMs/30yr spread widen. My quotes came in at 30y 3.25% vs 7y/6m ARM 2.325% (no points, 20% down). Offer fell through, but the ARM was clearly more attractive than it had been.

I wouldn't get hung on a specific product right now. Find your house, get the offer accepted, get a couple quotes from your lender, and then come back here with the options.

Happy hunting.

content:
This was cut from a similar thread where I calculated the return you must get from the lower payments to break even. Understand this math and I think you will get why the 15 year loan is a great option.

Assume a $100,000 loan. (Bankrate.com mortgage and savings calculators, deposit a .01 to start)

15 year at 2.15 percent payment of $782. The 30 year loan rate at 2.75 percent is $540 or $242 less. With this loan you will still owe $60,000 15 years out. See payment schedule.

What safe rate do you need to covert $242 per month in savings to grow to $60,000 in 15 years? 4.2 percent. That is a very good essentially risk free after tax tax free rate. A "satisfactory return. " (and if todays rates are used, this safe return will be closer to 5 percent). (In other words, if you put money in the bank, you would need a 6 + percent return (ish) that is taxed to get this equivalent -- that is very hard to find).

Of course, this depends on your ability to pay such loans / liquidity. This does not appear to be an issue.

I would add that this allows you to slowly increase your equity exposure and reduce bond exposure in other accounts over time as your "safe" asset of home equity rises.

I agree with others that keeping some money invested is the right action (i.e. take a mortgage) ... unless you are near retirement or something.

Finally, FWIW, IMHO the 30 year and the 15 year mortgage are the most competitively price mortgages available (best for consumers). The 10, 20 and 25 year equivalent loans are generally not as competitively priced and likely should be avoided.

I pretty much agree with everyone above me with regards to 30, 15, cash, stay invested, big down payment, small down payment, keep it simple, etc.

Another tiny but possible consideration is asset protection from anything other than divorce. In California, the location of the OP according to the forum profile, the house is protected from creditors up to $600k in a forced sale or bankruptcy. The money in ERISA accounts (401k, governmental 457, 403b) are protected from creditors in unlimited amounts. Up to low $1M in an IRA are supposedly protected, but the protection in California is actually weak because it depends on the judge deciding what is necessary for bare minimum survival support of the household. The money in taxable accounts can be levied by judgment creditors, so no asset protection at all. With adequate insurance, debt aversion, and lack of personal financial crisis, this is just a tiny consideration. Most people never get sued, but you see lawsuits flying left and right sometimes for big money when you randomly look at California superior court dockets.

I throw it out there because I think the optimal decision is probably some sort of middle ground between a low, risk-free return with asset protection and full risk in the 3-fund portfolio without asset protection in taxable accounts.

content:
We don’t know your location, age, and how long you think you’ll stay in your first house — all of which are relevant factors. At these ultra-low interest rates, I’d personally do a 30 year mortgage, especially if you live in a non-recourse state (e.g., California). With a 30 year mortgage you’ll likely do much better in the stock market long-term if you stay in the house long-term. Of course, you have to be disciplined to actually save the difference between the 15 and 30 years payments in the stock market, which many people aren’t. If you think you’re likely to over-spend, then a 15-year mortgage will force you into a smaller house and force you to save (in an illiquid asset).

Another thing to factor is career risk. For example, if you lose your job or if you might want to take some career risks that put your salary at risk in the short term (e.g., start a business, go to a commissioned sales role, etc.), then the lower required payment of the 30-year will be nice. You’d also have more liquid cushion with income volatility if you’re diligent about saving the delta in mortgage payments.

Good luck!

SantaClaraSurfer wrote:

The best advice I've received regarding age and tech is this mindset:

"You are either working or retired. There is no young and old. If you are working in tech, your age is irrelevant. Blend in, hone your skills, be a valuable resource to your team. Collaborate. Land projects."

This mindset is not saying that there are not headwinds, obstacles, or impacts.

This mindset IS saying that if you focus on your age as a barrier, especially if you focus on your age relative to others, you are quite possibly not going to be able to accurately see and assess the landscape, including your opportunities.
Are you on LinkedIn? (Do you have an upgraded account there with full access?) Do you network? That's a great way to get things moving.

With regards to doing well in interviews and landing a role that you want and would enjoy, these were my takeaways from my most recent experience:

1. Be focused on the road ahead and not the rearview mirror

2. Interviews are not for oversharing about your extensive qualifications, they are about showing, verbally and non verbally, that you have the skills and mindset to be an asset to the team

3. Demonstrating a flexible, problem-solving, collaborative mindset is key (not just talking about it, or dropping it into your interview as a buzzword)

4. It is completely possible for a 50 year old with 4 years of "key experience" for a role to be beat out on the grounds of experience by a 28 year old whose skills and 6 years of experience more directly match the role. Plenty of young people have direct relevant experience.

5. In general, stopping to ask or check in with your interviewer if you answered their question is never a bad idea. Ditto for sharing your thinking/thought process, and showing genuine enthusiasm and curiosity.


I can't speak directly to highly-technical, engineering-only roles out of direct experience, but I am adjacent to them in the work I do, and I see plenty of people of all ages, as well.

I started my job search by setting my LinkedIn status to "open to new opportunities" and then started replying to those recruiter messages. This led to a bunch of interviews and multiple offers.

If you're a software engineer, can you pass a coding interview? I did a bunch of those; I actually find them kind of fun. One of my coding interviewers said that he could really see the difference between me and the typical 20-something that he often interviews: I was able to formulate a clear algorithm in my head and just code it up. content:
maulermark wrote:

I submitted my resume for a couple of jobs thinking I'd be a shoe-in for the positions with my experience. I never got a callback for either job which surprised me. I did list over 25 years of experience on my resume which easily met the qualifications for the jobs. I thought that companies were desperate for employees???
As a 30-year-old SWE, I will say your ideas about how to get a job are comically outdated, and I mean that in the nicest way possible. There's a hilarious video from The Onion on YouTube titled "Report: 95% of Grandfathers Got Job By Walking Right Up And Just Asking". It was full of stereotypes about Baby Boomers telling Millennials how to get jobs. That was uploaded in 2014. You may as well have gotten your last job in Ancient Mesopotamia.

One of the first hurdles you would need to clear is understanding just how many automated and basic screens and filters there are in company hiring processes these days. I once had a recruiter send my resume back because I had listed "experience with mercurial"; he wanted me to change it to "experience with git" because that's what the company used. That's like getting hung up on a sales candidate because they prefer to drink cold water and the office water dispenser only has warm. After I was laid off from my first job as part of a restructuring, I took a year off to work on some personal projects before applying for jobs again. I applied for many dozens of jobs and didn't get a single reply. Someone suggested I stretch the truth about my employment history, which I didn't like doing because it felt unnecessarily dishonest, but I eventually listed my personal projects as work experience so my resume wouldn't show a gap in work history, and I almost immediately got an interview and job offer, suggesting I was just being automatically filtered out based on that. Later, I was involved with interviewing candidates for my team, and I remember there being so much unhelpful tension between our manager and recruiters. The recruiter would send a bunch of candidates who were probably very capable and trainable, but our manager wanted someone with direct experience on products like ours, even though it's really not necessary as long as someone has general software development skills in C and Linux. Eventually, our manager narrowed it down to 1 candidate, who subsequently accepted an offer somewhere else, and then our upper management rescinded our approval to hire a new member, so that position never got filled. I applied for another job once which was not only directly analogous to my product experience in the past, but I had very solid experience using a very particular debugging tool which is very niche in the industry and not many people know to this day but is present in the product for which I was applying, and I never heard from them. I was told later by friends that you basically need a referral to get a job there, and while I have certainly known people who went on to work there, I am very much anti-butt-kissing, so the idea of reaching out to old contacts knowing it's just for a referral makes me sick to my core, even though I know that's literally how most people get jobs these days.

My point is that it's waaaaay more of a numbers and networking game than the last time you changed jobs. You can't be the grandfather who just walked up and asked for the job because all it took was gumption and a strong handshake. You need to tick a bunch of really silly boxes and keywords on your resume to make it past the initial automated screens, get a referral if possible, brush up on newer tech skills (although after 33 years, I'd imagine you'd want to stick to familiar territory), and hope that ageism takes a back seat. I've heard of some older engineers not having such difficult interviews after a certain point, but that will certainly vary by company, and is probably more so the case in legacy tech companies that might struggle to find younger engineers with the required skill sets.

content:
Is there ageism, yes, but less than a lot of people here seem to think. Will it affect you? It depends, on what jobs you’re trying to get and what you’ve been doing for the past 33 years. I got hired at a FAANG in my 50’s. There are loads of companies out there that are dying to get some adults in the room. But they have expectations that you will have learned something in the course of getting the grey hair. They don’t want someone who’s just had the same couple of years of experience again and again. The question you need to ask yourself is what skills do you have that would make you worth what a new company would have to pay someone with your experience? If you can answer that question and sell yourself, you can get another job, and you shouldn’t have to take a big pay cut to do it.

That said, you’re planning on retiring in a year or less, and the alternative is to either go part time, or start a new job? I think you forget exactly how much work the first year at a new job is. I wouldn’t change jobs unless I was planning on staying long enough to make all that work pay off.

If you hate your job and are within a year of retirement, can you just quit now?

Does age discrimination really exist in Tech?
I'm 45 and have worked in IT for 21 years. I work for a state government and I have not seen any ageism where I work. I have many co-workers that are older than me.

I think in IT that the biggest reason why there are few people that are 40+ is because it is a profession where you can easily get burned out, and most people just don't want to do it long term.

You have to continually learn information that will be obsolete in five years or less. You have to be on-call a lot, and often work odd-hours to in order to perform maintenance when it will impact as few people as possible. Sometimes you have to work during holidays as that is the only time a system might not be in use. It can also be a very stressful occupation as downtime is not tolerated. Systems that go down can impact thousands of people. Its a lot of responsibility and you are not going to get paid a huge amount. I only make $75k as an example.

It is a descent middle income career. Its not that great, but not horrible either.

content: My brother is looking for a new job (not tech), late 40's. He hired someone to polish his resume and linked-in profile. I'm 45 and have worked in IT for 21 years. I work for a state government and I have not seen any ageism where I work. I have many co-workers that are older than me.
I think it varies a lot by the company environment. Most of the ageism I hear about is either in really tech-centric places like Silicon Valley, or in businesses that only have a technical focus (FAANG, software and computer hardware companies, maybe startups too). I'm not sure it's all of them, but in some of them it may be true.

Step outside of that world, and there are millions of technical roles at non-tech companies, where age probably isn't a big deal at all. I spent the last 15 years doing tech work for what was mostly a gas and oil company, and they definitely showed no age bias. In my mid-40's I was one of the youngest on my team and a third of the IT staff was in their 50s or 60s. I now work for a state government entity, and I've got three people on my team of six who are literally eligible for retirement, but still going strong, engaged, capable, learning new things, etc.

Does that mean some companies might reject an older applicant out of hand? No. Does that mean the OP might have to work a little harder to find a place that's a good fit? Possibly. But options are out there, for sure. The industry isn't one big monolith, all the same everywhere.

Edited to add: though I would 100% recommend finding a new job before leaving the old one, just as good practice at any age, but especially if there's any doubt about re-hireability.

Nail, meet head. At this point my experience and "institutional knowledge" is definitely valuable to an employer, but I'd argue it's not more than twice as valuable (but my compensation says it is). This is ratcheted up in tech, which moves so fast. I have a difficult time understanding how this is characterized as just prejudice.
Personally, I feel the opposite -- in my early 40s, I feel that I am a much better software engineer than I was when I started in this industry fresh out of my PhD. I now have over a decade of experience writing production code and maintaining said code. I understand which problems are worth solving, and which are not. I have experience leading teams, both as tech lead and as manager. I know how to run projects, how to manage cross-team relationships, how to play politics (I wish I didn't have to, but this is the world we live in), etc. I now have a combination of deep technical knowledge and real-world experience that makes me very valuable to the right team. I feel I am well worth the 3-4x I'm paid now vs. when I started.

Nobody wants to admit this. But it’s true for a lot of people. It’s true for me. And it’s dumb to pretend it isn’t.

Of course there are some people that stay strong, stay up to date, maintain great drive, etc. But they are a very slim minority.

I will gladly hire anybody who can do the job. But if you’re like me, with lower drive, outdated skills, and slowing cognitive ability, I’m passing on you, and not because of your age, it’s because there are better candidates.

And if the candidates are equivalent in terms of qualifications, I’m taking the lower priced one every single time.
I guess I'm agreeing with you.

One reason I early retired at 55 is that I saw in myself a dwindling interest in learning new stuff, and I struggled with the constant change. The "kids" come in and soak it up. I was like that, and I was on my game for the first 25 years just killing it. Then one day it got stale.

So I left on my own terms, head held high, and I'm doing things today that require learning in a completely different field (carpentry). I guess in my case I had seen too many goat rodeos and needed to watch dog agility competition. It got stale. I also saw the inner workings of Megacorp, and that poisoned my mind.

I would actually hire a 50-something brand new to tech as long as they didn't expect to come in at a high level. They'd still be in learning mode, with sponges still ready to soak up.

In my area, there is no reason to interview most people. There are only less than 10 employers that provide the kind of experience that we are looking for. In any specific sub-area, everyone knows everyone with less than 3 degrees of separation. Hence, LinkedIn and social networking is the way to find the candidate.

As per experience verification, we know the employer, the kind of project and the specific project name that you have to work on and know in order to have any possibility of doing the job. So, someone that is not an insider would not have that specific information in the resume and know the right person.

In summary, we look at the resume, look for the key project and search via LinkedIn as to how we are connected to the candidate. We contact our social network and ask about the person. So, way before the interview, we would know whether we want to hire this person.

30 seconds to 2 minutes into an interview, we would know whether we want to hire the candidate.

content:
I'm still catching up on the entire thread, but wanted to add my 2 cents....

I would definitely agree that tech is a young persons game. I am in a very niche B2B sub-field of tech that's mostly dominated by a bunch of smaller midcap firms but even here I see most new software developers and quality engineers are younger. Folks >40 tend to be senior managers, technical architects or have lateraled over to non directly coding roles such as product, program and project managers. The "PM" roles in particular tend to be good options to pursue in your 40s and 50s (assuming you have the aptitude) as these tend to benefit more from experience and industry/product knowledge and not dependent as much on knowing all the latest development stacks.

What I did was move into one of those non-tech roles after 40, and I am working hard to get to at least leanFI by 50~52 so I don't have to make some of those hard decisions when I'm older.

As to changing jobs. I think its certainly still doable up to your 50s, but as a lot of folks mentioned it takes a lot more than just sending out a bunch of resumes. Past entry level it becomes about your network and who you know and all my job changes have come from personal referrals. I mad a big role and company change at 42 and got my first choice role after applying to just 3 companies, but all where personal referrals where I had somebody on the inside to go to bat for me.

randomguy,

Basic Econ 101,

Supply versus Demand.

If it is not a niche hire and the employer can train someone to do a specific job, the supply is bigger. If not, the employer has a limited supply and have to pay the market price for the limited supply.

KlangFool
It is more generalist versus specialist. The specialist is harder to replace but by the same token, you don't need many of them. The supply&demand curve cuts both ways. You do well in good times, but the bad times can be brutal/permanent. Take you for example. How many times have you told us you were unemployed for a year during your career prime? The generalist looking at 100 companies instead of 10 has a much better chance of finding one that is hiring. I know during the dot.com bust that every laid off coworker had a job within a month of looking. It was standard when the news of layoffs hit to get calls/emails from everyone you knew asking if you were ready for a change. And the big fear is that your speciality basically goes away/loses value when something new comes along.

A similiar thing happens as your move up the ranks. Lots of jobs for senior software developers. Not as many for architects and the like.

For a person coming back to tech after a 7 year break, they probably aren't going to be the specialist unless they pick some random tech for a weekend project and the demand for that tech blows up.

I think the best advice I ever heard on this matter was find a job at 45 that you think you can do for the next 15 years and hope you can ride it out. Getting hired after 50 isn't impossible but it does get harder. And keeping a job is much easier than getting a new one.

Realistically as a manager, it takes 6 months for someone to get 80% ramped in their job. I'm giving you at least four weeks of vacation a year; you're probably negotiating five or six, so there's another 3 months off. We're down to me expecting 27 months of real service from you...

I'm not saying it can't be done but it is an uphill battle. I think the above advice of grabbing a good fit at 45 and hanging on for dear life is a good one. content:
OP,

You have gotten quite a variety of responses, some from hiring managers like myself.

Given that you said that you were bored, and only applied to 2 jobs, I would make these
observations:

1) Bored at this stage of your career is not a good reason to jump to another job. Frustration
with people blocking you from getting work done would be a reason.
I suspect that you have run out of energy, and you would be better off staying where
you are for the few months, and then retire and do whatever you want. If you are bored at
work, make sure you have something not boring for retirement, because otherwise
retiring will only exacerbate the problem.

2) If you really want to switch jobs, applying to 2 jobs is not nearly enough. That is
dabbling. Nobody is that fantastic that they are the obvious choice for a position.
Also, different hiring managers hire differently. You may look better to one than another.

dboeger1 wrote:

One of the first hurdles you would need to clear is understanding just how many automated and basic screens and filters there are in company hiring processes these days. I once had a recruiter send my resume back because I had listed "experience with mercurial"; he wanted me to change it to "experience with git" because that's what the company used. That's like getting hung up on a sales candidate because they prefer to drink cold water and the office water dispenser only has warm. After I was laid off from my first job as part of a restructuring, I took a year off to work on some personal projects before applying for jobs again. I applied for many dozens of jobs and didn't get a single reply. Someone suggested I stretch the truth about my employment history, which I didn't like doing because it felt unnecessarily dishonest, but I eventually listed my personal projects as work experience so my resume wouldn't show a gap in work history, and I almost immediately got an interview and job offer, suggesting I was just being automatically filtered out based on that.
I worked at a top-tier tech company and was very involved in interviewing, and ... yeah. Hiring is hard, and most people think their time is too precious for it, so you end up with this vicious cycle of automation that filters out a bunch of candidates for truly stupid reasons. Every couple years someone would have the clever idea of using machine-learning to automate the process, and we'd have an epic throw-down about how stupid of an idea that was, but I'm pretty sure at this point they're using machine-learning to automate the process. So now you could submit two resumes which would be identical to a human reviewer, but one would get binned because the PDF-extraction code interacts badly with the machine-learning model. And probably in many cases it's all outsourced, so even if someone noticed the problem there's no avenue for fixing it.

As a human, I might look at someone and say "Man, taking a year and a half off of C++ programming to train for and compete in the Olympic marathon trials is awesome!" But a computer is going to look at that and toss it in the bin. Which is why your network is so important.

topic_title: How difficult is it to get a job in Tech if you are "older"?
content: Hmm.. I don't know. It depends. I've been in Tech for a long time and at an age when ageism should matter, but I am also more sharper than ever and able to accomplish a lot more than my 30 year old self. Part of that is because my 30 year old self didn't know how to build relationships, push the right buttons, know what the executives wanted, how a business functions, how to position technology offerings to align with all of that. Now I know how to do, and usually is able to zoom in on the crux of the solution. I am able to tell other engineers what they should do to make a solution successful. I guess there is value in that. Basically a lot of that is just project management skills along with fine understanding of technology. I have also learned new things all along, and re-invented myself as the tech shifted, being able to speak the new lingo and deliver solutions that meets the new tech helps. If you want to do the same job as the 30 year old then they can do it a lot better.

content:
I hate the job search process, which is probably why I stuck with a contract agency so long. Let them do that work; they're the experts on the market, and they have the connections and inside info. Sure I've gotten the occasional assignment in a not great environment, but there's always the next one. Kind of like college; buck up, you'll get a new professor next semester.

Now that I'm full-time in a place I love, I'm hoping to make it a home and ride it into retirement. It could end sooner than I hope, but hey, every day work is becoming more an option, less a necessity. The great aspect of that is when I sit down in the evening to try to learn something new, I don't spin my wheels trying to second-guess what skills I might need at that next job. I just focus on what will help me in my current one. Feels liberating.

topic_title: How difficult is it to get a job in Tech if you are "older"?
content: I am 45. Am a high school dropout, and started as a software engineer at 19. I knew about the ageism in the industry from day one, and had set a goal to retire at 50. I live in Silicon Valley and have worked for some of the largest companies in the world. I'm highly specialized in security. I lost my job a year ago after being unable to adapt to WFH during the pandemic. I have been unemployed for 9 out of the last 13 months - 4 were a short-term contract, the first time I have ever worked contract. I have no problem getting interviews, my calendar is full of them daily. None of them ever results in any offer. Companies never disclose the reason why they choose not to hire for legal reasons, so I'm in the dark as to why, but I have to believe that age is part of it. I wonder if some HR departments are just interviewing older candidates in order to check a box, without any intention of hiring them. Some companies don't even have the courtesy to get back at all with a no, even after 5 or even 7 rounds of interview. Our house is paid off and we are debt-free, but the cost of maintaining it is quite high and rising with rampant inflation. We also have costly health issues. Even though my husband and I don't have kids, we are simply not financially independent even with a $3.5M net worth. I'm giving another 4 months, until my 46th birthday, before giving up on this industry in the area altogether. I have no idea what other less expensive part of the world I might to retire to, though.

content:
I came into this thread expecting some interesting replies, but I did not expect the:

1) Blatant Ageism and Discrimination by our own members, or rationalizing ageism, or toeing the line of "Well its not good but lets be real when you hit 50/60, I mean you will probably just die any day now, etc.

2) Unethical Recruitment, Hiring, and "Friend of a Friend" ask and tell for new recruits (reaching out to people outside of an interview loop for feedback, potentially jeopardizing the candidate)

Etc.

Maybe this is because I'm from the West coast and was on all of the technology teams I have been on the past 15 years, not once have I or any of my close colleagues even on a small scale discriminated based on age, race, sex, identity, religion, etc. Every team and org I have been in has been a beautiful mixture of people across all the spectrums of life.

And those companies were all better for it.

I'm so disappointed in the things so many of you have written about this. One thing that really stood out was "I have a hard time looking at someone and asking them about the long term at 62", what the actual heck is that? My dad is in his 60's and is on his 3rd career, better than ever. I have extensive groups of friends in my field who are in their 50's, 60's, and 70's who are fit, chipper, flexible, dynamic, and hard-working. Do you people think that life just ends when you hit 50? What do you think happens when you hit 62, that you will just cease to have any aspirations, career objectives, and life goals at all? Atrocious.

Your age is just a number. Discriminating against how old someone is, is the ultimate window into a persons lack of perspective and empathy. We all have one thing in common, we all die. If we don't, we eventually do, and in marching towards that shared fate we all age.

If this was actionable as a thread/topic, the action is revealing how embedded different forms of active bias, unconscious bias, and discrimination are still in our society at large.

Just disappointed and mad.

For any of you who have ever experienced Ageism and blatant discrimination, or even sub-text-oriented "Cultural Fit" discrimination, please DM me and I will be happy to provide a list of companies that are great to work for.

Gosh I'm so mad just writing this.

topic_title: How difficult is it to get a job in Tech if you are "older"?
content: Ageism and inertia (perceived or real) can be significant issues in your situation in Tech so tread carefully. If you are in a very technical role or in-demand technology perhaps less so (doesn't have to be the latest can be older technologies where people have retired out). If you really want to find a new role you will need to market yourself (linked in, social media) and perhaps do things you might consider beneath you. While a new career/role could be rejuvenating for you there's no guarantee the role or situation will be any better and you would be more vulnerable with organizational, management changes that frequently occur. I would examine why you are unhappy in your current role and see if you could change that given your commitment to the company which is hopefully valued as such.

I don’t believe ageism is the problem. I think “you don’t have the relevant skills” is the problem. At least in my company, there is zero incentive to discriminate based on age. We don’t offer pensions, etc.

But to turn it around. Everybody is desperate to hire. We are all looking to hire people. Given all of that, and that we all want to make ever increasing piles of money, why would anybody discriminate based on age? And since everybody is convinced this is happening, why do so many people do this?

It makes no sense to me. If these folks claiming discrimination were great, they should be snapped up instantly. Actually, even if they’re a eage, they should get offers. But they’re not. So what is the reason that people making hiring decisions won’t hire these very experienced, very successor professionals when they are desperate to fill these positions? Do they just hate everybody over 40?

This is one of those times when a lot of factors get confounded together, some real and some maybe less so.

Older employees are believed to be more likely to have the following characteristics:
Expensive compared to younger employees. Total compensation for a 40-year old is expected to be more than for a 25-year old. Often a lot more.
On average willing to work fewer hours per week. Everyone might be at 40+, but the belief is that the younger folks will work more.
Less current (on average) than the younger employees. The younger folks just learned whatever is trendy. Maybe. The older folks were working getting actual products out the door that often do not use the latest trendy tech.
There may be a few more.

The older folks have no credible way of signaling that they are as cheap, current and willing to work long hours as the younger kids.

This tends to look like age discrimination because it DOES track age.

But there is more.

Imagine that you are 45 and willing to work for the same wages that a 25 year old. This is a problem for the hiring manager because if you are willing to work that cheaply then you clearly can't be very good!

The hiring manager often doesn't actually know that you have been successful. He/she knows that you claim to have been successful. The two are not the same. And the hiring manager also doesn't know that you WILL BE successful. It is harder to credibly show senior level skill/talent than it is to show junior level smarts and enthusiasm.

Finally, in a well run organization you will often find that while you do need/want senior folks around to ride herd over the junior folks you don't necessarily want the same number of 30-year vets as 2-year junior folks. You'll notice that the military has a lot fewer senior sergeants than it has privates. The reasoning is similar.

In short, the senior folks often have a difficult time SHOWING during the hiring process that they will be worth the 2x or 3x total compensation versus the junior folks. Combine this will many companies needing (or thinking they need) fewer senior folks than junior folks and ...

What a sobering thread. And this is in a booming economy! I am a 44-year old attorney and am determined to do a career change (I'm fine with losing money doing so). Tech is an interesting field for sure and I've thought about going back to school for computer science to become a software engineer. I have a lot of friends in the industry who acknowledge ageism but say there's always room for (halfway) talented people who keep their skills up to date. On the outside looking in, one question about tech always come to mind. I imagine even "old" SWEs (60+) who keep their skills up to date can add a lot of value. Given all the ageism alleged in the tech industry, why don't more SWEs start their own businesses around when ageism rears its head?
I moved to the SF Bay Area from the upper Midwest, and back in the 90's I knew a LOT of people who had gone west to make their grubstake, then moved back to setup a small contracting business and start a family. I knew enough of that to be a little nervous about whether I was following that path (because I _already_ had a small contracting business at the time), but this did seem like a pretty sensible approach to the ageism problem.

I think part of the problem is mindset. I decided to retire from tech in my late 40's because I simply stopped caring about the work. I truly enjoyed trying to get a 100-horsepower app to run on a 15-horsepower computing system. But these days people are writing things like Electron apps which trade off fit and polish and 3GB of memory and two CPU cores for the ability to cut a couple engineers from your team. I mean, sure, that works, but it's not skillful, it's just applying brute force to export your problem onto your user's pocketbook. Sometimes brute force is interesting to me, I find being able to wire 2500 machines together to make a productive cluster super compelling. But the obvious next step is wiring 25,000 machines together, then 250,000 machines, and now resources are too cheap to meter and engineers are wasting them, and that's kind of boring. Wiring together 93 third_party dependencies and deploying to a huge AWS cluster to create "Uber for coffee" or "Uber for dog waste" is really really really not interesting.

I guess at root I just lost my ability to tolerate foolishness [stronger word omitted]. And there is a LOT of foolishness in tech these days, both in terms of foolish implementations, and in terms of foolish products. The actual tech isn't that challenging to wrap my head around, but it IS challenging to wrap my head around the attitudes implicit in current tech work.

content:
I can't speak directly to the every nuance of the debate at this point, but my work history post age 40 does give me direct experience relevant to this topic and job seeking more broadly. And I want to make one thing really clear for the readers of this thread.

If you are reading this and your work years after 50 years old are crucial to your financial well being and future retirement, my advice is please, by all means, do NOT get discouraged or take the wrong message from this discussion.

You can and will find meaningful work after 40 and 50, even if you have to change roles, or start over again and look for work multiple times.

It IS possible to reboot, revamp your resume and LinkedIn and switch ladders/careers/paths. I've done this more than once, been hired on to new titles more than once, and my compensation has increased multiple times.

It IS possible to retrain, learn new skills, platforms, and terminology. This is the new normal. Everyone is doing this.

Is is NOT the end of the world to work other jobs while you reboot. I temped over 40. I worked as an office admin. I worked at a grocery store popular with mid-career job switchers. I've been the oldest person on my team multiple times. I've worked as a contractor, as a vendor, and as a full-time employee with great benefits, (and I highly recommend full time work.)

I've also worked with multiple coaches. 5 to be exact. Each one had strengths and weaknesses. None of them was perfect or had all the answers. Each one of them was worth every single penny.

Over the last decade and a half, I've probably applied to more than 300 positions, and interviewed with more than 100 hiring managers, recruiters and teams, and I've rebooted my area of focus three times.

Before I landed my current role in 2021, I made final round multiple times during the height of Covid, and missed out multiple times. Almost every garden variety mishap or miscommunication that might happen in this process, I've experienced. Dropped from Zoom calls, hiring managers drinking Big Gulps on camera, been kept waiting in a lobby for an hour, having the employer decide not to hire anyone and start over, and worst, for those over 50, been subject to behavioral interview techniques that are VERY hard to take seriously when you are 30 years removed from college.

And that's not to mention feeling like I did not perform at my best. Which happened a lot.

I am sure that in the midst of that I've experienced some negative outcomes due to perceptions about my age, or how I represented my age. I'm also sure I've received huge benefits of the doubt I shouldn't have been given at other times.

The bottom line is that I don't think that there's any way to do this, at any age, other than by brute force, personal resilience, flexibility and smarts.

The one thing I would recommend doing is making a list of the top 20 things you are looking for in your next role and stack ranking them from "Must Have" "Nice to Have" and "Don't want." This allows you to be clear about what you want going in.

The last two roles I've landed, I hit 19 out of 20 items.

The other thing I would recommend doing if you're in an active job hunt is grab your phone and make a voice memo recording after every single interview when it's fresh. That 2-4 minutes of information, names and nuances can be worth gold if you make the next round, and all you have to do is hit play and listen.

Finally, if you're reading this thread, need a job, and are mid-career and feeling lost and hopeless, I'd recommend this book. It's a very solid playbook to get things back on track.

This is one of those times when a lot of factors get confounded together, some real and some maybe less so.

Older employees are believed to be more likely to have the following characteristics:
Expensive compared to younger employees. Total compensation for a 40-year old is expected to be more than for a 25-year old. Often a lot more.
On average willing to work fewer hours per week. Everyone might be at 40+, but the belief is that the younger folks will work more.
Less current (on average) than the younger employees. The younger folks just learned whatever is trendy. Maybe. The older folks were working getting actual products out the door that often do not use the latest trendy tech.
There may be a few more.

The older folks have no credible way of signaling that they are as cheap, current and willing to work long hours as the younger kids.

This tends to look like age discrimination because it DOES track age.

But there is more.

Imagine that you are 45 and willing to work for the same wages that a 25 year old. This is a problem for the hiring manager because if you are willing to work that cheaply then you clearly can't be very good!

The hiring manager often doesn't actually know that you have been successful. He/she knows that you claim to have been successful. The two are not the same. And the hiring manager also doesn't know that you WILL BE successful. It is harder to credibly show senior level skill/talent than it is to show junior level smarts and enthusiasm.

Finally, in a well run organization you will often find that while you do need/want senior folks around to ride herd over the junior folks you don't necessarily want the same number of 30-year vets as 2-year junior folks. You'll notice that the military has a lot fewer senior sergeants than it has privates. The reasoning is similar.

In short, the senior folks often have a difficult time SHOWING during the hiring process that they will be worth the 2x or 3x total compensation versus the junior folks. Combine this will many companies needing (or thinking they need) fewer senior folks than junior folks and ...
No, this makes too much sense, much easier just to blame it on plain discrimination.

I absolutely expect that it will be more difficult for me to find a job (in my non-tech industry) when I hit 50 (in a decade) and this pretty much explains why I believe that...I do not characterize this as "ageism".

OP, I would suggest you do your darnedest to stick it out with current employer as long as you can possibly stomach it. Maybe you are just going through a rough patch and it's just a matter of time until a good project will come along to reinvigorate you?

I think you have so many things going in your favor with the seniority you have with current employer...even if you throttle down a little.

My point is to look in to these things before making a decision. Don't leave by simply walking away if you can get a nice windfall if they let you go.

I likewise need to ask about your original plan - of doing something else 3 days a week for up to 6 months. Why do that when you could sit tight with no additional effort and have the same monetary result in less time?

In any case, again, I think you have many things in your favor staying put instead of looking for a new job now. If you do find a new job, you're going to be low man on the totem pole. You're going to have to work harder during the honeymoon period to prove yourself, and as you've seen, there are going to be kids who are able to outperform you. You have seniority, you don't have to prove anything to anyone. Enjoy the benefits you've earned by sticking with that employer for 33 years.
