Since you asked, I'm through the list that's under the maintenance category in Quicken. The top two lines are payments of $3000 to a general contractor for multiple services.

That $6K to GC covers parts & labor for the following, except where noted .
- install new water softener 5ft away (water softener purchased separately by me)
paint new exterior pipe
- dispose of old water softener
- master bathroom
purchase and deliver new toilet
I chose one of the top rated toilets according to Consumer Reports, which cost $250, and am extremely pleased with it. It flushes much better than the old wallmount model. At least it's a normal unit now, and any parts needed to fix it is probably only a $10-20 part from Home depot/Lowe's in the future, not a big job that involves opening walls and floors. The 4 remaining wallmount toilets don't have enough clearance in front to replace them all with regular toilets. Maybe a very short model would fit in one of the 4, but I'm not sure it would be up to code.
remove & dispose of wallmount built-in toilet
install new 15A dedicated circuit for bidet and GFCI outlet
extract water/sewer lines for bidet and toilet
install new standard toilet
install Biobidet seat (purchased by me in 2020; $300 unit, does not appear in 2021 expenses)
patch / texture / repaint drywall
dispose of old toilet
- half bathroom
fix drywall around wallmount flush mechanism
install new 15A dedicated circuit for bidet and GFCI outlet
extract water/sewer lines for bidet
install Biobidet seat (purchased by me in 2020; $300 unit, does not appear in 2021 expenses)
patch / texture / repaint drywall
replace existing non-working GFCI outlet

Yes, the $6K GC bill is very expensive for mostly labor, but I really had little choice. One wallmount toilet couldn't be repaired due to lack of parts. There was a small water leak that was getting costly. Replacing with another wallmount toilet of similar make would have been $3K+ in parts alone. I had it replaced with a regular toilet, but it was a major PITA. Wall had to be opened to extract water lines for it. Floor had to be modified also to add waste pipe. Drywall had to be redone, repainted, retextured. II had tried to get this job done in 2020, but nobody would touch wallmount toilets. There are 5 of them in the house. Only one was leaking, fortunately. I went through a general contractor who coordinated things with plumbers, painter, drywall and tile people, and could get the entire job done, as opposed to just one piece of it. It was very expensive, but it actually got done without headaches and any contractors blaming each other. If the electrical work didn't have to be done, and one wall didn't have to be open in the half bathroom, the cost would have gone down by about $1500, so that portion of it is discretionary.
I had talked to several electricians before who didn't want to run the new circuits at all. One wanted to charge $500 just to run a wire across the bathroom to a shared circuit, even though the bidet unit needs 1500W and would have tripped the breaker. The guy the GC hired was very good, and found a way to run the new lines to the main panel and not the subpanels far away.

- We had multiple pocket doors that were off their tracks completely, and others that could no longer slide open. Cost to fix four of them : $3200. I went through the only company that claimed to be able to do this without having to damage walls. They have a lifetime company on the new tracks. The other companies would have cost about the same, but would have had to open the walls and redo some framing, drywall, and paint; and no warranty on the new tracks. We have 7 more pocket doors in the house, almost all in very good shape. I almost had a 5th door replaced, but decided to wait until it was truly required.

- Whole house water softener was dead and had to be replaced. Parts cost was $650 from Lowe's.

- One of two water heaters had to be replaced. That was almost $1500 just for labor. The 75 gallon unit was under warranty and part was fully covered.

- $750 for 3 calls with a useless plumber related to WH issue

- Audio system in the hot tub was a $750 repair. Covered under CC warranty, there is a corresponding income line for the claim payment. The expense still shows up under maintenance.

- A small strip of sidewalk had to be repaired as it is homeowner responsibility in my city, and they sent me a bill for it. Cost: $700. Would have been - $800, but the contractor they used kept missing their deadlines, and city gave me a $100 refund on the permit fee.

- $700 for 9 wireless doorbells from 1-800-doorbell that actually reach across the entire property, both indoors and outdoors. The old system did not. One might consider this discretionary. I don't think of it that way, given issues with an important Fedex package being sent back on a month-long trip after doorbell wasn't heard several times.

- three Enphase M215 solar micro-inverters were failing and had to be replaced. Parts were covered under warranty. Labor was not. Cost : $500. I delay this repair for several years because I couldn't get anyone to do it for less than $1k before, and it didn't make economic sense at that price.

- HVAC regular maintenance was $425, for the two AC units and two furnaces. This was up from about $300 in previous years, and I didn't do it every year.

- Bar faucet failed. Parts alone was $350 from Amazon. This is a kitchen-style faucet.

- $300 to a handyman
Labor to replace reverse osmosis system in the bar that failed (it wasn't filters), replace a faucet in the lone bathroom downstairs that failed, fix some locks.

- $275 to Home Depot for another faucet and lock. Don't recall what location the faucet was for.

- $250 to a plumber to fix one of the two sinks in my master bathroom. Pipes underneath disintegrated and had to be replaced. Should have been about half, otherwise.

- another faucet from Lowe's for $200. I believe this was for the downstairs bathroom.

- Reverse osmosis system from Costco, $200

- $200 to an electrician to replace some broken electrical boxes on the side of the house

- $200 to fix a kitchen sink stoppage. This was an emergency after hours. Happened while my mother was visiting. Line had to be snaked quite far, over 100ft. No idea why that far, but it got unplugged.

- another $200 plumbing call that I didn't remember the reason for

Below $200, there are about 40 more expense lines, and they all really look like maintenance to me. Things like a garden hose, a rare double-turn pocket door lock, small dishwasher repair, filters for the hot tub, hot tub chemicals, water alarms for all the bathrooms & sinks, some LED tubes for the laundr roomy, water softener salt, water test kits for the hot tub, a new large deck box and labor to install it and haul the old broken one, dryer vent cleaning, I don't really see anything that shouldn't be there.

At best, you could probably say that $1500 of the GC work related to bidet seats was discretionary, and $700 for doorbells were improvements. But most of the $20k really is to keep existing systems in place working, not improvements.

The $4K that I categorized as improvements are related to installing surge protectors in each of the 4 electrical panels. Most of the money was spent on replacing some outlets with surge protector outlets. We have had some surges recently from the utilities that damaged equipment, I have a thread here on that. One some rare and very expensive quad breakers cost $270, and that was the only place I could find it nationwide. It was still a bargain versus replacing my main panel at $5k+ cost alone. There was some money spent on home automation also. A number of X10 switches, parts and labor. Maybe $600. Lots of small transactions to add up.

There is a still a ton of deferred maintenance. Example: One jetted tub in the bathroom downstairs failed. It's the electrical controls. No parts available. There are replacement kits. The local dealer wants $390 just for a trip charge to look at it. A part conversion kit is in the $1-2k range according to the manufacturer. No idea what install rate might be. I have not fixed it.

Hot tub cover got waterlogged during a storm. $800 parts and labor to fix and install on the lifter.

It's been 11.5 years since exterior was repainted. It's time for this year. In 2010, it cost $8k. I expect over $10k this time.

There are termites, and tenting is the best solution as the termites are multiple locations. I got bids between $3000 - $4000. We should have done this last year but delayed. We shouldn't delay more.

The list is quite long. Most really are maintenance items, not improvements.
14k property tax says you probably own a $1M+ house
It's assessed at about $1M due to Prop 13. Purchased for about $800k. Market value probably around $1.8M, but impossible to say unless it's put on the market and sells. Zillow says $1.8M - $2.2M.
$3kfor Gardner and housecleaner? We do that ourselves with dual full time jobs, kids and we volunteer in their youth programs too. You make the time.
We are back to cleaning ourselves again. We don't do gardening ourselves, and probably never will. To each their own.
How does one use $2000 of water? We pay bout $1k/yr of which $300 is a surcharge for a decade long water main replacement project. And my kids are NOT careful with water….
A combination of factors.
The base connection charge is $83 for 2 months, before consuming any water at all. So, $500 right there.
There was a small water leak in one toilet, also, which wasn't easy to fix (see above).
The rates are high due the California drought, with punitive rates when some consumption thresholds are exceeded, ie. it is a tiered rate.
San Jose Water is a for-profit company listed on the stock market.
There are various PUC and city taxes and other surcharges that apply on top of everything, which add roughly another 9%.

My most recent 2 months water bill includes the fix for the water leak, reduced irrigation from 7 days to 2 days a week, and only 30 minutes per day vs hours. Also includes 15 days with a 3rd person living in the house (mother was visiting from France). Usage went from 554 gallons/day down to 220 gallons/day. Previous bill as $366. Most recent bill is $197. I don't believe it's possible to go down much below that amount. Average American consumes about 100 gallon/water per day, and I believe that's for indoor consumption only. I don't think we can do a whole lot less than 220 gallons/day for 2 people + water used for landscaping. In summer, irrigation time will have to be a bit longer, and thus consumption and bill higher. Only real fix we could do to lower water consumption is to remove front, replace with native plants, and stop outdoor irrigation altogether.

I think realistically, with leak fixed and less outdoor watering, water bill will be down to about $1400 next year.
Your insurance is also extremely expensive… do you shop around? I pay 1800/yr for a pair of million dollar term policies we bought in our 30s. $1k for both cars (late model Japanese) for full boat 500k liability. 2M umbrella costs 400. Homeowners is 1400 (750k)
Neither of us can qualify for any life insurance except from employer. By age 30, both of us had HIV, and that's still an automatic decline regardless of being virally suppressed. We have policies converted/ported from employers. The premium increases every year. I think something like doubles every 5 years. This year is one of the major increases, for both of us. I will likely reduce the coverage amount, or drop it.

I shop around every single year for home/auto/umbrella. I recently switched from Safeco to Farmers, in December. For auto, the issue is that a lot of people in our zip code are uninsured. Our auto insurance rate nearly doubled when we moved from our previous one to this one 12 years ago. The rate I have is based on full coverage with the maximum deductible of $1000 on both cars, and perfect driving record. Only thing I could really do to lower the rate would be to move.

For home, only a few insurers will even touch it, because of the time to drive from the nearest fire station. That is not just for this house, but the neighborhood. There have been brush fires very close in recent years, especially 2020, which was never the case before. We almost had to evacuate that year, but didn't in the end.This is all due to climate change. The home insurance rate was $2373 with Safeco in 2013. I switched to Mercury a few years later due to rising premiums. Mercury wanted to raise the home policy rate to $4619 for 2022. I switched to Farmer's at $2803. The auto rate for 2022 is $2352 with Farmer's. Was going to be $2349 with Mercury.. Umbrella rate for 2022 is $784 for $2M. Umbrella was $414 with Mercury, half the price of Farmer's.
Insurance totals may have looked higher for 2021, because I switch insurer in mid-December, but hadn't received the refund from the previous insurer for all 3 policies that month. Some refunds happened in 2022. The auto premium isn't much different from what it was a decade ago. It's mainly the home premium that's massively increased, and umbrella too due to insurer change.

Obviously, I only know what I’ve seen, and what I’ve experienced. So I’m sure it’s not universal……

Companies constantly make decisions about how to allocate resources. Sometimes they do, it well, sometimes they screw it up. For me, I have pretty much free reign over compensation decisions for my very large group. I’m not the final decider, but I never get turned down.

At raise and bonus time, we make calculated bets as best we can to maintain our workforce. In a normal year, I have about 4% attrition. If I could waive a magic wand and give everybody a 25% raise, I’d probably still have 2% attrition. So we focus our compensation and bonuses on our most valuable people, our up-and-comers, and our perceived flight risks; and we hope that we keep most of them. The flip side of this, if you’re not in one of those groups, you’re getting less. And some of them will quit, but most of them won’t.

Also factoring in here, is that most people are absolutely terrible at understanding their actual value to the company, and how they are perceived. Dunning Krueger is real, but it’s more than that. A lot of people aren’t nearly as good as they think they are. Or they’re not nearly good as they used to be. And this is tech….. and a lot of people have much better relationships with their computers than they do with other human beings. So they are playing a game here that they just can’t comprehend…..

But also, some people are more valuable than they realize. And that is why, I advise everybody on these boards to get out there and do interviews every couple of years. Figure out what you are really worth in the market. Using that info, some of you will find out that you need to stay put, and some of you will find out that staying put is costing you a lot of money. And hopefully, you’ll also get a sense of how you need to change incrementally to stay relevant in the labor market.

But yeah, companies often times do stupid stuff. And some do cruel and unfair stuff. And some bosses are abusive and discriminatory. This is the world we are all in, and we each need to figure out for ourselves how to thrive in the world as it exists right now.

I'm currently leetcoding with an online group, and all the kids can run circles in leetcode around me (I'm now in mid 30s with no CS background), but I can absolutely crush them in system design. That way their algorithms and recruiter have no way to figure out how old I am, and on paper you will perpetually look like in your 30s-40s(maybe). Also, never use an up-to-date LinkedIn picture profile. I use mine from the 20s, and don't plan to change it ever.

3) My plan is also to move to M2 ASAP (managers of managers). I've read at that level there is no coding rounds.

content:
Tech is such a broad term that you'll need to be more specific. There's a huge difference between IT and coding.

Assuming you mean coding, because that's where age hits the hardest. If it's not for coding, disregard this. I

It's pretty rare in FAANG, AFAIK, if that's where you applied. I'd say your shots are about 0. They have way too many applicants to sacrifice in any way. They're selecting the best problem solvers and coders and will want young applicants with modern coding techniques and little bad habits from previous employers. They're that arrogant.

For 2nd tier software companies, like where I work, we hire people who are older but it's for senior positions and the fit has to be just about exact. If there is going to be any on-the-job training involved, it's just not worth it from a cost-perspective. Why would I hire an older person unless they have the exact experience or ability to do the job at that level on day 1? If I'm going to train up someone, it's going to be a younger coder with less salary demands and with a longer horizon for ROI on training. If I know that you're retiring soon, it either needs to be a perfect match, or you need to have experience in a very specific area that I wouldn't expect general coders to be able to perform.

In your particular case, I won't lie -- it will be pretty damn tough. Working at the same tech company for 33 years may sound like a positive in terms of loyalty, but it's actually a huge liability for you:

-By staying at one company, you've been doing things similarly for 33 years and haven't learned alternative techniques elsewhere or perhaps didn't need to learn additional skills that other companies would be expecting and you'd learn by bouncing around. Companies are expecting top talent to hop around every few years.
-Most coding tests nowadays revolve around puzzles needing to be solved by using algorithms, the ideal data structure, and optimized code -- things you learned in school. They're also going to expect you to code it in a modern, relevant language. If you haven't been putting in the work to stay current on the basics of algorithms or how to turn your puzzle solution from "a solution" to "the best solution," that's a long road ahead.

My advice, test the waters but don't get your hopes up. Keep your job if you need it and it's only for 2 years... I don't think the added stress of something new is going to help you. If it's really that boring/easy, take up a side job to get to retirement faster and keep yourself interested in working.

I wonder why not.

As it relates to the OP, perhaps it might be worth exploring opportunities in industries where a long tenure is considered a pro, not a con.
I think it may depend on what you consider the tech industry.

I work for a semiconductor equipment company (think ASML, Applied Material, LAM, KLA, ...) and our workforce tends to have a mix of younger kids and "lifers" as one of my co-workers called them. The lifers have often left the company once, so the term isn't totally literal, but the age distribution has a very bi-modal feel about it.

[And we do think we are in tech though we know we aren't a FAANG company]

I would not say that the lifers "throw out their decades of experience with the company as a badge of honor" but the company does not run only on folks who have been there for less than five years. And management tracks turnover at both the overall percentage level and also, for some employees, at the individual level. There is a list of senior folks that management really wants to keep, so there is some value seen here. Not *every* 50+ year old, but also management is fine losing a percentage of the 30-year-olds each year, too.

However, hiring into my employer with decades somewhere else *can* be an issue. For managers, especially in companies in our industry or related industries, age/experience can well be a plus. You worked at Cadence managing software teams for 15 years? Great! Come on in and lets talk!

Lots of experience managing a software team at Boeing might not be a plus. Probably depends on the details and also how well the resume presents the fit for us -- the first trick is to get through the initial resume filter to a phone screen so you do want to look at what *we* do and tailor your resume to what we care about [good advice for all ages].

Twenty years at Boeing as a programmer could be tough unless the developer had a skill match (partial is often enough) for the skills we care about that we believe take time to develop. Don't know git, but do know some other version control system? Fine. Don't know C++ and the hiring team uses it a lot? Problem. No, we don't/won't care that you have lots of experience with Ada. CUDA is a plus. Jovial is not.

But because we do have the "lifers" there is a willingness to at least consider the resumes of folks who haven't job-hopped every three years. But you (a) need to be mostly current in what we do [you don't have to be trendy in something we aren't using], and (b) have to have some story about how you are more than an expensive junior person. Examples of tech-lead where you help the team to be better are great! Examples of you using your experience and senior level skill to do things a junior person can't are great! Not having any of that and you are leaving your current company after 20+ years ... not so great.

But, yeah, I'd definitely recommend looking at companies that HAVE older workers. Those companies have already demonstrated a willingness to keep them and may well be open to hiring them as well.

IMHO, anyone working in IT/programming should make it a priority to be financially independent by 50. That is the only way to protect yourself.

I was able to pull it off by age 44 (which was in 2020) and my highest salary has been $75k and I was/am single. So I didn't have the benefit of a spouse to make it easier. I still work full time in IT (aws devops and systems administration). All this age discrimination stuff is not my concern.

Thats fine. The only think I took issue with was your implication (and apologies if you didnt intend to) that getting under 100k of annual expense is difficult to do for average middle class people. Your lifestyle is not average, or even close to it. Mine is not either. We are both above average, as are most people on this forum. Its *OK* to admit that.
I don't think I ever claimed anywhere to live a middle class lifestyle. However, the bay area in general is a very expensive place to live, even for middle class. The cost of living is estimated by this site to be about 2.4x the national average, and that's primarily driven by housing, which costs over 5x the national average.

https://www.bestplaces.net/cost_of_livi ... anta_clara

The majority of people in the Bay area who are middle class are paying either rent or a mortgage, which I don't have, and that can make many housing expenses just as high or higher than my $46k last year. Santa Clara is the #1 country by income in California, and #3 nationwide, but the expenses are commensurate with the income. A few searches I made have the median household income between $125,000 and $150,000; and average household income as high as $170,000. These are gross income numbers. I believe with our $103k of net expenses last year, we could make it work on the median income almost anywhere in that range without tapping our savings/investments, but wouldn't be saving anything additional for retirement near the bottom end of that range.

What I'm trying to say is that if we chose to downsize the house, but remained in the area to live a lifestyle closer to middle class, our overall expenses wouldn't enormously go down; at least, not by half. The average home price is listed in the site I mentioned as $1,395,000. If we sold the current home for $2M net and bought something at average price, we would have an extra $600k in the investment portfolio. The property tax would go up from $14k (based on current assessed value of $1M under Prop 13) to about $19k annually. Other home expenses would go down significantly, perhaps in half from $32k to $16k. So, the total housing expenses would go down from $46k to $35k/year. Total living expenses would go down from $103k to $94k.

The 30 year Firecalc success rate based on $103k expenses / $1.7M portfolio is 51%. 30 year for $94k expenses / $2.3M portfolio is $94%. So, this does make a pretty big difference.

topic_title: How difficult is it to get a job in Tech if you are "older"?
content:
Didn't work in the tech industry, but was in corporate life for 40 years. I climbed the ladder of management, but unfortunately the upper rungs were reserved for the children of the corporate officers, and each was groomed for a few years before being given the position. Notice I didn't say "earned" the position, because that's exactly how it was. Since I didn't like working in the office environment, being on the road handling clients and field staff was perfect for my situation. We went FI in 2014, and feathered the nest for the next eight years until opting to retire. I'd seen many "youth movement" hirings that resulted in them leaving in less than two years, while the veterans were overlooked and essentially taken for granted. Promoting from within was a fairy tale, and evoked gallows humor every time they went outside looking for the next "Rainmaker".

Get what you can out of this, but I would not resign out of boredom or spite. You have too much to lose. Given your age, I doubt your employer really cares all that much, and will be only too happy to show you the door if you announce your departure. Start a retirement budget, and see how well you can live it. Cobble together a financial plan given all of your resources and use a realistic SWR to determine it's feasiblity. When you hit the bricks, the reality of going it alone will become more clear and evident. Be ready for it.

topic_title: How difficult is it to get a job in Tech if you are "older"?
content:
Folks,

When you asked the wrong question, you would never get the right answer!

The correct question is

(A) Does your job and profession aged well?

Is your value increasing in your job when you work longer in the same job?

For example, the average career of an NFL running back is 4 years. Above 30 years old, the running back is disposable.

Ditto, if you are a software developer and the language that you use changes every 4 to 5 years, there are little carryover. Hence, years of experience helps some but not that great. But, if you are an IT Architect, years of experience helps.

Based on your answer to (A), you should plan your exit from your profession accordingly.

A quick and easy way to find out is to survey the age of folks working on your job in your employer. That would give you a rough idea how long you would last with the same job in your employer.

KlangFool

While I agree it's probably not worth arguing about whether that word applies, it is worth differentiating, as different causes factor into whether or not it is actually harder or whether it just doesn't happen. Furthermore, just because something is true at the population level doesn't mean that it's relevant to you. While many tech workers may face a decline in ability and relevant skill resulting in the general truth that it's harder to get a job in tech if you're older, that may not be true of particular people.
In some states, retained vs layoff data has to be handed to older employees upon layoff, so there is no need to speculate as seen above.
I'll donate a word or two for the wise:

High growth technical areas become commodities eventually, and it takes less time than most other fields of work. If one works in high tech, the first job out of school will likely be in a high growth area (where all the hiring is happening). If that area grows to full maturity, you'll end up being a (very busy) expert/specialist in that area just as the area cannot find anywhere to grow further. High tech workers should be prepared to reboot their career entirely before age 50 (or retire), because when that tech area reaches the commodification phase, the cost cutting will aim at the highly paid employees...which results in proportionally more older employees being laid off. Technically, the corporation is discriminating on the basis of cost, but cost is not just correlated with age...it is directly tied to age. This direct relationship between cost and age is why tech companies pay older people large sums of "exit money" to sign a doc saying they won't sue when laid-off. I know, I know...."it has never happened in my tech area X, so does not apply to me"....but that's only because area X just hasn't reached the commodity phase yet. This is why, when it hits, it's always a blindside hit to employees who spent their entire working lives in area X. Efforts to rationalize the cognitive dissonance usually grab onto the idea that an "expert/specialist" has become "stagnant/unable to learn". Yeah, no, that isn't really the reason. Plan accordingly.

content:
Contributing my recent experience as a software engineer on the younger side who has been interviewing with tech companies:
Generally, there isn't as many older people as individual contributors (IC) at the top tech companies because those roles are very demanding time and effort wise. The ones who are still ICs are usually senior members of their teams. Many people in tech transition to product management or people management as they move up. In addition, interviews at FAANGs consist of a lot of leetcode-like questions heavily weighed to algorithms, data structures, and system design questions. These questions strongly favor practice, repetition, and even memorization to a degree. It's much harder for older techies who haven't experienced this type of interview process compared to younger engineers who treat this as the norm. That's not to say that the material is necessarily harder for older engineers, but that it wasn't commonplace when they first started working.

I noticed several sweeping statements about FAANG companies regarding ageism and hiring. FAANG companies are behemoths and hiring processes aren't standardized across the whole company. Individual interviews and experiences will vary greatly across teams, organizations, and between FAANGs.

The share of mortgages that are adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) doubled to 10% in January, up from a 10-year low of 4% in January 2021, according to data from CoreLogic. ARMs offer an initial low rate for a period of years — typically anywhere from three to 10 years — and then the rate adjusts after that, usually annually, based on a fluctuating benchmark rate plus an additional margin, such as 2%.
I understand the desire for a nice house, but since mortgage rates for my first house were more than double current rates, my sympathy is pretty limited.

The news has been full of the expectation for multiple Fed rate hikes in the future. IOW, that ARM is going to get more expensive -- and anyone needing that lower rate to qualify may not be able to qualify for a refinance on better terms later.

But yes, if the difference between payments with an ARM and payments with a 30-year fixed is the difference between being able to afford the payments or not, then it is likely you are buying too much house. You should never have that little margin on mortgage payments.

content:
It is not market timing when you can re-fi with 0 point and $0 fees. I have bought 2 houses over the last ~13 years, and still own both of them.

For both houses, the initial mortgages were 30-year fixed and I did 0 point $0 fee refinance whenever the new 30-year fixed rate was at least 0.125% lower. For my first house, the initial rate was ~5-6%, and it became 3.375% after multiple re-fi before I bought and moved to my second house.

The second house started at around 4%, and it is now on a 2.25% 30-year fixed loan.

Between the 2 houses, I have done around 10 re-fi? And I stopped counting. With the 0 point and $0 fee re-fi, I knew I would pay 0.125-0.25% over the lowest possible rate if I pay for points and fees. However, I view it as a tail-I-win; head-they-lose kind of deal - I gave up timing the market, and I knew I would end up with the lowest possible rate + ~0.125-0.25%.

So far it has worked pretty well, and the chance to be able to re-fi to below 2.25% in the future seems low. Re-financing does extend the term of the loan, so whenever I re-fi, I save and invest the difference in payment, and by the end of 30 years since I bought the houses, I can pay them off if I choose to.

I think I am using terms incorrectly. Here's how I calculate the cost of my 30 year, 2.25% fixed rate mortgage in 2022 dollars:

1. I have all P&I payments entered in my model by year. Each year, I discount the P&I payment by inflation. I use the 10 year breakeven inflation rate of 2.9%. For example, my current year P&I payments are $23,041.20. In the last full year of the mortgage (2050), the P&I payments are $10,071 in 2022 dollars.
2. I add up all the payments using the discounted values.
3. I compare that total to the balance due on the mortgage.

Currently, my mortgage balance is $493,808. The total of the remaining payments in 2022 dollars is $450,940. So in my thinking, I am paying $450,940 for a $493,808 mortgage.

content:
I successfully filled out Form 2848 to help with my 83 year old mother's issues with the IRS. I also was requested to do this by the IRS after several joint phone conversations with my mother and the IRS.

The key elements of the form to me are:

Section 1 - Fill in Mother's details.

Section 2 - At the top where entering YOUR name and address - For CAF No. write "None". For PTIN write "None". Check YES to be sent copies of notices and communications.

Section 3 - I wrote "Income", "1040-SR" and "2019-2022" in the 3 columns. Obviously, you would adjust accordingly

Section 7 - Print name and get signature of Mother

Part II

Column 1 = f
Column 2 = Child

After a several weeks, I was sent a letter by the IRS containing my CAF Number. Now, I can call the IRS directly without my mother being on the phone at all. I start off the conversation by telling them I have a CAF Number and wish to discuss my mother's returns.

I have used the CAF Number many times over the last 2 years in my interactions with Mom's business. We've had an ongoing issue that has had to be dealt with. With the CAF, they will still ask you for more details about yourself each time you call in to verify you are who you say you are.

I also prepare my mother's returns using TurboTax, but I don't enter the CAF Number anywhere. I do list myself on the form as a "3rd Party designee". My mother is still on top of things, so we review her tax return before I hit "Submit" to file it.

I think the knee jerk on here is going to be "go get a new job". (and reading above, it is) A lot of people on here see work as strictly transactional, all about the money. That is important, but there are other factors.

Here's the deal - if you said "my boss is a jerk and they're unfair and inaccurate", I would tell you to run as fast as possible.

If you like the company, like you're peers, and make a good salary - then don't run away from your underperformance, particularly if you have upward potential (or desire for it). If you feel you have a good boss and someone who is working with you, cares about you, and wants to develop you, I'd recommend staying and learning, being sincere in trying to get better. If you feel you won't be given a fair shot moving forward or can do much better on salary elsewhere, move on.

The real takeaway is to search your soul and be better (if you want to be). You seem to have that attitude - you acknowledge that you underperformed, and very few people are honest enough to admit that. I see lots of posts on here about people griping about their job, and I just think to myself "I bet this person is a treat to work with". I do get where you might be frustrated that you weren't warned or given some slack, but very few managers are really good at handling these situations.

So good luck to you whatever you choose. If you're honest with yourself (and you seem to be), things will work out.

Precisely. We are cautioned by our HR not to make the PIP impossible. What we do instead in consultation with our legal team was ensure the quantifiable metrics associated with the PIP are based against a pace faster than normal -- for example, if you need to crank 50 widgets in a year, then during the 12 week PIP you need to crank 20 (as opposed to non-PIP employees cranking 12.5 in 12 weeks). Then we say to the employee, you've not performed up to par so to proceed here you must improve at this rate both to demonstrate your ongoing capabilities as well as to partially recover for unmet quotas from the period of poor performance.

We don't offer a severance alternative other than to cover health insurance for an additional month post termination, but we do that when we terminate anyway, so we don't have many people opt out of the PIP up front. Of my last 6 PIPs, 2 got new jobs within a month or two, 1 left the company of his own accord and I don't think he had anything lined up (but he saw the writing on the wall), and 3 ended up separated at the end of the PIP.

topic_title: Bad performance review. Time for a new job?
content:
It sounds like you had some issues early in the year. You worked with your manager to address those issues and your performance was back on track.

You got a "less than satisfactory" rating for the year, but it sounds like it wasn't a surprise. To use your words, you don't disagree with the rating.

It sounds like the people in your management chain didn't do anything wrong. Yes, it would have been nice to have been given the benefit of the doubt, but it sounds like you got a legitimate rating that is not tainted with bias or ulterior motive.

As far as whether you should get a new job, it depends upon your work culture. Where I work, a less than satisfactory rating for one review period isn't a big deal. I know of many people at my workplace who got future raises/promotions/etc despite such an occurrence. Now if you are less than satisfactory for multiple years, then you'll probably be put on PIP and potentially demoted or released.

The other thing to consider is the financial health of the company. Given the current tight job market, company's are trying to retain good talent. However, if they are under financial pressure, it certainly isn't outside the realm of possibility that they might have some sort of involuntary separations. Whether you would be included in that because of your one bad rating is speculation.

Finally, even without this bad performance rating, were you thinking of jumping ship? Were you already having doubts about your current job?

I guess the upshot of all this is that you need to consider all of these factors to make a decision of whether you would be better off staying or going. Good luck to you either way.

I would say unless there is some large benefit to trying to stay with this employer, find a new one.

First, you should always be looking for better opportunities both in your current job and elsewhere. Attend or speak at conferences and network as though you were on the hunt for a new job even if you feel like you on top of the world. If you are young, then look for opportunities to build your skillset and experiences. Your skills might stagnate if you work at the same place all the time. You need some discomfort in order to grow. I used to hate, hate, hate oral presentations, and still do not like them, but I can now do them. Lean into the discomfort of the review, and see what you can do to improve at your current job, but also start looking for a new job. I once gave my two weeks notice a few days after I was told that I was going to do the dog and pony show for the company I was at to be a partner. Why? Because I started interviewing when I had started to feel like I had reached a plateau, and in the process discovered a better opportunity.

Second, in a job market like this, it is a pain to hire and train new people. Unless your employer is shedding employees, most employers and managers do not want to do a recruitment if they can avoid it. While it is possible that the review might have been motivated by a desire to justify compensation and bonus decisions, it is tough game to play in this type of job market. So, listen to the feedback and try to see things from the perspectives of your managers and co-workers. Assuming that they are just planning to terminate you can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. Listen to the feedback. Perhaps the feedback to pick-up the phone and problem solve with a co-worker, rather than exchanging passive aggressive chat messages is not motivated by a conspiracy to make you feel horrible, but because you are starting to act like a toxic co-worker. As someone said, do some soul searching and work to improve even if it is not necessarily at your current employer.

Third, always have a Plan B. Once when I did not get a promotion, although I was ticked off, I looked for opportunities to improve. Mentally, my thought process was that I needed to polish my resume just in case I needed to interview, and even engaged in some informational interviews at some places that I really liked (but would have had to take a pay cut). In the end, I was promoted on the next go around, and that might have been because at the confidence of knowing that I had a Plan B set up. Even now, when things feel pretty good, I try to keep in mind what are my options if there is change in upper management or the economy goes South.

content:
Let me offer a contradictory opinion.

A negative performance review, if it is not documented as a behavior trend, is not necessarily a corporate death sentence. Senior leadership changes over time, too; some retire and others move to other departments, reorganizations shuffle everyone, etc.

I was a high performer for decades. One year, I was moved out of my Opco after a project and into the business unit's Opco into a support role (I was a developer). I was the "outsider," in that I was new in an organization of people who had worked together for years doing the business (not developing the IT tools for the business). Their performance was based on forced ranking, my prior Opco was based on relative performance versus a baseline standard. Needless to say, I was put in the lowest ranking category because it was "safe" for them to put me there, despite me single-handedly developing a product support process and tools that enabled them to have a 90+% on-time bug fix delivery that allowed them to build a reputation with the different user groups that didn't trust IT. The following year, they eliminated my role, I went back to my "home" organization, their production support efficiency collapsed, and my performance was back to its high trend in my home org.

I heard through the grapevine that the following year, someone else was designated as the low performer, and then someone else after that, and so on and on. These were all good performers who had the one year of bottom performance for no apparent reason. Maybe their leaders thought they could absorb the hit without long-term impact because of their prior reputations, but it really pissed off those people when it happened. Eventually, they eliminated the forced ranking and the MegaCorp standardized their performance evaluations across all the organizations.

-B

topic_title: 401k / what is responsibility of employer to pick best(ish) plan?
content:
Curious. In for the ride.

Recalling past topics, so quick searches:
Forum: https://www.google.com/search?q=bad+ret ... rg%2Fforum
General: https://www.google.com/search?q=ERISA
General: https://www.google.com/search?q=erisa+fiduciary+duty
General: https://www.google.com/search?q=employe ... ement+plan

Assuming your employer's retirement plan falls under ERISA, could search for employer's fiduciary responsibilities. Ask you employer how switching to a less-than-the-best plan falls under "meeting his fiduciary duty".

See: https://www.repairerdrivennews.com/2021 ... nsibility/
“It is the responsibility of the owner of the company, or anyone who’s helping in administration of that 401(k) plan, to act in the best interests of the participants of that plan."
In any resulting lawsuit, it is the employer who is hurt for accepting a bad plan, not the salesmen who sold him the bad plan. But if it takes a lawsuit for your employer to learn that his "friend" is a salesman first, and a (rented) friend second, then so be it.

You could ask your employer leading questions.
"Does employer's retirement fall under ERISA?"
"Does employer know he has a fiduciary duty to act in best interest of the retirement plan participants?"
"How will employer make plan participants whole for the extra fees charged by his friend's plan?"



Rhetorical question. Curious why your current advisor found a better plan... after your employer thought about moving to a friend's plan? Just curious.

I am pointing this out because I think it is worth thinking big picture about this. $100K is a lot of money to many people/organizations. You don't need it, so what do you want to do with it?

Using the $35K to pay off the car loans isn't really answering the question, because that just means you need less from your investments, and within rough approximation this means you have just "hidden" the $35K you don't need in your investments instead. But it is still there.

Now, one notable possibility is you just do that with all $100K: invest it despite not needing it. And then basically that is a choice to invest it on behalf of your eventual heirs, and again that is true whether you use the $35K to pay off the loans, or invest it and then pay the loans off from your investments.

And that is not an irrational choice, but is that REALLY what you want to do with it? Are your heirs who you want to give it to? And is making them wait for it until you die really what you want as well??

One obvious alternative would be giving it to loved ones or charity now, rather than making them wait. And again, to many people/organizations, that could be a lot of money, and indeed just a piece of it could be a lot of money. And you might find it pretty cool to actually be alive when it is given and used.

So again, my point is I would suggest you really think about not what you want to do with this money in the short-term, but rather who you ultimately want to get it, and when.

Because if what you do is simply add it to your savings without any plan to spend it on yourself, that is providing an answer to these questions, but not necessarily the answer you would really prefer.

Expenses definitely related to US income are not listed in either category; see the Form 1116 instructions.

The logic is that you need to determine your US and foreign net income. If your gross income was $90K US and $10K foreign, and you have $10K of deductions not related to either, your net income is $81K US and $9K foreign. If you instead have $10K of deductions which are related specifically to the US income, your net income is $80K US and $10K foreign, which would allow you a foreign tax credit of 1/9 rather than 1/10 of your foreign tax. If you have $10K of deductions which are related specifically to the foreign income, your net foreign income is zero; you have no foreign tax credit because the foreign income was not taxed by the US.

TurboTax puts (or at least used to put) charitable contributions on Line 3b; TaxAct does not put them on either line.

The Form 1116 instructions say that the itemized deductions for medical expenses, sales taxes, and real estate taxes do not relate to either US or foreign income; these are entered on Line 3a. Most adjustments to income also do not relate to either US or foreign income, such as alimony paid and HSA deductions; they are entered on line 3b. Interest needs to be apportioned on Line 4 if your foreign income exceeds $5000; home mortgage interest is prorated based on gross income, while investment interest (no longer deductible for individuals) would be prorated based on the investment assets.

State income taxes are special. Tax software normally puts state income taxes on line 3a, but the correct procedure is to compute what fraction of the income taxed by the state was foreign, and treat that part as definitely related to the foreign income and the rest as definitely related to the US income.

IRS Publication 514, Foreign Tax Credit has more detail than the Form 1116 instructions. It also gives the official definition:

A deduction is definitely related to a specific class of gross income if it is incurred either:
•
As a result of, or incident to, an activity from which that income is derived; or
•
In connection with property from which that income is derived

You will have to ask your tax advisor, but the logic here doesn't make sense. The IRA contribution is not a result of having US source income, as it is an independent decision. (In contrast, state taxes on the US source income are directly connected with the US source income, because you cannot have this income without the deduction).

An alternative argument is that the IRA contribution must be made from earned income, and thus it is directly connected with the country where you have the earned income, which is the US if all your foreign income is from investments.

HDHPs are not just offered through employers; you can buy them as an individual, either from the ACA marketplace or on your own. However, if your employer makes a contribution to your HSA (including by payroll deduction), this changes it from an adjustment to income into a reduction of salary, so it does reduce your US source income just as a 401(k) contribution would.

Neither the Form 1116 instructions nor Publication 514 are helpful here. Publication 514 just says that all deductions and adjustments to income must be prorated if not connected with US or foreign income. The Form 1116 instructions say, "Enter on line 3b any other deductions that don't definitely relate to any specific type of income (for example, the deduction for alimony paid from Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 18a)," without enumerating the other lines.

topic_title: Form 1116 3b
content:
Here is the current IRS wording:
IRS Publication 514 wrote:
You should also apportion any other deductions that are not definitely related to a specific class of income, including deductions shown on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), Part II, Adjustments to Income.
This clearly does not mean that you should apportion all adjustments as not definitely related to a specific class of income, because some of them are definitely related to certain income. For example, deductible business expenses (limited to certain classes of employees now) are related to that employment, and half the self-employment tax is related to the self-employment income. Therefore, it must mean that you must apportion these adjustments in the same way that you apportion other deductions.

I don't know how the IRS views HSAs, and this is not tax advice, but a logical analogy would be the way that medical insurance is handled. If your employer provides medical insurance by payroll deduction, this reduces your salary, so it reduces your US-source income (and is not reported on Form 1116 at all). If you pay for it on your own, the deduction must be apportioned between US and foreign income. Similarly, if your employer contributes to your HSA by payroll deduction, this reduces your US-source income; if you contribute your cash, it would make sense to apportion.

content:
Let me suggest a slightly different tack.

Bear in mind that these people are often very personable and they know, either from training or just intuitively, that the more time they spend with you, the better the chance is of making the sale. You've invested time yourself, and so have a kind of bias towards this time not being wasted. Recognizing that can help.

There's a need in such cases to slow things down. One objective there is to move toward a position where it's easier to get out. You've spent time with him, he's personable, and it's naturally difficult for many people to tell them to forget it.

One approach that can help here is to ask them to send you full copies of the contracts, so you can read what's written, what a person is signing. At that stage, they really need to pony up. If they don't, you're obviously out, with the ball in their court. If they do send the stuff, you let it sit a while until you hear from them and then say you're going to get your attorney and your tax preparer to review things. You could also bring in a financial advisor! Actually, it's probably best to tell them when asking for copies of contracts that you're going to review them and maybe ask for some trusted 3rd party advice. They might say there's no need for that, but you can easily insist. After all, 3rd parties with no agenda are good, right? The more advice the better, etc.

At some point, the smart sales people will know they're losing you and will move on. The less savvy ones? Well, you just haven't heard back from the tax preparer and the lawyer... they're just really busy. And those financial advisors at Bogleheads? No word. You get the idea. Eventually you'll feel fine about not going forward, the more time and distance you put between them and you.

Also, it seems to me someone your age could get a better deal on term life. Look around.

topic_title: Struggling with TurboTax and the Foreign Tax Credit
content:
Yes, you should take the total dividend and distribution for each fund and multiply it by the foreign income %. Add those two funds up to get your Form 1116 box 1a total. Some of these Vanguard International funds have dividends that come from the USA in addition to the expected foreign countries so form 1116 is looking for the foreign component, not the foreign component + the USA component.

The Qualified dividends come into play with regards to the $20K cutoff for the adjustment exception that must be done if you are in the 32% tax bracket or your Qualified dividends hit the $20K threshold. So Vanguard gives you the percentage so you can figure out if you need to do the adjustment for Form 1116. It would be a good idea to read the instructions for Form 1116, but even reading them doesn't help you make some decisions such as....

I anticipate offers coming through relatively quickly and the house going under contract a week or two after listing

Assuming that I'll have cash offers and conventional loan offers to choose from:
1. Do I (the seller) have to contact a title company now to secure escrow services? Or is that done by the lender of the buyer?
2. I'm assuming the escrow agent will apply the sale proceeds first to the balance of my current mortgage and then the rest would go to an account of my choice?
3. Is there anything else I need to watch out for in the sale, closing, and escrow process?
1. It depends on your state. In my state, closings are done by attorneys representing the buyer's lender so the lender handles that. If your state uses title companies to close or it is a cash transaction, you'll want to discuss this with your realtor (or better yet, your real estate attorney).

2. Sale proceeds are applied to any indebtedness on the property (primary mortgage, home equity loans and other liens), seller-paid items per contract (closing costs and such), pro-rated property taxes if those taxes are paid in arrears, other taxes and fees associated with the sale for which the seller is responsible by law or per contract, real estate commissions, and so on. Once all of that is paid, the net sale proceeds, if any, are disbursed to the seller.

3. There are many moving parts to a real estate transaction so it is hard to pick out specifics. Problems can pop-up anywhere...everything from disclosures, inspections, negotiations, contract terms, contingencies, closing, buyer breach and so on. Most transactions go relatively smoothly. However, it is always wise to retain a real estate attorney to advise you concerning real estate transactions. They are best equipped to advise you and their loyalty is only to you. Realtors cannot give legal advice and their loyalties can often conflict...their overriding interest is in closing the sale so they are paid. Fees for consultation with a real estate attorney are often very modest.

Good luck!

topic_title: First time home seller: closing and escrow questions
content:
I'm speaking of home sales in California (may not be applicable in other states).
Stick close to your realtor. They are hired to not only sell your home but manage the process.
The realtor will most likely have companies they typically work with for each step of the transaction. For example, they will have a title insurance company with which they typically work. By funneling their transactions through the same set of companies they can get discounts (not all of which will go to you, but some will). They will also have an escrow company. Once an escrow company is in the process, then see if your realtor is ok with you being in contact with them directly (the realtor will probably want you to do this because there will be lots of small questions going back and forth with escrow). Escrow will tell you when everything has completed and they will provide you with accounting statements (how much was paid to things like existing mortgage, pro-rated property tax, title search company, realtor, etc). The remaining money will then be directed to wherever you want it (your bank account) or provided to you as a cashiers/bank check.

content:
Thinking through how to pay for a second home and whether it makes sense to tap Roth assets rather than mortgage or sell taxable assets. I'm 71, DW is 66. Current assets are $8M, broken down as follows: $600K Roth, $3.6M IRA, $3M taxable, $300K non-emergency cash, $500K fully paid house. Investments are mostly mutual funds with 65/35 stock/bond allocation. 24% federal tax bracket. Purchase price for second home is $800K.

Pulling $500k from Roth will allow cash purchase and no tax hit. Selling $500k taxable assets will incur capital gains and higher IRMAA. Taking $500K pretax IRA distribution will get us to 35% marginal bracket and higher IRMAA. Mortgage rates as I write are 4-5%, cost would be partially offset by itemized deductions.

Any thoughts?

topic_title: Mortgage vs Roth assets for second home purchase
content:
Serendipity wrote:
Tue Mar 22, 2022 10:54 am
Current assets are $8M....
....
Investments are mostly mutual funds with 65/35 stock/bond allocation.
....
Mortgage rates as I write are 4-5%,
With your asset allocation you would have almost $3 million in bonds that are likely paying in the ballpark of 2% right now.

If you get a mortgage then in effect you would be borrowing money at 4%+ to lend it out at around 2%.

It is not exact but in some ways a mortgage is like a negative bond and there are lots of threads about that which you can look up. When looking at it that way having a mortgage would change your asset allocation from 35% bonds to more like 25% bonds and make your overall asset allocation more agressive.

I don't see where getting a mortgage would make sense.

One big factor is how this fits into your estate planning. With the current laws your heirs will get the taxable accounts at a stepped up cost basis so not selling the taxable invest could be good for them.

I didn't try to crunch the numbers but I would take a hard look at making enough traditional IRA withdrawals to get you to the top of the 24% tax bracket then make a Roth withdrawal for the rest.

Next year you may want to look at doing Roth conversions up to the top of the 24% federal tax bracket since federal tax brackets will revert to the old higher rates in 2026. If one of you survives the other then they will be filing tax returns in the higher single tax brackets so that 24% rate could look pretty good compared to what they will be paying then.

topic_title: Estimated tax payments: specific spouse or doesn’t matter which?
content:
Yes, it matters to the IRS. My son had this problem with his 2020 return. His spouse’s name was the first name on the 1040 form. He made estimated tax payments one quarter for a huge capital gain from their joint banking account, and used his SS #, instead of his spouse’s SS #. And was later assessed IRS tax penalties for not promptly making estimated or withholding payments. It took him 4 hours of time to get this straightened out with the IRS over the phone, most of which was wait time.

I’d take a proactive approach and call them after tax season has ended and within the quarter the estimated payment was made.

topic_title: Estimated tax payments: specific spouse or doesn’t matter which?
content: As stated by others, it definitely does matter. On a federal tax return the IRS considers the first person listed on the tax return as the taxpayer and the other as the spouse. Future tax returns should reflect those persons in the same sequence. Good luck as you attempt to clear up the situation. Let us know how it all works out please.

In tax year 2019, we made a tax payment for a Trust, form 1041, by check with our return. Check wasn’t cashed for 6 months. We get a notice from the IRS to pay up within 30 days after the date of the letter, which we received 3 weeks from the date of the letter. We place a stop payment on this check and send them another one. IRS cashes second check and evidently tried to cash the first check, and then sends us a Treasury check at the end of the year for the amount of the tax payment with interest! We keep that check uncashed until we get guidance from the IRS, which occurs 6 months later. We then recount our experience with them and we sent them back the Treasury check. They should have had no trouble in finding out stuff, right? BTW, we no longer make any payments by check to the IRS as a result of this experience.

In 2012, before we learnt our lesson about snail mail payments, we sent in our joint returns with a tax payment. A year later we get the dreaded CP Notice that we owe the IRS much more than we paid at a figure that precisely mirrors the amount of money withheld from my wife’s salary by her employer, plus interest and penalties. The IRS tells us that we didn’t withhold anything from her salary. We say we did and the W-2 attached to the 1040 shows that. The IRS agent tells us that she doesn’t have the W-2 and that it relies on the tax withholding data dumps of employers, and this impacts on what gets reported as earnings to the SSA. The IRS agent asks us to send her another copy of the W-2, information they should have found — why the heck does the IRS even want us to attach W-2 if it’s relying on electronic submissions by employers and the W-2 is not even read into the IRS system? We also got stuff corrected by the SSA for Social Security benefits.

Sorry for the rant.

topic_title: Secure CC and Less-Secure?
content:
I have been thinking about using a cashback CC for bigger ticket relatively secure purchases and another CC for "other". Does anyone else do this and have suggestions on how to do so? For example would a large chain grocery store be considered secure? Any restaurants, or none? Should I put the secure card into an RF-proof sleeve if I carry it in my wallet.

I'm not so worried about liability for fraud but rather the hassle of changing autopay for the "secure" transactions such as health insurance premiums, utility bills etc. It is nice to have get the cashback on these.

Perhaps for online do the split based on the transaction amount, say for over $150 use the cashback card. And/or 3 categories: secure, less secure, and cash-only.

topic_title: Secure CC and Less-Secure?
content: You have no liability for fraud. Usually the card number is hacked from within the bank network, or through the reader, nothing you can do about either. I just use whatever card gives me the best rewards on the place I'm shopping. In the event there's fraud on the card, they send me a new one and cover the charges. It's happened to me maybe 5 times over the last 30 years. I've never paid a cent. Don't overthink it too much, do what you feel gets you the most rewards and the least stress

topic_title: Secure CC and Less-Secure?
content: I do not worry about this as credit cards protect you from being liable. I've had cards that were activated and never even used anywhere still end up with fraudulent charges, so I think you are taking many steps toward protecting against something that may not be 100% secure anyway.

topic_title: Secure CC and Less-Secure?
content:
Sometimes I feel like am posting in a foreign language. Liability from fraud is not at all concern for me. I don't know how to make that any clearer. However, it is an additional nuisance (but not end of the world) dealing with replacement credit cards with new numbers when they are used for automatic payments, in addition to the "given" nuisance of disputing all fraudulent transactions. I prefer to keep using an existing cashback card for automatic payments, plus some other big ticket relatively secure transactions, but plan to avoid using it for transactions that may have a higher risk of my number being stolen.

Possibly online game outfits and small software outfits may be risky. Gas stations and restaurants that take your card away have bad reps (pretty much all sit-down restaurants in the USA) though I usually buy gas with cash. I probably should ask my CC provider about this. Restaurants that take your card away again have bad reps. Are RF skimmers a reality; should I RF-proof my cards or wallet?

topic_title: Secure CC and Less-Secure?
content: As I said, you can end up with fraudulent activity even if you go through these steps. Even if you never even use the card. To me it is more of a nuisance to try to maintain one card as extra secure and still need to replace cards anyway. In fact you introduce more chance of fraudulent activity with more accounts (I am not against multiple cards, but I would not maintain one as being extra "secure"). Yes it is a foreign language to me to go through these extra steps without a tangible benefit.

topic_title: Secure CC and Less-Secure?
content:
Most recurring subscription vendors subscribe to the account updater services from the card networks. When you get a new card number, those merchants automatically get updates and you don't need to update them manually.

Nobody is skimming your card using RFID.

Most online vendors outsource credit card processing to someone like Stripe or Authorize.net and are never even in possession of your card number. There's literally nothing an attacker could steal from the vendor that would allow them to make fraudulent charges.

(I used to lead the payments team for a major tech company, this stuff was literally my day job for a while)

I wouldn't say this is an exhaustive list but as far as major brands I think virtual card number support has actually been declining. Just recently PayPal announced they were discontinuing their Key product. My Discover card used to offer it, but no more. Capital One now only supports it when you install their privacy questionable browser extension.
https://wallethub.com/edu/cc/virtual-credit-card/65981

I think it's somewhat due to the prevalence of the digital wallets available now. Entering credit card numbers into a random website for a one time purchase should be viewed with suspect just like a merchant using a mag stripe reader. The card networks have made the penalties for storing actual card numbers which get breached pretty severe. Anyone reputable doing recurring billing where you "save" your credit card info is tokenizing the card which makes it only useable with that merchant. That is, Netflix isn't storing your actual credit card number but a different version of it only they can use. As was mentioned above the networks also have updater services available so a merchant doing recurring billing can get a new number when the card expires.

Bottom line should be, no mag stripe readers. Use a digital wallet if at all possible online. Virtual card number online if you happen to still have one available.

content:
You are not alone. I tried filing my federal return on Friday. Rejection code FD-31-13.

For reasons that I don't understand, my Federal e-filed return via HR Block keeps getting rejected by the IRS despite the fact that the final review by the program finds no errors. The "solution" proposed by HR Block is that I review all the myriad of forms and look for the error, which I have done and I can't find any errors either. That said, HR Block software did all the calculating, not me, so it's not like reviewing the forms for errors is easy.

So my next step will be to forego e-filing and mail my returns in instead. At least if there is some issue, and it is not just a software thing, the IRS will get back to me and tell me what I have to do...I have already spent several hours wasted trying to solve this.

Additional hassles....
I paid my taxes electronically in advance, plus $5K so I could get a refund in I-bonds.
I wanted to check if the IRS processed the funds, thinking that may have something to do with my e-return being rejected. (I assume they did receive them because the money was debited from my bank account).
Starting this year the IRS is using a private security firm (ID.me) that forces you to trust them with all of your personal data (phone number, tax return, drivers license/photo ID, pound of flesh closest to the heart, etc) in order to access the IRS page to have access to your account.
It's a long verification process, and for unknown reasons, after I gave them all they requested (leaving me feeling uneasy), I could still not get verified because their program could not read the barcode on the back of my driver's license (I photographed it 3 times).
So now they have my demographics to do with as they wish and I still have no access to my IRS page. I called the IRS and went through an excessively long menu, only to be finally told by a recording that they are too busy to take my call and to call back later. Using a machine to talk to another machine. Arggghhhh.....

So a tip for all of you that I learned too late...if you are requesting an I-bond refund, give them a little more money than the amount you are requesting in I-bonds and ask for the balance in cash (like direct deposit). I read in some online blog that, though the IRS will not confirm processing your I-bond refund, it will when they process your cash refund, and they will email you to let you know they processed your cash refund...thus you can be pretty sure they processed your I-bond refund as well. $5001 should work.

topic_title: What do you wish you knew before you retired you know now!
content:
I didn’t know that by converting my 403(b) to an IRA I’d be depriving myself of access to a liquid, 3%+ stable-value fund. That access is all the more valuable for those of us wary of bond funds, especially in the current environment.

On the nonfinancial side, if that’s of interest, I overestimated my largely untested enthusiasm for hiking and moved across country to a location where I could hike in beautiful landscapes. A year later I’d had my fill of hiking and moved again. In general, I’ve found that interests I had pursued for an extended time at some point in life were easily rekindled. If I had never in the past made much time for an activity, I’ve found that I’m still not moved to do so in retirement. No doubt some retirees are different in this respect.

Two things to consider about when to claim SS. First, If you have a spouse, the survivor gets to assume the higher SS benefit of the two. This is why most folks recommend that the higher wage earner claim at 70. Second, SS is about the best longevity insurance you can find. If you can afford to wait to 70, you are rewarded with an inflation protected payment for the remainder of your life. If you die young, you're just dead.

content:
I wish I had known about index fund investing and how easy it is to manage your own portfolio before I retired from megacorp in 2009 with a lump sum retirement and a very low 6 figure 401k. Luckily I found this site in mid 2011 before I permanently retired in early 2016. I stopped the bleeding by getting out of PAS at Fidelity and transferring to Vanguard with a 3 fund portfolio.

At Fidelity they had me in a 5 year 200k fixed annuity in a market that was on fire and a single Ginnie Mae initially, then after talking me into PAS, 20 constantly churning funds of stocks and bonds with high ER's, total hit about 2.5% yearly.

Woulda coulda shoulda, if I had that knowledge in 2009 at the beginning of this raging bull I would have been able to permanently retire even earlier than when I did at 63.5. Can't complain though, so many know nothing about how AUM fees and high ER's eat away at their accounts.

The other thing I learned in the nick of time was the value of delaying SS until age 70 in our situation. I would have likely filed at 63.5 and my wife at 62 when she retired if I had not found Bogleheads. Instead, she filed at 65 and I simultaneously filed a restricted application on her benefit and will file for my own benefit next year at age 70 (we share the same birthday, me at 1 year older).

Back at Fidelity now because of the brick and mortar aspect, competent clerks, and no hassle mistake-free transactions. The difference between then and now? I pay them zero and hold the same VG funds at the same ER as I did at VG for a combined cost of .032%. I never talk to my assigned representative, but I do drink their coffee if I ever feel the need to visit. They handled the wire transfer for the cash purchase of our new home flawlessly for no charge. The coffee was good then too.

Bogleheads should get the prestigious Taylor Larimore Award for the most helpful forum for prospective retirees on the internet.

As a reminder, SS goal is effectively equal payments to a given individual that aligns with the longevity assumptions.

In other words, for the average person who "dies on schedule", it shouldn't matter when you claim - you'll get roughly the same overall payments. (Either more smaller payments if you claim early or fewer larger payments if you claim late, but the total is intentionally roughly the same.)

For someone single, they basically need to figure out if they'll live longer or shorter than the average estimate. Someone in bad health probably should claim early, as they might not live long enough to hit the "average". For others, it's more subjective.

If married, the analysis is arguably simpler. The highest earner (especially if by a large margin) should try to delay claiming (assuming finances allow). So long as one of you beats the average life expectancy, you likely come out ahead. (Since the survivor gets to effectively keep the higher payment of the two spouses. [In reality, I think they keep their payment and then get a 2nd check for the difference.])

Beyond that consider what happens if you "guess wrong" related to how long you live.
If you die sooner, sure from an SS viewpoint you'll have been paid less (maybe nothing if you delayed SS). But presumably your portfolio has unused assets since you had less expenses vs your "planned" lifetime expenses. So you'll probably leave more assets to your heirs than planned (OK, maybe less as they didn't grow as long, but they'll get them much sooner).
If you live longer, you risk living beyond your saved assets. This is where SS can really shine as "longevity insurance". Delaying your SS as long as possible - combined with its COLA helping to keep pace with inflation, will drastically reduce the risk of running out of money.
Between the two options, I'd rather err on the side of delayed SS. If we both die young, our heirs will get plenty (even if we never get $1 from SS). If one of us lives to 100+, it's likely their expenses will be fully covered by SS (and we are lucky that spouse has a small inflation adjusted pension as well).

On the contrary!!!

Why you need to have a Roth IRA
Let’s look at your future self. Suppose you are age 70, would you be glad you had tax-deferred accounts that had grown to $2M or would you be glad that you had $1.5M in a Roth IRA? Or would you like half of each? [Forget the math for the moment and decide your answer before continuing]

If all/most of your retirement money is in tax-deferred, you will have to start withdrawing RMDs and pay taxes on every dollar withdrawn, regardless if you need the money for spending or not and regardless of what your tax bracket is at that time. By the time you pay the taxes, there will less left over and the tax bracket will be unknown until then. There is also a surcharge on those Medicare beneficiaries with higher income. Instead of paying $2K in premiums each year like the vast majority pay, you could be one of those paying $11K in premiums just because the RMDs made your income higher. Double those amounts if Married.

In addition, if you are MFJ now, when you are widowed, you will have to file as Single. The space in each tax bracket for Single is half as much as MFJ, so you could easily be bumped into a higher tax bracket.

Now, if you were half (or all) Roth, all your Roth withdrawals would be tax-free. You could leave them in your Roth or spend them as you want. Withdrawals would not raise your Medicare premiums or push you into higher tax brackets when widowed.

[Stop and ask yourself again which kind of accounts you would rather have at age 70.]

How to contribute to Roth IRAs
Everyone with earned income (wages) or with a spouse with earned income can contribute to a Roth each year. Instead of deducting your income on your taxes when contributing to tax-deferred accounts, you contribute money that was NOT deducted. If your current income is too high to contribute directly, you can contribute indirectly by doing a Backdoor Roth instead.

After reading that page, if you have questions, ask them in a new thread you start.

What's more important to you?

Getting the "most" out of social security, especially if your are concerned you might not make it to the "average" life span? If so, claiming early might be an advantage, as we aren't guaranteed a tomorrow...

But if your most concerned with "not running out of money", especially if you happen to live longer than the "average" life span? If so, delaying is probably better...

However, there's "more to the story"...

Maybe you have a high 401k balance that will end up with massive RMDs if you don't do years of Roth conversions. That might be a case to delay, so that you have less "income" and thus can do more Roth conversions.

Ultimately, you have to balance multiple considerations, and make a judgement call on what's best for yourself. Resources like opensocialsecurity.com can help, as can things like retirement calculators (preferably ones that include taxes), so you can test out different scenarios with different SS dates / benefits, assets, etc. and find what works for you.

I estimate that a Single with $500K in tax-deferred or MFJ with $1M in tax-deferred, should project their finances past age 72 to see what might happen tax-wise. (Actually, everyone should do that.) It is far better to understand your age 72+ situation in early retirement, when you have an opportunity to change it, than being surprised at 72 because you weren’t pro-active.
