content:
Using the metaphor of the "big rocks first" (for reference, see, for example, http://www.appleseeds.org/big-rocks_covey.htm ), I prepared my big rocks for retirement well:
1. Sufficient assets, approximate retirement budget
2. Good health insurance
3. Several project ideas

Now in retirement, I am noticing and taking care of small rocks. For example:
1. In retirement, I need more strict time planning than when I was working. I have more control of my time, but I don't have more free time.
2. When I can do anything I want, I am missing the constraints that were tying me to specific projects for long enough to complete them. The freedom to choose causes me to move from one activity to another without completing them.
3. I did not anticipate that I'd be spending so much time learning about health and implementing various health measures. There is a huge amount of information about genetic predispositions, supplements, self-directed blood tests and their interpretations, various exercise systems, food related approaches such as ketogenic diet and intermittent fasting, and brain stimulating exercises. All of them are useful for preserving one's health, and all of them take a lot of time.

Knowing what I know now, I don't think I'd do anything differently before I retired. But I would mentally prepare for the need to be more organized than ever.

Victoria

Why you need to have a Roth IRA
Let’s look at your future self. Suppose you are age 70, would you be glad you had tax-deferred accounts that had grown to $2M or would you be glad that you had $1.5M in a Roth IRA? Or would you like half of each? [Forget the math for the moment and decide your answer before continuing]

If all/most of your retirement money is in tax-deferred, you will have to start withdrawing RMDs and pay taxes on every dollar withdrawn, regardless if you need the money for spending or not and regardless of what your tax bracket is at that time. By the time you pay the taxes, there will less left over and the tax bracket will be unknown until then. There is also a surcharge on those Medicare beneficiaries with higher income. Instead of paying $2K in premiums each year like the vast majority pay, you could be one of those paying $11K in premiums just because the RMDs made your income higher. 'AUM' is assets under management. It's a fee schedule for how a money manager is compensated. If their fee is 1%, your account is reduced by that much each year. A place like Edward Jones may charge this.

'ER' is expense ratio. That is a fee mutual fund charges to keep the lights on and pay wages. Places like Fidelity, Schwab and Vanguard have the lowest ER's. If you use an S&P 500 fund, why pay more than necessary?

You could pay an AUM and a high ER. Double whammy!

content:
Having retired at 55, just to get away from my job, I had no idea of how joyous those early years of retirement freedom could be. We traveled extra for the off-season prices then stayed home to avoid the holiday crowds, so even our "vacation" travels in retirement were better. Hawaii in October is not crowded.

In your late 50s, you can still backpack with today's ultralight gear. It was unimaginable when I was working, that I could always have enough flexible time to wait for the good weather days to go backpacking, between the periodic bad weather days. There is about a weekly cycle of weather events, some years with more wet weekends, and some years with more wetness on the mid-week days. People make calendar-based plans, and the weather gods laugh, but retirees have time to adapt.

Thank you to Bogleheads and the older Vanguard Diehards site for the steady financial info on retirement spending. We started to do the post-retirement Roth conversions (something new but not difficult to learn), because several said we should (special thanks to poster Celia), and now the Roth IRA is all stock funds while the currently no-growth bond funds are all in the tIRA. The formerly dreaded RMDs are now just a reasonable withdrawal amount for spending. Experiencing the promised results after more than a dozen years of paying extra tax on Roth conversions, is very nice.

Fully delayed SS is now enough that it is a partial buffer for my 16 year old, no-COLA pension, as inflation is starting to heat up. At retirement, I did not see how the almost tag team effect would be such a good benefit in my 70s. Do all those financial recommendations for the initial and the continuing years of retirement, because they do work well, same as immediately starting retirement contributions at your first career job, as if we knew anyone who did that.

I do not intend to derail the thread. I thought this may be of interest to some. It is a common belief that the experience of time shortens as we age. There is a field of research on this topic and this does not appear to be a function of age itself. One of the most important variables is the volume of new stimuli to the brain. When a child is 4, one year is 25% of their life and nearly everything is new. After so many years many of us end up in routines where very little is new. There is no need for the brain to assimilate every near identical commute to work for example. Upon recalling the proceeding time it feels as if it has flown by. In actuality the memory timeline is punctuated with gaps. But I challenge you that the next time you travel for a weekend to place you've never been, pay attention to how long those two days feel compared to two days of a mundane week. The same goes for really getting into something new as far as education. The subjective experience of the passage of time is mostly a function of new experiences and knowledge. It still works this way in older age. The field of neurobiology is called chronoception if you're interested to dive deeper.

I do not intend to derail the thread. I thought this may be of interest to some. It is a common belief that the experience of time shortens as we age. There is a field of research on this topic and this does not appear to be a function of age itself. One of the most important variables is the volume of new stimuli to the brain. When a child is 4, one year is 25% of their life and nearly everything is new. After so many years many of us end up in routines where very little is new. There is no need for the brain to assimilate every near identical commute to work for example. Upon recalling the proceeding time it feels as if it has flown by. In actuality the memory timeline is punctuated with gaps. But I challenge you that the next time you travel for a weekend to place you've never been, pay attention to how long those two days feel compared to two days of a mundane week. The same goes for really getting into something new as far as education. The subjective experience of the passage of time is mostly a function of new experiences and knowledge. It still works this way in older age. The field of neurobiology is called chronoception if you're interested to dive deeper.
[/quote]

What a fascinating topic. Thanks for mentioning the topic and it’s name, chronoception. I will read more on this topic.

Claim $2270 at 62 = 490K (live till 80)
Claim $3300 at 67 = 514K (live till 80)
Claim $4100 at 70 = 492K (live till 80)

Social Security payouts were designed to pay out the same amount of money regardless of whether you start collecting early or later. The unknown factor off course is how long a specific person lives. If you happen to make it to a very old age, deferring can have dramatic improvements in your overall payout. If you live to the average age, it won't make much difference either way.

I wish I had known about index fund investing and how easy it is to manage your own portfolio before I retired from megacorp in 2009 with a lump sum retirement and a very low 6 figure 401k. Luckily I found this site in mid 2011 before I permanently retired in early 2016. I stopped the bleeding by getting out of PAS at Fidelity and transferring to Vanguard with a 3 fund portfolio.

At Fidelity they had me in a 5 year 200k fixed annuity in a market that was on fire and a single Ginnie Mae initially, then after talking me into PAS, 20 constantly churning funds of stocks and bonds with high ER's, total hit about 2.5% yearly.

Woulda coulda shoulda, if I had that knowledge in 2009 at the beginning of this raging bull I would have been able to permanently retire even earlier than when I did at 63.5. Can't complain though, so many know nothing about how AUM fees and high ER's eat away at their accounts.

The other thing I learned in the nick of time was the value of delaying SS until age 70 in our situation. I would have likely filed at 63.5 and my wife at 62 when she retired if I had not found Bogleheads. Instead, she filed at 65 and I simultaneously filed a restricted application on her benefit and will file for my own benefit next year at age 70 (we share the same birthday, me at 1 year older).

Back at Fidelity now because of the brick and mortar aspect, competent clerks, and no hassle mistake-free transactions. The difference between then and now? I pay them zero and hold the same VG funds at the same ER as I did at VG for a combined cost of .032%. I never talk to my assigned representative, but I do drink their coffee if I ever feel the need to visit. They handled the wire transfer for the cash purchase of our new home flawlessly for no charge. The coffee was good then too.

Bogleheads should get the prestigious Taylor Larimore Award for the most helpful forum for prospective retirees on the internet.

topic_title: What do you wish you knew before you retired you know now!
content:
What a great question!

Most cops are not good at retirement…well, based on my two-plus years of experience in retirement, ‘most people’ in general are not great at retirement. My personal stat…at least 50% of the people I know extremely well, are not happy in retirement. Heck, they actually say it…or their hung over blood-shot eyes scream it.

I’m excellent at retirement and that isn’t bragging. Simple math - how many times a day, week or month does that little voice inside my head utter the words, “I’m bored.” For me it doesn’t happen.

Average life expectancy for cops (57), is 6 to 8 years less than coal miners. I turned 57 this year and I’m thankful as of yet I have ensured the average ‘retire cop life expectancy.’

Pre retirement… I wish I knew or had better awareness of how badly and cluttered my occupation (I allowed it…my fault) would effect my ability to personally connect with family and friends in a completely, zen-like unobstructed way.

I was a very motivated field officer, then went through the ranks and did the Chief thing for 13 years, 30 years LE total. Once that spam or crud or how ever you want to quantify it, left my brain, oh boy did my relationships with family and friends open up. …Almost like a new set of eyes or a 7th sense.

All that said, if I had better managed the crud of a career, I would have seen what I see clearly now…numerous depressed and broke human beings who were right in front of me and I didn’t know it. Heck, five years prior to retiring my 18 year old within a 10 minute span told me he was gay and had been depressed for five years. I wasn’t shocked he was gay but I was floored that he had been depressed that long and my ‘crap brain’ missed it. That hurt bad!

My ‘retired brain’ has become, for the better, a relationship sponge and now I can see clearly and can help my family and friends through those moments with a deeper uncluttered understanding. They tell me stuff now that during my career they hadn’t, though I should have easily seen. They were perhaps too loyal and not wanting to add to my existing career crud.

‘…leave your work at the office’…I was well aware of the saying!!! And call it luck but several of my close friends and my son, who were on the cusp of taking their lives somehow managed to hang on without much help from me and my understanding.

The gift of a clear retired head, may just end up saving the life of a close relative or friend.

In the mean time; pre retirement, figure out and get trained, get counseling, however it happens, remove that career/job plaque from your brain. I thought I managed it well during my career. But looking back, the evidence clearly states otherwise and my brain lied to me back then.

I love my newly retired relationship brain and would give up my entire portfolio to keep it! It’s value is immeasurable.

As a reminder, SS goal is effectively equal payments to a given individual that aligns with the longevity assumptions.

In other words, for the average person who "dies on schedule", it shouldn't matter when you claim - you'll get roughly the same overall payments. (Either more smaller payments if you claim early or fewer larger payments if you claim late, but the total is intentionally roughly the same.)

For someone single, they basically need to figure out if they'll live longer or shorter than the average estimate. Someone in bad health probably should claim early, as they might not live long enough to hit the "average". For others, it's more subjective.

If married, the analysis is arguably simpler. The highest earner (especially if by a large margin) should try to delay claiming (assuming finances allow). So long as one of you beats the average life expectancy, you likely come out ahead. (Since the survivor gets to effectively keep the higher payment of the two spouses. [In reality, I think they keep their payment and then get a 2nd check for the difference.])

Beyond that consider what happens if you "guess wrong" related to how long you live.
If you die sooner, sure from an SS viewpoint you'll have been paid less (maybe nothing if you delayed SS). But presumably your portfolio has unused assets since you had less expenses vs your "planned" lifetime expenses. So you'll probably leave more assets to your heirs than planned (OK, maybe less as they didn't grow as long, but they'll get them much sooner).
If you live longer, you risk living beyond your saved assets. This is where SS can really shine as "longevity insurance". Delaying your SS as long as possible - combined with its COLA helping to keep pace with inflation, will drastically reduce the risk of running out of money.
Between the two options, I'd rather err on the side of delayed SS. If we both die young, our heirs will get plenty (even if we never get $1 from SS). If one of us lives to 100+, it's likely their expenses will be fully covered by SS (and we are lucky that spouse has a small inflation adjusted pension as well).
Thank you very much for this concise explanation. I know this information is out there and I've kind of looked at it out of the corner of my eye off and on but it has never really "sunk in" until I read this post.

Much clearer to me now - thanks!

A few of observations

1) ACA plans are made available at a County level, so quality and cost of plans can vary quite a bit even within a state

2) In general, states that have been friendly towards the ACA have better ACA plans than states that have been hostile to it

3) ACA plans change periodically, almost yearly in less stable markets.

content:
Things change from year-to-year. That's the issue. When we moved over from COBRA to ACA in 2021, we had a gold plan with a monthly premium under $300 for us and our two dependents. It was a really good plan, albeit the larger deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. Fast forward to 2022 plans and more insurance companies added plans in the marketplace where we live. I thought it would be really good with more options to choose from, but the gold plan we were on in 2021 was now going to have a premium of $1,500 a month in 2022 and our income not expected to increase. We were not going to pay $1,500 a month for the "privilege" of carrying health insurance. So, we switched to a bronze plan with the same insurance company that have co-pays that are a little higher, prescriptions that are a little higher, etc., with a smaller monthly premium.

We stayed with the same insurance company under ACA because we really didn't have many issues. They paid the claims. We had to call them once in a while about something, but that was about it. Customer service is pretty good; if we email them asking if something is covered, they respond promptly (within a day).

So, you see how pricing of premiums, co-pays, prescription medicines, etc. can change from year-to-year no matter where you live.

The biggest factor getting a private plan is federal: whether you qualify for ACA subsidy. Totally different picture in what you get for what you personally pay if you qualify for those subsidies or not. It's a way bigger effect than difference nowadays in features of plans state by state* which all have to meet ACA standards. Although some states have additional requirements, and some allow cheaper lower coverage 'temporary' plans others don't allow to be offered. As with most things definitely don't decide based on average statistics like 'there's higher medical debt in X state'. That's also a factor that seems to confuse people about where health care is better for *you*: you can't accurately judge that by average outcomes in a state, because you won't automatically become the average person in AL, VT or NJ just because you move there, just like you're not automatically the average person in CA now.

The common benchmark 'Second Lowest Cost Silver Plan' in NJ for age 55 is $674/mo/person (just $1348 if 'we' is two people that age), second lowest cost gold $1,093 per person. If $700 is a 'great plan' and that cost is for 2 people, it's going to be a lot more unsubsidized in NJ and many other states I believe. In fact we're early retired in NJ and have the cheapest Bronze plan (would be $588 each at your age). If we couldn't afford the copay/dedutibles we should probably still be working, and on unsubsidized basis the extra coverage of the better plans is not worth it. Again ACA subsidies (and now NJ has additional state premium subsidies) could completely change the comparison, but we don't come close to qualifying for either. I agree with the post saying this isn't likely to end up the main reason you'd choose to live one state rather than another (health insurance cost that is, living in an area remote from major healthcare providers could be a real factor if you plan to live in this next place from 55 to the end). But to the extent it factors in you have to determine what subsidies you'd get and what the final cost would be.

*somebody said it varies locally but that's not true in NJ for private health plans, features and cost are both standard statewide.

If we couldn't afford the copay/dedutibles we should probably still be working, and on unsubsidized basis the extra coverage of the better plans is not worth it. You are mistaken.
1. I just looked at the state of NJ exchange.
Looking at plans in Newark vs. Cape May, the former shows 65 different health plans to choose from, the latter shows only 45 plans available.
Several companies serve one area but not the other. Most states of any size are like this. ACA was designed to create markets at a County level, that is why the signup process specifically asks for that information.

2. I don't understand the point you are trying to make about the different tier plan in your last paragraph.

3. You are also quite mistaken about the main issue being about federal subsidies, and that state to state variations are not meaningful.
There was another thread recently discussing access to top tier hospitals (Mayo, MD Anderson, Sloan Kettering, etc.) Many people lamented about how all the plans available in their area only have narrow networks that do not provide any coverage at such places, while other living in different states have access to broad PPO plans that cover those facilities. That can be more important than few thousand dollars of tax savings.
1. These are the private plans available in NJ and the pricing for each age:
https://www.nj.gov/dobi/division_insura ... ccd67b1570

I don't believe it's true you can't buy any of these plans, either on exchange or from the provider directly, if you live in NJ. Assuming you're unsubsidized, that's again a huge difference.

2. The points were two. First, depending what OP meant by '$700/mo' (for one person or two?) and 'great plan' OP could at most save marginally for probably a worse plan in NJ than the employer/retiree one in CA. If $700 is for two people that's a big advantage for the CA plan. Second, if you do not qualify for ACA subsidies and are at least fairly old (like OP, 55) it seldom makes sense to pay for a more expensive individual plan with better coverage. The difference is mainly deductible/out of pocket limit, fixed number of $'s, but the premium price difference in $'s expands with the age multiplier. Young people might benefit to consider gold/silver/bronze but for unsubsidized older people only bronze makes economic sense. Again if you're subsidized, different story.

3. Which is why subsidized or not is the really big difference. But it's rare nowadays to find a plan at a practical cost which gives coverage outside the state you live in, ie. a plan that covers you at Mayo *and* Sloan Kettering, prior to getting Medicare. Whereas in-state I don't know about Mayo vs. MN plans, but the relatively less expensive plans in NY and NJ include the respective locations of Sloan Kettering in those states.

*by reputation anyway, actually analyzing what difference it would make to one's health outcome might be complicated, but a person might feel better off, in particular being able to send a loved one to a big name place.

The individual plan market is really Horizon and Amerihealth, for an older unsubsidized person it's really Horizon's cheapest Bronze or Amerihealth's, 2 plans that make sense, not 40 or 60-some. content:
We are in one of those areas (Illinois side of the St. Louis metro) that two years ago only had one insurer, BCBS with a decent but more limited PPO. The broad PPO network they usually sell to their group clients is not available. At the beginning of last year two new insurers came in, Ambetter (which is Centene, a major provider of managed Medicaid plans) and First Health (the Catholic Hospital network in St. Louis). Their plans are both HMO/EPO options and came in significantly below BCBS. The downside is the cost for the lower cost silver plan after subsidy has doubled from before when BCBS was the only carrier.

I guess the message is if you're going to be higher income and not relying on a premium subsidy, more competition / more plans choices is good. If you're trying to keep your costs lower by taking the subsidy, more choices often mean very limited networks which drive down the silver plan cost vs the broader network carrier and can substantially increase the final cost to you.

The biggest factor getting a private plan is federal: whether you qualify for ACA subsidy. Totally different picture in what you get for what you personally pay if you qualify for those subsidies or not. It's a way bigger effect than difference nowadays in features of plans state by state* which all have to meet ACA standards. Although some states have additional requirements, and some allow cheaper lower coverage 'temporary' plans others don't allow to be offered. As with most things definitely don't decide based on average statistics like 'there's higher medical debt in X state'. That's also a factor that seems to confuse people about where health care is better for *you*: you can't accurately judge that by average outcomes in a state, because you won't automatically become the average person in AL, VT or NJ just because you move there, just like you're not automatically the average person in CA now.

The common benchmark 'Second Lowest Cost Silver Plan' in NJ for age 55 is $674/mo/person (just $1348 if 'we' is two people that age), second lowest cost gold $1,093 per person. If $700 is a 'great plan' and that cost is for 2 people, it's going to be a lot more unsubsidized in NJ and many other states I believe. You are mistaken.
1. I just looked at the state of NJ exchange.
Looking at plans in Newark vs. Cape May, the former shows 65 different health plans to choose from, the latter shows only 45 plans available.
Several companies serve one area but not the other. Most states of any size are like this. ACA was designed to create markets at a County level, that is why the signup process specifically asks for that information.

2. I don't understand the point you are trying to make about the different tier plan in your last paragraph.

3. You are also quite mistaken about the main issue being about federal subsidies, and that state to state variations are not meaningful.
There was another thread recently discussing access to top tier hospitals (Mayo, MD Anderson, Sloan Kettering, etc.) Many people lamented about how all the plans available in their area only have narrow networks that do not provide any coverage at such places, while other living in different states have access to broad PPO plans that cover those facilities. That can be more important than few thousand dollars of tax savings.
1. These are the private plans available in NJ and the pricing for each age:
https://www.nj.gov/dobi/division_insura ... ccd67b1570

I don't believe it's true you can't buy any of these plans, either on exchange or from the provider directly, if you live in NJ. Assuming you're unsubsidized, that's again a huge difference.

2. The points were two. First, depending what OP meant by '$700/mo' (for one person or two?) and 'great plan' OP could at most save marginally for probably a worse plan in NJ than the employer/retiree one in CA. If $700 is for two people that's a big advantage for the CA plan. Second, if you do not qualify for ACA subsidies and are at least fairly old (like OP, 55) it seldom makes sense to pay for a more expensive individual plan with better coverage. The difference is mainly deductible/out of pocket limit, fixed number of $'s, but the premium price difference in $'s expands with the age multiplier. Young people might benefit to consider gold/silver/bronze but for unsubsidized older people only bronze makes economic sense. Again if you're subsidized, different story.

3. Which is why subsidized or not is the really big difference. As far as absolute top care providers* it could be that you'd choose to live in MN to find a network that included Mayo, or in NY or NJ for Sloan Kettering**. But it's rare nowadays to find a plan at a practical cost which gives coverage outside the state you live in, ie. a plan that covers you at Mayo *and* Sloan Kettering, prior to getting Medicare. Whereas in-state I don't know about Mayo vs. MN plans, but the relatively less expensive plans in NY and NJ include the respective locations of Sloan Kettering in those states.

*by reputation anyway, actually analyzing what difference it would make to one's health outcome might be complicated, but a person might feel better off, in particular being able to send a loved one to a big name place.
**which has a branch in NJ, included in the networks of the by far most common individual plan provider Horizon, and the second place one Amerihealth; back to point 1, if you choose an individual plan in NJ from other than Horizon or Amerihealth you'll have a significant problem finding providers that take it. The individual plan market is really Horizon and Amerihealth, for an older unsubsidized person it's really Horizon's cheapest Bronze or Amerihealth's, 2 plans that make sense, not 40 or 60-some. Oscar, WellCare, Oxford are more expensive and few doctors take them, somewhat mysterious who buys them if anyone.
1) If you want access plans sold by Oscar or WellCare, which seems like a significant portion of offered plans, you can't get them on the exchange in Cape May County

2) I agree that it seldom makes sense to buy the higher tier plans. What you typically see is that the Bronze plans come out ahead for either little, or a lot of healthcare spending. The higher tier plans usually only have a narrow sliver of spending where they come out ahead. That does not change whether you get subsidies or not. So, not sure what you mean by it being a different story if you are subsidized.

3) You are simply mistaken about this. The fact that you can get coverage at Sloan in your NJ plan (Sloan in NYC, or some "affiliated" facility, not the same) while others living in say Texas can't get access to MD Anderson just proves my point about how much impact your location can have on the plans you can get. It might be illustrative for you to take a look at the extensive research linked to by FinanceGeek in the post just above yours. For example, I live in Hawaii and have access to a nationwide PPO plan. I can get coverage at MD Anderson while people living around the corner from the facility have no such options. Others have indicated the same is true for them with respect to Sloan. That is true whether it is subsidized or not.
1. You can see on the chart not all those plans are offered on exchange but they are all available to NJ residents directly from the companies and price/features are standard statewide. There is no such thing as different price or features of a given plan by county in NJ. And like I said the providers besides Horizon and Amerihealth are uniformly more expensive and many/most providers don't accept them. A poster knowledgeable about the NJ market from the inside gave a corporate game theory reason they are offered, but they have not been real alternatives in the years I've actually been shopping in the NJ market.

2. It does change depending on whether you are subsidized, as well as by age. For a double-subsidized (federal and NJ subsidy) person the difference in deductible and OOP limit between gold and bronze is the same in $'s as for me, but the premium difference in $'s is a lot more for me. Likewise even among unsubsidized 18 yr old pays 1/3 what I do in premium, but again the deductible/OOP limit difference is the same. Gold or silver could conceivably make sense for them, basically could not for me.

3. I'm not 'mistaken' how this works in either NJ or NY (where one of my kids looked at private insurance last year). Also as people pointed out on the other thread, 'PPO' no longer means there's any out of network coverage or the network extends beyond the state. AFAIK that's becoming unusual nationally and it's not true of almost any plan in NJ or NY, only otherwise totally uneconomical gold plans in NJ have any out-of-state coverage now, but the state has a lot of good health providers so it's not a fatal flaw unless you insist on a famous hospital somewhere else in the country (though it is a drawback that we now could not go to Sloan Kettering in Manhattan which is a couple of air miles from us, at one time a family member did, back when economical plans included limited out of state coverage). But sure if you could find a place with real national PPO plans that are a reasonable value proposition for normal circumstances, that would be an advantage.

However still, the two basic pieces of info missing from OP's summary are:
1. is $700/mo per person or for two people?
2. would they be subsidized? That is a huge difference, can't see any reasonable argument how it isn't on an individual financial planning basis. It would greatly change the economics vs. a fixed cost like $700/$1400, it would greatly change it in any state, though more so in a state like NJ with additional state premium subsidies if you qualify for those.

But it's really the network and the consistency year-to-year that is the deal breaker for most people. If I could have my old cadillac plan with an $8900 ACA max OOP instead of $3500, I'd still take that deal because I could count on what would be available to me.

Kaiser is always kaiser, as far as the network goes. The "mega corporate" Kaiser plans may offer lower/better copays, out of pocket costs, etc. I've only had "small company" Kaiser, and those plans are identical and use the same language (gold/bronze/etc.)
